So "it is of faith, that it might be by grace; to the end the promise might be sure to all the seed." Paul closes with a portrait of what such faith actually looked like. Abraham stood "before him whom he believed, even God, who quickeneth the dead, and calleth those things which be not as though they were." He "against hope believed in hope"; "being not weak in faith, he considered not his own body now dead" at "about an hundred years old, neither yet the deadness of Sara’s womb"; he "staggered not at the promise of God through unbelief; but was strong in faith, giving glory to God," "being fully persuaded that, what he had promised, he was able also to perform." "And therefore it was imputed to him for righteousness." The record is not antiquarian: "it was not written for his sake alone," but "for us also, to whom it shall be imputed, if we believe on him that raised up Jesus our Lord from the dead; Who was delivered for our offences, and was raised again for our justification." Paul's argument turns on a date, not a debate. Genesis credits Abraham with righteousness before the covenant mark is given, so Paul can ask "How was it then reckoned? when he was in circumcision, or in uncircumcision?" and answer from the record itself: "Not in circumcision, but in uncircumcision." The sequence, not merely the principle, makes Gentile inclusion structural rather than a later concession. Circumcision is not dismissed but reclassified. It is "the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of the faith which he had yet being uncircumcised" — a visible ratification of something already given, not the instrument that produced it. That distinction between what confers and what confirms shapes every later Christian argument about signs, marks, and sacraments. The faith Paul praises is not bare assent to a proposition but sustained trust against evidence. Abraham "considered not his own body now dead" nor "the deadness of Sara’s womb"; he "staggered not at the promise" and was "fully persuaded" — and the object of that trust is defined theologically as "God, who quickeneth the dead, and calleth those things which be not as though they were." Faith here is measured by the God it holds onto. Grace and certainty are linked, not opposed. "Therefore it is of faith, that it might be by grace; to the end the promise might be sure to all the seed." A promise contingent on law-keeping would be as unstable as the keepers; resting it on grace is what makes it "sure" and what makes it extend beyond one people. The chapter ends by making Abraham's story a template for Christian faith with a specific content: righteousness is imputed "if we believe on him that raised up Jesus our Lord from the dead." The same God who quickens the dead womb raises the crucified Son, "delivered for our offences, and was raised again for our justification" — resurrection is not an appendix to justification but part of its ground. What shall we say then that Abraham our father, as pertaining to the flesh, hath found? For if Abraham were justified by works, he hath whereof to glory; but not before God. For what saith the scripture? Abraham believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness. Now to him that worketh is the reward not reckoned of grace, but of debt. But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness. Even as David also describeth the blessedness of the man, unto whom God imputeth righteousness without works, Saying, Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin. Cometh this blessedness then upon the circumcision only, or upon the uncircumcision also? for we say that faith was reckoned to Abraham for righteousness. How was it then reckoned? when he was in circumcision, or in uncircumcision? Not in circumcision, but in uncircumcision. And he received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of the faith which he had yet being uncircumcised: that he might be the father of all them that believe, though they be not circumcised; that righteousness might be imputed unto them also: And the father of circumcision to them who are not of the circumcision only, but who also walk in the steps of that faith of our father Abraham, which he had being yet uncircumcised. For the promise, that he should be the heir of the world, was not to Abraham, or to his seed, through the law, but through the righteousness of faith. For if they which are of the law be heirs, faith is made void, and the promise made of none effect: Because the law worketh wrath: for where no law is, there is no transgression. Therefore it is of faith, that it might be by grace; to the end the promise might be sure to all the seed; not to that only which is of the law, but to that also which is of the faith of Abraham; who is the father of us all, ( As it is written, I have made thee a father of many nations,) before him whom he believed, even God, who quickeneth the dead, and calleth those things which be not as though they were. Who against hope believed in hope, that he might become the father of many nations; according to that which was spoken, So shall thy seed be. And being not weak in faith, he considered not his own body now dead, when he was about an hundred years old, neither yet the deadness of Sara’s womb: He staggered not at the promise of God through unbelief; but was strong in faith, giving glory to God; And being fully persuaded that, what he had promised, he was able also to perform. And therefore it was imputed to him for righteousness. Now it was not written for his sake alone, that it was imputed to him; But for us also, to whom it shall be imputed, if we believe on him that raised up Jesus our Lord from the dead; Who was delivered for our offences, and was raised again for our justification.

label: Romans 5
text: Paul draws the consequence of everything argued so far with a single word, "Therefore," and states the result: "being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ." Justification is not left as a verdict filed away; it opens a door, for "by whom also we have access by faith into this grace wherein we stand, and rejoice in hope of the glory of God." That standing turns even affliction into ground for boasting: "we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience; And patience, experience; and experience, hope." The chain does not end in wishful thinking, because "hope maketh not ashamed; because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us" — the love is poured in, not merely announced. Paul then proves that love from its timing rather than from our worthiness: "when we were yet without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly," and where "scarcely for a righteous man will one die," "God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." Twice he argues from the greater to the greater still — "Much more then, being now justified by his blood, we shall be saved from wrath through him," and "if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son, much more, being reconciled, we shall be saved by his life" — so that the death reconciles and the risen life saves. The present result is joy: "we also joy in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom we have now received the atonement." From verse twelve the argument widens to the whole race. "As by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned," and the proof that sin is deeper than any statute is that "death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over them that had not sinned after the similitude of Adam’s transgression." Adam is therefore "the figure of him that was to come," a likeness broken by asymmetry: "not as the offence, so also is the free gift," for "the judgment was by one to condemnation, but the free gift is of many offences unto justification." Where one offence let death reign, "they which receive abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness shall reign in life by one, Jesus Christ" — reigning, not merely surviving. The parallel is stated twice in full, once in terms of act — "as by the offence of one judgment came upon all men to condemnation; even so by the righteousness of one the free gift came upon all men unto justification of life" — and once in terms of person and will: "as by one man’s disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous." The law's entrance did not reverse the ruin but exposed it, "that the offence might abound"; yet exposure is overwhelmed by gift, "where sin abounded, grace did much more abound." The chapter closes with two reigns and only one survivor: "as sin hath reigned unto death, even so might grace reign through righteousness unto eternal life by Jesus Christ our Lord." Peace with God is described as an accomplished state rather than a mood: "we have peace with God" and "we have access by faith into this grace wherein we stand." The verbs are of position and entry, so justification is presented as admission into a standing place, not only as a charge dismissed. The love of God is not merely reported to the believer but placed inside him — "shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us" — which is why suffering can produce hope rather than cynicism. Tribulation refines what has already been poured in; it does not manufacture it. Paul grounds assurance in chronology, not in self-assessment. Christ died "when we were yet without strength" and "while we were yet sinners," so the worst possible moment has already been survived, and the twin "much more" arguments reason from the harder thing accomplished to the easier thing promised. Adam and Christ are set as two heads of one race, and the comparison is deliberately unequal. One offence brought condemnation upon all, but the gift answers "many offences unto justification," so grace is not a repair returning us to the starting line but an overflow that ends in reigning "in life by one, Jesus Christ." The law is given a diagnostic role, entering "that the offence might abound," which makes it the servant of grace rather than its rival. The final image is governmental — sin "reigned unto death," grace reigns "through righteousness unto eternal life" — so salvation is a change of sovereignty, not merely a change of record. Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ: By whom also we have access by faith into this grace wherein we stand, and rejoice in hope of the glory of God. And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience; And patience, experience; and experience, hope: And hope maketh not ashamed; because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us. For when we were yet without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly. For scarcely for a righteous man will one die: yet peradventure for a good man some would even dare to die. But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us. Much more then, being now justified by his blood, we shall be saved from wrath through him. For if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son, much more, being reconciled, we shall be saved by his life. And not only so, but we also joy in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom we have now received the atonement. Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned: ( For until the law sin was in the world: but sin is not imputed when there is no law. Nevertheless death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over them that had not sinned after the similitude of Adam’s transgression, who is the figure of him that was to come. But not as the offence, so also is the free gift. For if through the offence of one many be dead, much more the grace of God, and the gift by grace, which is by one man, Jesus Christ, hath abounded unto many. And not as it was by one that sinned, so is the gift: for the judgment was by one to condemnation, but the free gift is of many offences unto justification. For if by one man’s offence death reigned by one; much more they which receive abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness shall reign in life by one, Jesus Christ.) Therefore as by the offence of one judgment came upon all men to condemnation; even so by the righteousness of one the free gift came upon all men unto justification of life. For as by one man’s disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous. Moreover the law entered, that the offence might abound. But where sin abounded, grace did much more abound: That as sin hath reigned unto death, even so might grace reign through righteousness unto eternal life by Jesus Christ our Lord.

label: Romans 6
text: Paul answers the objection his own gospel invites. If grace abounds where sin abounds, then "Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound?" His reply is not an argument about consequences but about identity: "God forbid. How shall we, that are dead to sin, live any longer therein?" The ground of that death is baptism, and Paul appeals to it as something the Romans already know: "Know ye not, that so many of us as were baptized into Jesus Christ were baptized into his death?" The rite is not a symbol laid alongside the cross but a real joining to it — "we are buried with him by baptism into death" — and it carries the whole shape of Easter with it, so that "like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life." Those united to the death are promised the resurrection: "if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall be also in the likeness of his resurrection." What died is named plainly, "our old man is crucified with him, that the body of sin might be destroyed," with the purpose stated as freedom for service, "that henceforth we should not serve sin," since "he that is dead is freed from sin." Paul then grounds the believer's security in Christ's own finished pattern: "Christ being raised from the dead dieth no more; death hath no more dominion over him," for "he died unto sin once: but in that he liveth, he liveth unto God." From this comes the chapter's hinge command, an act of the mind followed at once by acts of the body: "reckon ye also yourselves to be dead indeed unto sin, but alive unto God through Jesus Christ our Lord," then "Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body," and "yield yourselves unto God, as those that are alive from the dead, and your members as instruments of righteousness unto God." The promise "sin shall not have dominion over you" is not license, and Paul raises the objection a second time — "shall we sin, because we are not under the law, but under grace? God forbid" — answering now with the logic of servitude: "to whom ye yield yourselves servants to obey, his servants ye are." There is no neutral ground, only "sin unto death, or of obedience unto righteousness." The Romans have changed masters, having "obeyed from the heart that form of doctrine which was delivered you," and "being then made free from sin, ye became the servants of righteousness." Paul concedes the image is homely — "I speak after the manner of men because of the infirmity of your flesh" — but presses it into a command with a direction and a destination: "yield your members servants to righteousness unto holiness." The two lives are weighed by their fruit. The old yields what "ye are now ashamed" of, and "the end of those things is death"; the new yields "fruit unto holiness, and the end everlasting life." The chapter closes on an asymmetry that refuses to make salvation a transaction: "the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord" — death is earned, life is given. Paul refutes the charge that grace encourages sin not by threatening the sinner but by describing what has already happened to him. "How shall we, that are dead to sin, live any longer therein?" treats continuing in sin as incoherent rather than merely forbidden, an attempt to live a life that has already been buried. Baptism here is not illustration but incorporation. Paul says believers "were baptized into his death" and "are buried with him," language of real union rather than resemblance, and he argues from the sacrament as an accomplished fact the Romans can be reminded of rather than persuaded into. The chapter holds together two things easily separated: an indicative and an imperative. Believers are told to "reckon ye also yourselves to be dead indeed unto sin" — to count as true what God has done — and in the same breath to stop yielding their "members as instruments of unrighteousness." Grace is received by faith and then worked out in the body's actual members. Freedom in Paul is never autonomy but transferred allegiance. "To whom ye yield yourselves servants to obey, his servants ye are" leaves no third option; the choice is not between service and independence but between masters, and "being then made free from sin, ye became the servants of righteousness." The closing contrast is deliberately unbalanced. Death is called "wages," something owed and earned by the one who works for it; eternal life is called "the gift of God," never earned, always given. Holiness is commanded throughout the chapter, yet its end is never described as a paycheck. What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid. How shall we, that are dead to sin, live any longer therein? Know ye not, that so many of us as were baptized into Jesus Christ were baptized into his death? Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life. For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall be also in the likeness of his resurrection: Knowing this, that our old man is crucified with him, that the body of sin might be destroyed, that henceforth we should not serve sin. For he that is dead is freed from sin. Now if we be dead with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with him: Knowing that Christ being raised from the dead dieth no more; death hath no more dominion over him. For in that he died, he died unto sin once: but in that he liveth, he liveth unto God. Likewise reckon ye also yourselves to be dead indeed unto sin, but alive unto God through Jesus Christ our Lord. Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, that ye should obey it in the lusts thereof. Neither yield ye your members as instruments of unrighteousness unto sin: but yield yourselves unto God, as those that are alive from the dead, and your members as instruments of righteousness unto God. For sin shall not have dominion over you: for ye are not under the law, but under grace. What then? shall we sin, because we are not under the law, but under grace? God forbid. Know ye not, that to whom ye yield yourselves servants to obey, his servants ye are to whom ye obey; whether of sin unto death, or of obedience unto righteousness? But God be thanked, that ye were the servants of sin, but ye have obeyed from the heart that form of doctrine which was delivered you. Being then made free from sin, ye became the servants of righteousness. I speak after the manner of men because of the infirmity of your flesh: for as ye have yielded your members servants to uncleanness and to iniquity unto iniquity; even so now yield your members servants to righteousness unto holiness. For when ye were the servants of sin, ye were free from righteousness. What fruit had ye then in those things whereof ye are now ashamed? for the end of those things is death. But now being made free from sin, and become servants to God, ye have your fruit unto holiness, and the end everlasting life. For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.

label: Romans 7
text:
Paul argues from a case his readers already grant, since he speaks "to them that know the law": "the law hath dominion over a man as long as he liveth." A wife "is bound by the law to her husband so long as he liveth," but a death dissolves the bond, and "if her husband be dead, she is free from that law." The application is startling, because it is the believer who has died: "ye also are become dead to the law by the body of Christ; that ye should be married to another, even to him who is raised from the dead." The purpose is fruitfulness, "that we should bring forth fruit unto God" — set against the old yield, when "the motions of sins, which were by the law, did work in our members to bring forth fruit unto death." What replaces the old bondage is not lawlessness but a new mode of obedience: "that we should serve in newness of spirit, and not in the oldness of the letter."

Paul then heads off the obvious slander. "Is the law sin? God forbid." The law is the instrument of diagnosis, not the disease: "I had not known sin, but by the law: for I had not known lust, except the law had said, Thou shalt not covet." The real culprit is named and personified — "sin, taking occasion by the commandment, wrought in me all manner of concupiscence" — and the commandment that arrived as a gift became an executioner by sin's misuse: "the commandment, which was ordained to life, I found to be unto death," for "sin, taking occasion by the commandment, deceived me, and by it slew me." The verdict on the law itself is unambiguous and glowing: "the law is holy, and the commandment holy, and just, and good." Its very goodness is what exposes sin, "that sin by the commandment might become exceeding sinful."

The chapter's last movement turns from argument to anguish, spoken in the present tense and the first person. "The law is spiritual: but I am carnal, sold under sin." The speaker is divided against himself: "what I would, that do I not; but what I hate, that do I," and again, "the good that I would I do not: but the evil which I would not, that I do." That very failure vindicates the law — "I consent unto the law that it is good" — and locates the trouble deeper than the will's approval: "to will is present with me; but how to perform that which is good I find not," for "in me ( that is, in my flesh,) dwelleth no good thing." Paul describes two laws at war, "another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind," while "I delight in the law of God after the inward man." The cry that follows is not despair but appeal — "O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?" — and it is answered before the chapter closes: "I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord." The summary line holds both halves together without resolving the tension prematurely: "with the mind I myself serve the law of God; but with the flesh the law of sin." Paul's marriage analogy makes freedom from the law a matter of death, not of the law's failure. It is not the commandment that dies but the believer — "ye also are become dead to the law by the body of Christ" — so that release is a remarriage "to him who is raised from the dead," and its aim is fruitfulness rather than autonomy. The chapter is the New Testament's strongest defense of the law by the very man accused of abolishing it. Twice Paul answers an objection with "God forbid," and his verdict is that the law is "holy, and the commandment holy, and just, and good." What killed him was sin exploiting a good thing, not a defect in the thing exploited. Sin is described as an agent, not merely an act: it "taking occasion by the commandment" deceived, slew, and now "dwelleth in me." That grammar rules out treating the divided self as an excuse. Paul never says the indwelling of sin makes him innocent — he still cries "O wretched man that I am!" The anatomy of moral failure Paul gives is precise and uncomfortable: the problem is not ignorance of the good or even reluctance toward it, since "to will is present with me," but the gap between willing and performing — "how to perform that which is good I find not." Knowledge and good intention are shown to be insufficient without deliverance from outside the self. The chapter ends in thanksgiving rather than in defeat. The question "who shall deliver me from the body of this death?" expects a person, not a technique, and receives one: "I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord." The remaining tension between mind and flesh is real, but it is now carried inside gratitude. Know ye not, brethren, ( for I speak to them that know the law,) how that the law hath dominion over a man as long as he liveth? For the woman which hath an husband is bound by the law to her husband so long as he liveth; but if the husband be dead, she is loosed from the law of her husband. So then if, while her husband liveth, she be married to another man, she shall be called an adulteress: but if her husband be dead, she is free from that law; so that she is no adulteress, though she be married to another man. Wherefore, my brethren, ye also are become dead to the law by the body of Christ; that ye should be married to another, even to him who is raised from the dead, that we should bring forth fruit unto God. For when we were in the flesh, the motions of sins, which were by the law, did work in our members to bring forth fruit unto death. But now we are delivered from the law, that being dead wherein we were held; that we should serve in newness of spirit, and not in the oldness of the letter. What shall we say then? Is the law sin? God forbid. Nay, I had not known sin, but by the law: for I had not known lust, except the law had said, Thou shalt not covet. But sin, taking occasion by the commandment, wrought in me all manner of concupiscence. For without the law sin was dead. For I was alive without the law once: but when the commandment came, sin revived, and I died. And the commandment, which was ordained to life, I found to be unto death. For sin, taking occasion by the commandment, deceived me, and by it slew me. Wherefore the law is holy, and the commandment holy, and just, and good. Was then that which is good made death unto me? God forbid. But sin, that it might appear sin, working death in me by that which is good; that sin by the commandment might become exceeding sinful. For we know that the law is spiritual: but I am carnal, sold under sin. For that which I do I allow not: for what I would, that do I not; but what I hate, that do I. If then I do that which I would not, I consent unto the law that it is good. Now then it is no more I that do it, but sin that dwelleth in me. For I know that in me ( that is, in my flesh,) dwelleth no good thing: for to will is present with me; but how to perform that which is good I find not. For the good that I would I do not: but the evil which I would not, that I do. Now if I do that I would not, it is no more I that do it, but sin that dwelleth in me. I find then a law, that, when I would do good, evil is present with me. For I delight in the law of God after the inward man: But I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind, and bringing me into captivity to the law of sin which is in my members. O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death? I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord. So then with the mind I myself serve the law of God; but with the flesh the law of sin.

label: Romans 8
text: Paul opens with the verdict that answers the anguish of the chapter before it: "There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit." The ground of that freedom is not human strength but "the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus," because "what the law could not do, in that it was weak through the flesh," God did by "sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and for sin," so that he "condemned sin in the flesh" and "the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us." He then draws a line between two whole orientations of a life: "they that are after the flesh do mind the things of the flesh; but they that are after the Spirit the things of the Spirit," and "to be carnally minded is death; but to be spiritually minded is life and peace." The carnal mind "is enmity against God: for it is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be," so "they that are in the flesh cannot please God." What marks the Christian is indwelling rather than agreement — "if so be that the Spirit of God dwell in you" — with a sharp test attached: "if any man have not the Spirit of Christ, he is none of his." That indwelling reaches even the body, for he who raised Jesus "shall also quicken your mortal bodies by his Spirit that dwelleth in you." The consequence is obligation, not license: "we are debtors, not to the flesh, to live after the flesh," and "if ye live after the flesh, ye shall die: but if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live." The Spirit's work is naming as much as power. "Ye have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear; but ye have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father," and "the Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God." Sonship then carries inheritance and a condition in one breath: "if children, then heirs; heirs of God, and joint-heirs with Christ; if so be that we suffer with him, that we may be also glorified together" — and against that inheritance "the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us." Paul widens the frame to the whole cosmos: "the whole creation groaneth and travaileth in pain together until now," having been "made subject to vanity, not willingly," and it waits for "the manifestation of the sons of God" so that it too "shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the glorious liberty of the children of God." Believers groan with it, for even those who "have the firstfruits of the Spirit" are still "waiting for the adoption, to wit, the redemption of our body." Because "we are saved by hope: but hope that is seen is not hope," the present posture is patient waiting. Into that weakness the Spirit comes: "we know not what we should pray for as we ought: but the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered," and he does so "according to the will of God." From there the chapter climbs. "All things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose"; "whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brethren"; "whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified." The close is a courtroom with every accuser removed — "If God be for us, who can be against us?", "He that spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not with him also freely give us all things?", "Who shall lay any thing to the charge of God’s elect? It is God that justifieth" — and the judge's place is held by one who "maketh intercession for us." Paul then names every candidate for separation and finds none that qualifies: not "tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword," under which "we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter" and yet "are more than conquerors through him that loved us"; not "death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come"; not "height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord." The chapter defines a Christian by possession rather than performance — "if so be that the Spirit of God dwell in you" — and then makes that indwelling the sole boundary line: "if any man have not the Spirit of Christ, he is none of his." Freedom from condemnation is not a legal fiction laid over an unchanged life but the presence of a new occupant who produces a new walk. Paul never lets "no condemnation" drift into passivity. In the same breath as the indwelling he writes "if ye live after the flesh, ye shall die: but if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live," and makes glory conditional in form — "if so be that we suffer with him, that we may be also glorified together." Mortification is the Spirit's work done through the believer's willing act, not instead of it. Adoption is presented as both already given and not yet finished. Believers already "cry, Abba, Father" and already have the Spirit's inward witness, yet those same believers, holding only "the firstfruits of the Spirit," are still "waiting for the adoption, to wit, the redemption of our body." The Christian life is lived in the gap between a name conferred and a body not yet raised. Redemption in this chapter is cosmic, not merely personal. "The creature was made subject to vanity, not willingly," and its release is tied to ours — creation "waiteth for the manifestation of the sons of God" before it enters "the glorious liberty of the children of God." Matter is not discarded in Paul's hope; it is delivered along with the bodies of the saints. The unbreakable love of the closing verses is described entirely in terms of what comes at the believer from outside — sword, powers, height, depth, "any other creature" — while the warnings of verse 13 concern what the believer chooses from within. The chapter's confidence is aimed squarely at fear of hostile forces, not at the question of a will that turns away. There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit. For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus hath made me free from the law of sin and death. For what the law could not do, in that it was weak through the flesh, God sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and for sin, condemned sin in the flesh: That the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit. For they that are after the flesh do mind the things of the flesh; but they that are after the Spirit the things of the Spirit. For to be carnally minded is death; but to be spiritually minded is life and peace. Because the carnal mind is enmity against God: for it is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be. So then they that are in the flesh cannot please God. But ye are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit, if so be that the Spirit of God dwell in you. Now if any man have not the Spirit of Christ, he is none of his. And if Christ be in you, the body is dead because of sin; but the Spirit is life because of righteousness. But if the Spirit of him that raised up Jesus from the dead dwell in you, he that raised up Christ from the dead shall also quicken your mortal bodies by his Spirit that dwelleth in you. Therefore, brethren, we are debtors, not to the flesh, to live after the flesh. For if ye live after the flesh, ye shall die: but if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live. For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, they are the sons of God. For ye have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear; but ye have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father. The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God: And if children, then heirs; heirs of God, and joint-heirs with Christ; if so be that we suffer with him, that we may be also glorified together. For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us. For the earnest expectation of the creature waiteth for the manifestation of the sons of God. For the creature was made subject to vanity, not willingly, but by reason of him who hath subjected the same in hope, Because the creature itself also shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the glorious liberty of the children of God. For we know that the whole creation groaneth and travaileth in pain together until now. And not only they, but ourselves also, which have the firstfruits of the Spirit, even we ourselves groan within ourselves, waiting for the adoption, to wit, the redemption of our body. For we are saved by hope: but hope that is seen is not hope: for what a man seeth, why doth he yet hope for? But if we hope for that we see not, then do we with patience wait for it. Likewise the Spirit also helpeth our infirmities: for we know not what we should pray for as we ought: but the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered. And he that searcheth the hearts knoweth what is the mind of the Spirit, because he maketh intercession for the saints according to the will of God. And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose. For whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brethren. Moreover whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified. What shall we then say to these things? If God be for us, who can be against us? He that spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not with him also freely give us all things? Who shall lay any thing to the charge of God’s elect? It is God that justifieth. Who is he that condemneth? It is Christ that died, yea rather, that is risen again, who is even at the right hand of God, who also maketh intercession for us. Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword? As it is written, For thy sake we are killed all the day long; we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter. Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him that loved us. For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, Nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

label: Romans 9
text: Paul opens under oath — "I say the truth in Christ, I lie not, my conscience also bearing me witness in the Holy Ghost" — because what follows will sound like an accusation against his own people, and it is instead a grief: "great heaviness and continual sorrow in my heart." So deep is it that he "could wish that myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh," to whom belong "the adoption, and the glory, and the covenants, and the giving of the law, and the service of God, and the promises," and from whom "as concerning the flesh Christ came, who is over all, God blessed for ever." The problem is not that God's word failed but that it never ran along bloodlines: "they are not all Israel, which are of Israel," for "In Isaac shall thy seed be called," and "the children of the promise are counted for the seed." Paul presses the point past Ishmael to twins of one mother, chosen "being not yet born, neither having done any good or evil, that the purpose of God according to election might stand, not of works, but of him that calleth" — "The elder shall serve the younger," "Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated." To the objection "Is there unrighteousness with God?" he answers "God forbid," and grounds mercy in God's own freedom: "I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy," therefore "it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy." Pharaoh is the counterweight — "Even for this same purpose have I raised thee up, that I might shew my power in thee" — leading to the hardest line in the chapter, "whom he will he hardeneth." When the reader protests "Why doth he yet find fault? For who hath resisted his will?", Paul refuses to argue on those terms: "Nay but, O man, who art thou that repliest against God?" "Hath not the potter power over the clay, of the same lump to make one vessel unto honour, and another unto dishonour?" Yet the sentence that follows is conditional and asymmetric — God "endured with much longsuffering the vessels of wrath fitted to destruction," while the vessels of mercy he "had afore prepared unto glory," "Even us, whom he hath called, not of the Jews only, but also of the Gentiles." The prophets are then read as forecasting exactly this shape: "I will call them my people, which were not my people," and "a remnant shall be saved," for "Except the Lord of Sabaoth had left us a seed, we had been as Sodoma." The chapter closes by naming the actual mechanism of the reversal, and it is not a decree but a stumble: the Gentiles "which followed not after righteousness, have attained to righteousness, even the righteousness which is of faith," while Israel "sought it not by faith, but as it were by the works of the law. For they stumbled at that stumblingstone" — Christ himself, of whom it is written "whosoever believeth on him shall not be ashamed." Paul's argument is bracketed by love, not cold determinism. It begins with a man willing to be "accursed from Christ" for his kinsmen and ends with an open promise to "whosoever believeth on him." Any reading of the middle that makes the beginning insincere or the ending unreal has lost the chapter's frame. The election Paul defends is first about vocation and covenant lineage rather than the private eternal fate of individuals: the pairs he cites are Isaac and Ishmael, Jacob and Esau, patriarchs whose roles in salvation history are assigned before birth so "the purpose of God according to election might stand, not of works, but of him that calleth." The potter passage is a rebuke of the questioner's standing, not an answer to the question — "who art thou that repliest against God?" Paul is asserting that the creature has no court in which to summon the Creator, which is a different move from explaining how mercy and responsibility fit together. The grammar of verses 22-23 is deliberately uneven. God "endured with much longsuffering" the vessels of wrath "fitted to destruction," but the vessels of mercy he "had afore prepared unto glory." Glory is credited to God's preparation; destruction is described as a fitting God patiently bore, and no verse here says he authored it. Verses 30-32 supply Paul's own explanation of who missed the righteousness, and it is a human failure rather than a divine exclusion: Israel "sought it not by faith, but as it were by the works of the law." The chapter's mystery of divine freedom is answered on the human side by the mystery of unbelief. I say the truth in Christ, I lie not, my conscience also bearing me witness in the Holy Ghost, That I have great heaviness and continual sorrow in my heart. For I could wish that myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh: Who are Israelites; to whom pertaineth the adoption, and the glory, and the covenants, and the giving of the law, and the service of God, and the promises; Whose are the fathers, and of whom as concerning the flesh Christ came, who is over all, God blessed for ever. Amen. Not as though the word of God hath taken none effect. For they are not all Israel, which are of Israel: Neither, because they are the seed of Abraham, are they all children: but, In Isaac shall thy seed be called. That is, They which are the children of the flesh, these are not the children of God: but the children of the promise are counted for the seed. For this is the word of promise, At this time will I come, and Sara shall have a son. And not only this; but when Rebecca also had conceived by one, even by our father Isaac; ( For the children being not yet born, neither having done any good or evil, that the purpose of God according to election might stand, not of works, but of him that calleth;) It was said unto her, The elder shall serve the younger. As it is written, Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated. What shall we say then? Is there unrighteousness with God? God forbid. For he saith to Moses, I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I will have compassion. So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy. For the scripture saith unto Pharaoh, Even for this same purpose have I raised thee up, that I might shew my power in thee, and that my name might be declared throughout all the earth. Therefore hath he mercy on whom he will have mercy, and whom he will he hardeneth. Thou wilt say then unto me, Why doth he yet find fault? For who hath resisted his will? Nay but, O man, who art thou that repliest against God? Shall the thing formed say to him that formed it, Why hast thou made me thus? Hath not the potter power over the clay, of the same lump to make one vessel unto honour, and another unto dishonour? What if God, willing to shew his wrath, and to make his power known, endured with much longsuffering the vessels of wrath fitted to destruction: And that he might make known the riches of his glory on the vessels of mercy, which he had afore prepared unto glory, Even us, whom he hath called, not of the Jews only, but also of the Gentiles? As he saith also in Osee, I will call them my people, which were not my people; and her beloved, which was not beloved. And it shall come to pass, that in the place where it was said unto them, Ye are not my people; there shall they be called the children of the living God. Esaias also crieth concerning Israel, Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved: For he will finish the work, and cut it short in righteousness: because a short work will the Lord make upon the earth. And as Esaias said before, Except the Lord of Sabaoth had left us a seed, we had been as Sodoma, and been made like unto Gomorrha. What shall we say then? That the Gentiles, which followed not after righteousness, have attained to righteousness, even the righteousness which is of faith. But Israel, which followed after the law of righteousness, hath not attained to the law of righteousness. Wherefore? Because they sought it not by faith, but as it were by the works of the law. For they stumbled at that stumblingstone; As it is written, Behold, I lay in Sion a stumblingstone and rock of offence: and whosoever believeth on him shall not be ashamed.

label: Romans 10
text: Paul opens not with an argument but with an ache: "my heart’s desire and prayer to God for Israel is, that they might be saved." What follows is a diagnosis offered by a man who loves the patient. His kinsmen "have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge" — the failure is not indifference but misdirected fervor, for "being ignorant of God’s righteousness, and going about to establish their own righteousness," they "have not submitted themselves unto the righteousness of God." The verb is submission: righteousness is a gift to be received, not a wage to be earned, and the refusal is at root a refusal to be given to. Against this Paul sets the hinge of the chapter: "Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believeth" — end as goal and completion, the point the law was always aiming at. He then stages two voices. Moses speaks for "the righteousness which is of the law": "the man which doeth those things shall live by them." But "the righteousness which is of faith" speaks differently, and Paul puts Moses' own words from the wilderness into its mouth: "Say not in thine heart, Who shall ascend into heaven?" and "Who shall descend into the deep?" No one must storm heaven to fetch Christ down or ransack the grave to bring him up, because the Incarnation and the Resurrection have already happened. Therefore "The word is nigh thee, even in thy mouth, and in thy heart: that is, the word of faith, which we preach." Salvation is not remote and heroic; it is as close as a confession. Hence the chapter's most quoted line: "if thou shalt confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus, and shalt believe in thine heart that God hath raised him from the dead, thou shalt be saved," balanced immediately by "with the heart man believeth unto righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation" — inward belief and outward, bodily, public profession held together as one act, never one without the other. From this Paul draws the universal reach: "there is no difference between the Jew and the Greek: for the same Lord over all is rich unto all that call upon him," and "whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved." The second half of the chapter then works that promise backwards into a chain of necessity: "How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher? And how shall they preach, except they be sent?" Calling depends on believing, believing on hearing, hearing on preaching, preaching on being sent — so the gospel is not a private discovery but a commissioned mission, and its messengers wear the prophet's blessing: "How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace." Yet sending does not compel: "they have not all obeyed the gospel," and the prophet's complaint stands, "Lord, who hath believed our report?" Paul distills the whole sequence into a single principle: "faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God." He then closes the escape routes. Did they not hear? "Yes verily, their sound went into all the earth." Did Israel not know? Moses himself warned, "I will provoke you to jealousy by them that are no people," and Isaiah dared even more: "I was found of them that sought me not; I was made manifest unto them that asked not after me." The chapter ends not in condemnation but in a posture — God with open arms and a wounded patience: "All day long I have stretched forth my hands unto a disobedient and gainsaying people." Zeal is not self-validating. Paul grants his kinsmen a genuine "zeal of God" and still calls it "not according to knowledge," which means sincerity, effort, and religious seriousness can all be present while the one necessary thing — submission to "the righteousness of God" — is absent. The gravest religious error in this chapter is committed by devout people. The failure Paul names is not lawbreaking but self-construction: "going about to establish their own righteousness." A righteousness one builds remains one's own possession and therefore cannot be received as gift; the sin is not that the effort is too small but that it is claimed rather than accepted. "Christ is the end of the law for righteousness" reads as fulfillment rather than abolition. Paul does not discard Moses — he quotes him twice, and puts the words of the wilderness covenant into the mouth of "the righteousness which is of faith." The law's own voice testifies that the word is already "nigh thee." Faith in this chapter is never purely interior. Heart and mouth are named together twice, and the confession is bodily, audible, and public: "with the heart man believeth unto righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation." A faith that never surfaces in word and act is not the faith Paul describes. The chain "call — believe — hear — preach — sent" makes salvation structurally ecclesial and missionary. Because "faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God," no one is expected to generate faith privately; God binds the gift to a word carried by messengers he sends, and the last word of the chapter is his own stretched-out hands. Brethren, my heart’s desire and prayer to God for Israel is, that they might be saved. For I bear them record that they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge. For they being ignorant of God’s righteousness, and going about to establish their own righteousness, have not submitted themselves unto the righteousness of God. For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believeth. For Moses describeth the righteousness which is of the law, That the man which doeth those things shall live by them. But the righteousness which is of faith speaketh on this wise, Say not in thine heart, Who shall ascend into heaven? ( that is, to bring Christ down from above:) Or, Who shall descend into the deep? ( that is, to bring up Christ again from the dead.) But what saith it? The word is nigh thee, even in thy mouth, and in thy heart: that is, the word of faith, which we preach; That if thou shalt confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus, and shalt believe in thine heart that God hath raised him from the dead, thou shalt be saved. For with the heart man believeth unto righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation. For the scripture saith, Whosoever believeth on him shall not be ashamed. For there is no difference between the Jew and the Greek: for the same Lord over all is rich unto all that call upon him. For whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved. How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher? And how shall they preach, except they be sent? as it is written, How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace, and bring glad tidings of good things! But they have not all obeyed the gospel. For Esaias saith, Lord, who hath believed our report? So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God. But I say, Have they not heard? Yes verily, their sound went into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world. But I say, Did not Israel know? First Moses saith, I will provoke you to jealousy by them that are no people, and by a foolish nation I will anger you. But Esaias is very bold, and saith, I was found of them that sought me not; I was made manifest unto them that asked not after me. But to Israel he saith, All day long I have stretched forth my hands unto a disobedient and gainsaying people.

label: Romans 11
text: Paul puts the hardest question of his letter directly: "Hath God cast away his people? God forbid." His first evidence is himself, "an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin" — the apostle to the Gentiles is living proof that God "hath not cast away his people which he foreknew." He reaches for Elias, who thought himself "left alone," and for the answer that corrected him: "I have reserved to myself seven thousand men, who have not bowed the knee to the image of Baal." So too now, "at this present time also there is a remnant according to the election of grace" — and Paul immediately guards the word grace from being emptied: "if by grace, then is it no more of works: otherwise grace is no more grace." The rest, he says, "were blinded," given "the spirit of slumber, eyes that they should not see." But blindness is not the end of the story: "Have they stumbled that they should fall? God forbid." Their stumble has become the Gentiles' opening — "through their fall salvation is come unto the Gentiles, for to provoke them to jealousy" — and if that fall is "the riches of the world," Paul asks, "how much more their fulness?" He magnifies his Gentile office precisely so as to "provoke to emulation them which are my flesh, and might save some of them," for if their casting away reconciles the world, their receiving will be "life from the dead." Then comes the olive tree. "If the root be holy, so are the branches"; some branches "be broken off," and the Gentile, "being a wild olive tree," was "graffed in among them" to partake "of the root and fatness of the olive tree." The warning is sharp and personal: "Boast not against the branches... thou bearest not the root, but the root thee." They fell "because of unbelief"; the Gentile "standest by faith" and must "be not highminded, but fear," since "if God spared not the natural branches, take heed lest he also spare not thee." Both attributes of God stand together — "the goodness and severity of God: on them which fell, severity; but toward thee, goodness, if thou continue in his goodness: otherwise thou also shalt be cut off" — and the door swings the other way too, for "they also, if they abide not still in unbelief, shall be graffed in: for God is able to graff them in again." Paul then names a "mystery" against Gentile conceit: "blindness in part is happened to Israel, until the fulness of the Gentiles be come in. And so all Israel shall be saved," with the promise that "There shall come out of Sion the Deliverer." Israel is at once "enemies for your sakes" as concerns the gospel and "beloved for the fathers’ sakes" as touching the election, because "the gifts and calling of God are without repentance." The whole tangled history resolves into one purpose: "God hath concluded them all in unbelief, that he might have mercy upon all." Paul can only end in worship — "O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments" — with no creature ever God's "counsellor" or creditor, since "of him, and through him, and to him, are all things." Paul answers the question of Israel's rejection not with a theory but with his own body: "For I also am an Israelite." The existence of a believing remnant "according to the election of grace" is itself the disproof of any claim that God has revoked his choice, and it means the Church is not a replacement people but the tree Israel's own root still feeds. The olive tree makes Gentile inclusion an act of sheer grafting mercy, never of merit or superiority: "thou bearest not the root, but the root thee." Paul's pastoral aim in the whole chapter is to kill Christian arrogance toward the Jewish people at the root, warning against being "wise in your own conceits." Verse 22 refuses to let grace become presumption. "Goodness" and "severity" are held in one sentence, and continuance is made a condition — "if thou continue in his goodness: otherwise thou also shalt be cut off." The grafted branch is genuinely in the tree and genuinely warned, which is why fear and faith are commanded together: "Be not highminded, but fear." God's severity is never terminal by design. "God is able to graff them in again" and blindness is only "in part" and only "until the fulness of the Gentiles be come in." Judgment in this chapter is instrumental, aimed at mercy, not at a permanent write-off of anyone. The chapter's logic ends in doxology rather than in a system. Having reduced every party to the same condition — "God hath concluded them all in unbelief, that he might have mercy upon all" — Paul admits the judgments are "unsearchable" and "past finding out," a built-in rebuke to any reader who thinks he has fully mapped the mechanics of election. I say then, Hath God cast away his people? God forbid. For I also am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin. God hath not cast away his people which he foreknew. Wot ye not what the scripture saith of Elias? how he maketh intercession to God against Israel, saying, Lord, they have killed thy prophets, and digged down thine altars; and I am left alone, and they seek my life. But what saith the answer of God unto him? I have reserved to myself seven thousand men, who have not bowed the knee to the image of Baal. Even so then at this present time also there is a remnant according to the election of grace. And if by grace, then is it no more of works: otherwise grace is no more grace. But if it be of works, then is it no more grace: otherwise work is no more work. What then? Israel hath not obtained that which he seeketh for; but the election hath obtained it, and the rest were blinded (According as it is written, God hath given them the spirit of slumber, eyes that they should not see, and ears that they should not hear;) unto this day. And David saith, Let their table be made a snare, and a trap, and a stumblingblock, and a recompence unto them: Let their eyes be darkened, that they may not see, and bow down their back alway. I say then, Have they stumbled that they should fall? God forbid: but rather through their fall salvation is come unto the Gentiles, for to provoke them to jealousy. Now if the fall of them be the riches of the world, and the diminishing of them the riches of the Gentiles; how much more their fulness? For I speak to you Gentiles, inasmuch as I am the apostle of the Gentiles, I magnify mine office: If by any means I may provoke to emulation them which are my flesh, and might save some of them. For if the casting away of them be the reconciling of the world, what shall the receiving of them be, but life from the dead? For if the firstfruit be holy, the lump is also holy: and if the root be holy, so are the branches. And if some of the branches be broken off, and thou, being a wild olive tree, wert graffed in among them, and with them partakest of the root and fatness of the olive tree; Boast not against the branches. But if thou boast, thou bearest not the root, but the root thee. Thou wilt say then, The branches were broken off, that I might be graffed in. Well; because of unbelief they were broken off, and thou standest by faith. Be not highminded, but fear: For if God spared not the natural branches, take heed lest he also spare not thee. Behold therefore the goodness and severity of God: on them which fell, severity; but toward thee, goodness, if thou continue in his goodness: otherwise thou also shalt be cut off. And they also, if they abide not still in unbelief, shall be graffed in: for God is able to graff them in again. For if thou wert cut out of the olive tree which is wild by nature, and wert graffed contrary to nature into a good olive tree: how much more shall these, which be the natural branches, be graffed into their own olive tree? For I would not, brethren, that ye should be ignorant of this mystery, lest ye should be wise in your own conceits; that blindness in part is happened to Israel, until the fulness of the Gentiles be come in. And so all Israel shall be saved: as it is written, There shall come out of Sion the Deliverer, and shall turn away ungodliness from Jacob: For this is my covenant unto them, when I shall take away their sins. As concerning the gospel, they are enemies for your sakes: but as touching the election, they are beloved for the fathers’ sakes. For the gifts and calling of God are without repentance. For as ye in times past have not believed God, yet have now obtained mercy through their unbelief: Even so have these also now not believed, that through your mercy they also may obtain mercy. For God hath concluded them all in unbelief, that he might have mercy upon all. O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out! For who hath known the mind of the Lord? or who hath been his counsellor? Or who hath first given to him, and it shall be recompensed unto him again? For of him, and through him, and to him, are all things: to whom be glory for ever. Amen.

label: Romans 12
text: After eleven chapters of argument that end in doxology, Paul turns to the life that mercy makes: "I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service." The appeal rests on "therefore" — everything asked here follows from what has already been given. The altar is the body, the victim stays alive, and the worship is called "reasonable service," a phrase that binds mind and flesh into one offering. From that follows the double command "be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind," with a stated purpose: "that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God." Discernment is not a preliminary to obedience but its fruit; the renewed mind learns God's will by living it. Paul then applies the renewed mind first to self-estimate, warning "every man that is among you, not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think soberly, according as God hath dealt to every man the measure of faith" — and he says this "through the grace given unto me," measuring even his own authority as gift rather than rank. Humility is grounded in an image: "as we have many members in one body, and all members have not the same office: So we, being many, are one body in Christ, and every one members one of another." The differences are not accidents to be tolerated but the body's design, and the belonging is mutual, member to member, not merely each to the head. Out of that comes the list of charisms — "Having then gifts differing according to the grace that is given to us, whether prophecy," then "ministry," "he that teacheth," "he that exhorteth," "he that giveth," "he that ruleth," "he that sheweth mercy" — each with its own manner attached: "with simplicity," "with diligence," "with cheerfulness." The gift is measured by grace, and even the temper in which it is exercised is prescribed. The chapter then opens into a rapid series of clipped imperatives that read as the anatomy of charity in practice: "Let love be without dissimulation," love that neither pretends nor flatters, joined to a sharp moral edge — "Abhor that which is evil; cleave to that which is good." Life inside the body is described as competitive honor rather than competitive standing, "in honour preferring one another," sustained by an interior fire, "Not slothful in business; fervent in spirit; serving the Lord," and by three braided disciplines, "Rejoicing in hope; patient in tribulation; continuing instant in prayer." It becomes concrete in goods shared and doors opened: "Distributing to the necessity of saints; given to hospitality." Then the horizon widens past the Church to the hostile world, and the commands become harder: "Bless them which persecute you: bless, and curse not." Paul asks for an emotional solidarity that costs on both sides — "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep" — and a deliberate refusal of status, "Mind not high things, but condescend to men of low estate. Be not wise in your own conceits." Retaliation is forbidden not because evil does not matter but because judgment belongs elsewhere: "Recompense to no man evil for evil," and "avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord." Peace is commanded with a realist's qualification, "If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men," acknowledging that the other party may refuse. The alternative to vengeance is not passivity but active kindness aimed at the enemy's need: "if thine enemy hunger, feed him; if he thirst, give him drink: for in so doing thou shalt heap coals of fire on his head." The whole chapter closes in a single line that gathers the living sacrifice, the body, and the enemy into one strategy: "Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good." The word "therefore" governs everything that follows. Paul does not begin the moral section with a command but with an appeal "by the mercies of God," so that the "living sacrifice" is the answer to grace already received rather than the price of grace still to be earned. Worship here is not an hour but a body, and it is called "reasonable service" — offered by a creature who understands what he is doing. Discernment is presented as a consequence of transformation, not a substitute for it. The renewed mind is not first told what God's will is; it is told to be renewed "that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God." Knowing what God wants follows from no longer being "conformed to this world," which means moral clarity is downstream of conversion. The body image is pressed further than mere teamwork. Paul writes that "all members have not the same office" and that believers are "every one members one of another" — the belonging is horizontal as well as vertical, so that difference of function is not inequality of worth and no member can be surplus without the body being maimed. Every gift is named with its manner as well as its content: giving "with simplicity," ruling "with diligence," showing mercy "with cheerfulness." The chapter refuses to separate what a Christian does from how it is done, and it places even prophecy under a limit, "according to the proportion of faith," so that no charism becomes a law unto itself. Non-retaliation is grounded in theology, not temperament. "Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord" means that refusing revenge is an act of faith that justice exists and is God's, which is why the alternative offered is not withdrawal but feeding and giving drink — the enemy is met with active good in the confidence that evil is defeated by being outlived, not matched. I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service. And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God. For I say, through the grace given unto me, to every man that is among you, not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think soberly, according as God hath dealt to every man the measure of faith. For as we have many members in one body, and all members have not the same office: So we, being many, are one body in Christ, and every one members one of another. Having then gifts differing according to the grace that is given to us, whether prophecy, let us prophesy according to the proportion of faith; Or ministry, let us wait on our ministering: or he that teacheth, on teaching; Or he that exhorteth, on exhortation: he that giveth, let him do it with simplicity; he that ruleth, with diligence; he that sheweth mercy, with cheerfulness. Let love be without dissimulation. Abhor that which is evil; cleave to that which is good. Be kindly affectioned one to another with brotherly love; in honour preferring one another; Not slothful in business; fervent in spirit; serving the Lord; Rejoicing in hope; patient in tribulation; continuing instant in prayer; Distributing to the necessity of saints; given to hospitality. Bless them which persecute you: bless, and curse not. Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep. Be of the same mind one toward another. Mind not high things, but condescend to men of low estate. Be not wise in your own conceits. Recompense to no man evil for evil. Provide things honest in the sight of all men. If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men. Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord. Therefore if thine enemy hunger, feed him; if he thirst, give him drink: for in so doing thou shalt heap coals of fire on his head. Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good.

label: Romans 13
text: Having spent the previous chapter on the shape of life in the body of Christ, Paul turns outward to the Christian standing before the magistrate: "Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God." The argument is not that rulers are good but that authority itself is derivative — it exists because God ordained order, so "whosoever therefore resisteth the power, resisteth the ordinance of God." Paul then gives the ruler's job description twice over in a single title: "he is the minister of God to thee for good," and again "he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil." The office is defined by its purpose — restraining evil and praising good — and the sword is real, for "he beareth not the sword in vain." But Paul refuses to leave obedience at the level of fear. "Wherefore ye must needs be subject, not only for wrath, but also for conscience sake": the Christian pays taxes and gives honour not because he is watched but because he answers to God in the paying. Hence the ledger of verse 7 — "tribute to whom tribute is due; custom to whom custom; fear to whom fear; honour to whom honour" — a settling of accounts that immediately opens onto the one debt that is never settled: "Owe no man any thing, but to love one another: for he that loveth another hath fulfilled the law." Paul then walks through the second table of the commandments — "Thou shalt not commit adultery, Thou shalt not kill, Thou shalt not steal, Thou shalt not bear false witness, Thou shalt not covet" — and gathers them all into one line, "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself," concluding with the logic that makes the gathering possible: "Love worketh no ill to his neighbour: therefore love is the fulfilling of the law." The chapter closes on urgency rather than administration. "Knowing the time," Paul says, "now it is high time to awake out of sleep: for now is our salvation nearer than when we believed." The imagery turns to dawn — "The night is far spent, the day is at hand" — and with it a change of clothing: "cast off the works of darkness," "put on the armour of light," "walk honestly, as in the day; not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness, not in strife and envying." The final command names the garment itself: "put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof." Civil duty, the debt of love, and the coming day are one argument — the Christian lives an ordinary public life under authority while dressed for a morning the world has not yet seen. Paul grounds submission in the origin of authority, not the virtue of the officeholder: "there is no power but of God." What is honoured is an office God ordained for order, which is why he can write this to Christians in Rome, under a state that would later kill him. The phrase "minister of God" is applied to the civil ruler twice, and both times it is tied to a function — "to thee for good" and "a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil." Authority is described by its purpose, which quietly supplies the standard by which any particular exercise of it can be measured. "Not only for wrath, but also for conscience sake" moves obedience out of the realm of prudence. Paying tribute becomes an act done before God rather than merely under surveillance, which both dignifies civic duty and makes conscience — not the magistrate — the Christian's final internal court. Love is not presented as an alternative to the commandments but as their sum: the prohibitions against adultery, killing, stealing, false witness, and covetousness are "briefly comprehended" in loving the neighbour, because "love worketh no ill to his neighbour." The law is fulfilled, not discarded. The ethics of the chapter are eschatological, not merely civic. Because "the night is far spent, the day is at hand," ordinary conduct — sobriety, chastity, peaceableness — is dressing for the coming day, and the final imperative is not a rule but a Person: "put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ." Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God. Whosoever therefore resisteth the power, resisteth the ordinance of God: and they that resist shall receive to themselves damnation. For rulers are not a terror to good works, but to the evil. Wilt thou then not be afraid of the power? do that which is good, and thou shalt have praise of the same: For he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil. Wherefore ye must needs be subject, not only for wrath, but also for conscience sake. For for this cause pay ye tribute also: for they are God’s ministers, attending continually upon this very thing. Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due; custom to whom custom; fear to whom fear; honour to whom honour. Owe no man any thing, but to love one another: for he that loveth another hath fulfilled the law. For this, Thou shalt not commit adultery, Thou shalt not kill, Thou shalt not steal, Thou shalt not bear false witness, Thou shalt not covet; and if there be any other commandment, it is briefly comprehended in this saying, namely, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. Love worketh no ill to his neighbour: therefore love is the fulfilling of the law. And that, knowing the time, that now it is high time to awake out of sleep: for now is our salvation nearer than when we believed. The night is far spent, the day is at hand: let us therefore cast off the works of darkness, and let us put on the armour of light. Let us walk honestly, as in the day; not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness, not in strife and envying. But put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof.

label: Romans 14
text: Paul turns from doctrine to the table, where a mixed congregation of Jewish and Gentile believers was quietly tearing itself apart over food and calendar. His opening rule is hospitality without interrogation: "Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations." The dispute is named plainly — "one believeth that he may eat all things: another, who is weak, eateth herbs" — and the two parties are given symmetrical corrections, because each has its own characteristic sin: "Let not him that eateth despise him that eateth not; and let not him which eateth not judge him that eateth." The free man is tempted to contempt, the scrupulous man to condemnation, and both are silenced by the same fact: "for God hath received him." Paul presses it with a household image — "Who art thou that judgest another man’s servant? to his own master he standeth or falleth" — and adds a promise that removes the anxiety underneath the judging: "Yea, he shall be holden up: for God is able to make him stand." On the calendar he refuses to legislate, saying only, "Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind," because what matters is the direction of the act rather than its form: the one who keeps the day "regardeth it unto the Lord," and both the eater and the abstainer alike "giveth God thanks." The whole argument is then anchored in Christ's lordship over life and death — "none of us liveth to himself, and no man dieth to himself" — and in a judgment already assigned to another: "we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ," and "every one of us shall give account of himself to God." From that Paul draws the practical turn, replacing one verdict with another: "Let us not therefore judge one another any more: but judge this rather, that no man put a stumblingblock or an occasion to fall in his brother’s way."
