He states his own conviction without hedging — "there is nothing unclean of itself" — and immediately limits its use, since "to him that esteemeth any thing to be unclean, to him it is unclean," and a right that wounds has already stopped being love: "if thy brother be grieved with thy meat, now walkest thou not charitably. Destroy not him with thy meat, for whom Christ died." The controlling principle is a reordering of what religion is about: "the kingdom of God is not meat and drink; but righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost." So the strong are told to "follow after the things which make for peace, and things wherewith one may edify another," to grant that "All things indeed are pure" while conceding that "it is evil for that man who eateth with offence," and even to forgo flesh and wine rather than make a brother stumble. The chapter ends by moving the whole question inward to conscience before God: "Hast thou faith? have it to thyself before God. Happy is he that condemneth not himself in that thing which he alloweth" — while the doubter who acts against his own conscience is condemned, "because he eateth not of faith: for whatsoever is not of faith is sin." Paul rebukes both sides with equal force but for different faults — the free are told not to "despise," the scrupulous not to "judge" — which forbids the common move of treating one's own party's temptation as the only real danger in a disputed matter. The chapter separates two questions that are constantly confused: what is true in itself and what is safe for this person to do. "There is nothing unclean of itself" is stated as fact, yet "to him that esteemeth any thing to be unclean, to him it is unclean" — objective liberty does not license an act performed against one's own conscience. Liberty is bounded by charity rather than by a longer list of rules. The strong are not told they were wrong about meat; they are told that "if thy brother be grieved with thy meat, now walkest thou not charitably," so the limit on a real right is the good of a brother "for whom Christ died," not a revised verdict about food. "The kingdom of God is not meat and drink; but righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost" gives a working test of proportion: practices are ranked beneath the ends they serve, so a community that fights hardest over its secondary observances has inverted its own faith. Judgment is not abolished but reassigned. Because "we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ" and each "shall give account of himself to God," the energy spent auditing a brother is redirected into a single permitted verdict — "that no man put a stumblingblock or an occasion to fall in his brother’s way." Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations. For one believeth that he may eat all things: another, who is weak, eateth herbs. Let not him that eateth despise him that eateth not; and let not him which eateth not judge him that eateth: for God hath received him. Who art thou that judgest another man’s servant? to his own master he standeth or falleth. Yea, he shall be holden up: for God is able to make him stand. One man esteemeth one day above another: another esteemeth every day alike. Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind. He that regardeth the day, regardeth it unto the Lord; and he that regardeth not the day, to the Lord he doth not regard it. He that eateth, eateth to the Lord, for he giveth God thanks; and he that eateth not, to the Lord he eateth not, and giveth God thanks. For none of us liveth to himself, and no man dieth to himself. For whether we live, we live unto the Lord; and whether we die, we die unto the Lord: whether we live therefore, or die, we are the Lord’s. For to this end Christ both died, and rose, and revived, that he might be Lord both of the dead and living. But why dost thou judge thy brother? or why dost thou set at nought thy brother? for we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ. For it is written, As I live, saith the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to God. So then every one of us shall give account of himself to God. Let us not therefore judge one another any more: but judge this rather, that no man put a stumblingblock or an occasion to fall in his brother’s way. I know, and am persuaded by the Lord Jesus, that there is nothing unclean of itself: but to him that esteemeth any thing to be unclean, to him it is unclean. But if thy brother be grieved with thy meat, now walkest thou not charitably. Destroy not him with thy meat, for whom Christ died. Let not then your good be evil spoken of: For the kingdom of God is not meat and drink; but righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost. For he that in these things serveth Christ is acceptable to God, and approved of men. Let us therefore follow after the things which make for peace, and things wherewith one may edify another. For meat destroy not the work of God. All things indeed are pure; but it is evil for that man who eateth with offence. It is good neither to eat flesh, nor to drink wine, nor any thing whereby thy brother stumbleth, or is offended, or is made weak. Hast thou faith? have it to thyself before God. Happy is he that condemneth not himself in that thing which he alloweth. And he that doubteth is damned if he eat, because he eateth not of faith: for whatsoever is not of faith is sin.

label: Romans 15
text: Paul finishes the argument about the strong and the weak by refusing to let strength be a privilege: "We then that are strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak, and not to please ourselves," and every man is to "please his neighbour for his good to edification." The warrant is not prudence but imitation, "For even Christ pleased not himself," who took upon himself the psalmist's words, "The reproaches of them that reproached thee fell on me." Scripture is enlisted for the same endurance: "whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning, that we through patience and comfort of the scriptures might have hope." The aim of all this forbearance is worship in common — that God would "grant you to be likeminded one toward another according to Christ Jesus: That ye may with one mind and one mouth glorify God" — and the rule of admission into that assembly is set by Christ himself: "receive ye one another, as Christ also received us to the glory of God." Paul then grounds the union of Jew and Gentile in God's own fidelity rather than in tolerance. "Jesus Christ was a minister of the circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm the promises made unto the fathers: And that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy" — promise kept to one, mercy extended to the other, one purpose in both. He piles up four Scriptures to prove the Gentiles were always in view: "I will confess to thee among the Gentiles," "Rejoice, ye Gentiles, with his people," "Praise the Lord, all ye Gentiles," and Isaiah's "root of Jesse" in whom "shall the Gentiles trust." The doctrinal body of the letter then closes in benediction: "Now the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, that ye may abound in hope, through the power of the Holy Ghost." Turning personal, Paul softens his boldness by crediting his readers — they are "full of goodness, filled with all knowledge, able also to admonish one another" — and explains that he has written "because of the grace that is given to me of God, That I should be the minister of Jesus Christ to the Gentiles, ministering the gospel of God, that the offering up of the Gentiles might be acceptable, being sanctified by the Holy Ghost." The vocabulary is deliberately liturgical: he serves at an altar, and the converted nations are the sacrifice laid on it, made acceptable not by his skill but by the Spirit. His glorying is therefore strictly bounded — "I will not dare to speak of any of those things which Christ hath not wrought by me" — and his method is pioneering, "not where Christ was named, lest I should build upon another man’s foundation," a course that has carried him "from Jerusalem, and round about unto Illyricum." Rome has waited because of that work, but now he means to pass through on his way "into Spain," hoping to be "somewhat filled with your company." First, though, "I go unto Jerusalem to minister unto the saints," carrying the "contribution for the poor saints which are at Jerusalem" gathered in Macedonia and Achaia — a gift Paul calls a debt: "if the Gentiles have been made partakers of their spiritual things, their duty is also to minister unto them in carnal things." He will "have sealed to them this fruit" and then come, "in the fulness of the blessing of the gospel of Christ." The chapter ends not in confidence but in requested struggle: "strive together with me in your prayers to God for me; That I may be delivered from them that do not believe in Judaea; and that my service which I have for Jerusalem may be accepted of the saints" — the apostle fearing both the hostility outside and the cool reception within — and then rests in a blessing, "Now the God of peace be with you all. Amen." Strength in the Church is defined as load-bearing, not as license. The strong "ought to bear the infirmities of the weak," and the standard is set by a Christ who "pleased not himself" and absorbed reproach that was aimed elsewhere, so that yielding to a weaker conscience is conformity to the cross rather than a concession to error. The unity Paul wants is liturgical before it is social: the goal of being "likeminded one toward another" is "that ye may with one mind and one mouth glorify God." Mutual reception is not politeness among believers but the precondition of a single voice in worship, which is why the rule is "receive ye one another, as Christ also received us." Verse 8 keeps Jew and Gentile inside one divine action without collapsing the difference. To Israel Christ comes as "a minister of the circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm the promises made unto the fathers"; the Gentiles "glorify God for his mercy." Promise kept and mercy shown are two motions of one fidelity, and the four quoted Scriptures show the Gentile praise was written into Israel's own books long before it happened. Paul describes apostolic work in the language of the sanctuary: he is a "minister of Jesus Christ," "ministering the gospel," so that "the offering up of the Gentiles might be acceptable, being sanctified by the Holy Ghost." Preaching is presented as an act of sacrificial service in which converted peoples are the offering and the Holy Ghost, not the preacher, is what makes them acceptable. The collection is theology in money. Gentile churches owe Jerusalem because "the Gentiles have been made partakers of their spiritual things," so a material gift becomes the visible proof that the two halves of the Church are one body — which is why Paul asks prayer not only that he survive Judaea but "that my service which I have for Jerusalem may be accepted of the saints." We then that are strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak, and not to please ourselves. Let every one of us please his neighbour for his good to edification. For even Christ pleased not himself; but, as it is written, The reproaches of them that reproached thee fell on me. For whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning, that we through patience and comfort of the scriptures might have hope. Now the God of patience and consolation grant you to be likeminded one toward another according to Christ Jesus: That ye may with one mind and one mouth glorify God, even the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Wherefore receive ye one another, as Christ also received us to the glory of God. Now I say that Jesus Christ was a minister of the circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm the promises made unto the fathers: And that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy; as it is written, For this cause I will confess to thee among the Gentiles, and sing unto thy name. And again he saith, Rejoice, ye Gentiles, with his people. And again, Praise the Lord, all ye Gentiles; and laud him, all ye people. And again, Esaias saith, There shall be a root of Jesse, and he that shall rise to reign over the Gentiles; in him shall the Gentiles trust. Now the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, that ye may abound in hope, through the power of the Holy Ghost. And I myself also am persuaded of you, my brethren, that ye also are full of goodness, filled with all knowledge, able also to admonish one another. Nevertheless, brethren, I have written the more boldly unto you in some sort, as putting you in mind, because of the grace that is given to me of God, That I should be the minister of Jesus Christ to the Gentiles, ministering the gospel of God, that the offering up of the Gentiles might be acceptable, being sanctified by the Holy Ghost. I have therefore whereof I may glory through Jesus Christ in those things which pertain to God. For I will not dare to speak of any of those things which Christ hath not wrought by me, to make the Gentiles obedient, by word and deed, Through mighty signs and wonders, by the power of the Spirit of God; so that from Jerusalem, and round about unto Illyricum, I have fully preached the gospel of Christ. Yea, so have I strived to preach the gospel, not where Christ was named, lest I should build upon another man’s foundation: But as it is written, To whom he was not spoken of, they shall see: and they that have not heard shall understand. For which cause also I have been much hindered from coming to you. But now having no more place in these parts, and having a great desire these many years to come unto you; Whensoever I take my journey into Spain, I will come to you: for I trust to see you in my journey, and to be brought on my way thitherward by you, if first I be somewhat filled with your company. But now I go unto Jerusalem to minister unto the saints. For it hath pleased them of Macedonia and Achaia to make a certain contribution for the poor saints which are at Jerusalem. It hath pleased them verily; and their debtors they are. For if the Gentiles have been made partakers of their spiritual things, their duty is also to minister unto them in carnal things. When therefore I have performed this, and have sealed to them this fruit, I will come by you into Spain. And I am sure that, when I come unto you, I shall come in the fulness of the blessing of the gospel of Christ. Now I beseech you, brethren, for the Lord Jesus Christ’s sake, and for the love of the Spirit, that ye strive together with me in your prayers to God for me; That I may be delivered from them that do not believe in Judaea; and that my service which I have for Jerusalem may be accepted of the saints; That I may come unto you with joy by the will of God, and may with you be refreshed. Now the God of peace be with you all. Amen.

label: Romans 16
text: After eleven chapters of argument and four of exhortation, Paul closes the letter with names. He begins by commending "Phebe our sister, which is a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea," asking that the Romans "receive her in the Lord, as becometh saints" and "assist her in whatsoever business she hath need of you," for "she hath been a succourer of many, and of myself also." Then comes the roll: "Priscilla and Aquila my helpers in Christ Jesus," who "have for my life laid down their own necks"; "the church that is in their house"; Epaenetus, "the firstfruits of Achaia unto Christ"; "Mary, who bestowed much labour on us"; "Andronicus and Junia, my kinsmen, and my fellowprisoners, who are of note among the apostles, who also were in Christ before me"; "Tryphena and Tryphosa, who labour in the Lord" and "the beloved Persis, which laboured much in the Lord"; "Rufus chosen in the Lord, and his mother and mine." Some twenty-six people are named, whole households are addressed, and the greeting is meant to be enacted physically: "Salute one another with an holy kiss. The churches of Christ salute you." Into this warmth Paul drops a single sharp warning: "mark them which cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine which ye have learned; and avoid them," since such teachers "serve not our Lord Jesus Christ, but their own belly; and by good words and fair speeches deceive the hearts of the simple." His wish for them is discernment without corruption, "wise unto that which is good, and simple concerning evil," and his assurance is that "the God of peace shall bruise Satan under your feet shortly." The scribe himself breaks in — "I Tertius, who wrote this epistle, salute you in the Lord" — followed by Gaius the host and "Erastus the chamberlain of the city." The letter ends in doxology, praising "him that is of power to stablish you according to my gospel" and "the revelation of the mystery, which was kept secret since the world began, But now is made manifest, and by the scriptures of the prophets... made known to all nations for the obedience of faith: To God only wise, be glory through Jesus Christ for ever. Amen." The heaviest doctrinal letter in the New Testament ends in a list of names, and that is not an accident of form. Righteousness by faith is shown landing in actual households — "the church that is in their house" — among people known by nickname, kinship, and what they suffered, so that doctrine is never abstract from the community it creates. The labour of the gospel in this chapter is conspicuously shared by women. Phebe is "a servant of the church" entrusted with "business" among the Romans, Priscilla is named before her husband as a fellow "helper in Christ Jesus," Mary "bestowed much labour," Tryphena, Tryphosa, and Persis "labour in the Lord," and Junia is "of note among the apostles." Paul uses the same working vocabulary for them that he uses for himself. The one command in an otherwise affectionate chapter is a command of separation: "mark them which cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine which ye have learned; and avoid them." The test given is not eloquence but appetite and effect — such men "serve not our Lord Jesus Christ, but their own belly" and "by good words and fair speeches deceive the hearts of the simple." Paul's prayer that they be "wise unto that which is good, and simple concerning evil" refuses both naivety and worldly cunning. Christian discernment is meant to be expert in what is good and deliberately inexperienced in what is not, which is the exact reversal of the wisdom Eden offered. The closing doxology gathers the whole letter into one word: the "mystery, which was kept secret since the world began, But now is made manifest." The gospel is presented as neither novelty nor secret knowledge, since it is attested "by the scriptures of the prophets" and published "to all nations for the obedience of faith" — faith that obeys, not faith set against obedience. I commend unto you Phebe our sister, which is a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea: That ye receive her in the Lord, as becometh saints, and that ye assist her in whatsoever business she hath need of you: for she hath been a succourer of many, and of myself also. Greet Priscilla and Aquila my helpers in Christ Jesus: Who have for my life laid down their own necks: unto whom not only I give thanks, but also all the churches of the Gentiles. Likewise greet the church that is in their house. Salute my wellbeloved Epaenetus, who is the firstfruits of Achaia unto Christ. Greet Mary, who bestowed much labour on us. Salute Andronicus and Junia, my kinsmen, and my fellowprisoners, who are of note among the apostles, who also were in Christ before me. Greet Amplias my beloved in the Lord. Salute Urbane, our helper in Christ, and Stachys my beloved. Salute Apelles approved in Christ. Salute them which are of Aristobulus’ household. Salute Herodion my kinsman. Greet them that be of the household of Narcissus, which are in the Lord. Salute Tryphena and Tryphosa, who labour in the Lord. Salute the beloved Persis, which laboured much in the Lord. Salute Rufus chosen in the Lord, and his mother and mine. Salute Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermas, Patrobas, Hermes, and the brethren which are with them. Salute Philologus, and Julia, Nereus, and his sister, and Olympas, and all the saints which are with them. Salute one another with an holy kiss. The churches of Christ salute you. Now I beseech you, brethren, mark them which cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine which ye have learned; and avoid them. For they that are such serve not our Lord Jesus Christ, but their own belly; and by good words and fair speeches deceive the hearts of the simple. For your obedience is come abroad unto all men. I am glad therefore on your behalf: but yet I would have you wise unto that which is good, and simple concerning evil. And the God of peace shall bruise Satan under your feet shortly. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. Amen. Timotheus my workfellow, and Lucius, and Jason, and Sosipater, my kinsmen, salute you. I Tertius, who wrote this epistle, salute you in the Lord. Gaius mine host, and of the whole church, saluteth you. Erastus the chamberlain of the city saluteth you, and Quartus a brother. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen. Now to him that is of power to stablish you according to my gospel, and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery, which was kept secret since the world began, But now is made manifest, and by the scriptures of the prophets, according to the commandment of the everlasting God, made known to all nations for the obedience of faith: To God only wise, be glory through Jesus Christ for ever. Amen.

label: 1 Corinthians 1
text: Paul opens with his credentials and a co-sender — "Paul, called to be an apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God, and Sosthenes our brother" — and writes "Unto the church of God which is at Corinth, to them that are sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints," immediately widening the address to "all that in every place call upon the name of Jesus Christ our Lord, both theirs and ours," so that a quarrelling congregation is never permitted to think of itself in isolation. The thanksgiving that follows is generous and, read against the rest of the letter, pointed: he thanks God "for the grace of God which is given you by Jesus Christ," that "in every thing ye are enriched by him, in all utterance, and in all knowledge," and that "ye come behind in no gift; waiting for the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ." These are the very endowments the Corinthians will shortly be rebuked for mishandling, yet Paul names them as gifts before he names them as problems, and he grounds their perseverance not in their gifting but in the God "Who shall also confirm you unto the end, that ye may be blameless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ," summing it up in four words of assurance: "God is faithful, by whom ye were called unto the fellowship of his Son Jesus Christ our Lord." Then the trouble surfaces. "Now I beseech you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you; but that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment." The report has come "by them which are of the house of Chloe, that there are contentions among you," and the contentions have hardened into slogans of allegiance: "every one of you saith, I am of Paul; and I of Apollos; and I of Cephas; and I of Christ." Paul answers with three questions that demolish all four parties at once — "Is Christ divided? was Paul crucified for you? or were ye baptized in the name of Paul?" — and is relieved to have personally baptized so few of them, "none of you, but Crispus and Gaius" and "the household of Stephanas," precisely "Lest any should say that I had baptized in mine own name." He then states the shape of his own commission: "For Christ sent me not to baptize, but to preach the gospel: not with wisdom of words, lest the cross of Christ should be made of none effect." That last clause opens the chapter's great argument, and the argument is about the cross rather than about church politics. "For the preaching of the cross is to them that perish foolishness; but unto us which are saved it is the power of God." Scripture had already announced the reversal — "I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and will bring to nothing the understanding of the prudent" — so Paul taunts the recognized authorities of the age: "Where is the wise? where is the scribe? where is the disputer of this world? hath not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?" The strategy behind the reversal is deliberate: "after that in the wisdom of God the world by wisdom knew not God, it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe." Both halves of Paul's world are scandalized by the result, since "the Jews require a sign, and the Greeks seek after wisdom: But we preach Christ crucified, unto the Jews a stumblingblock, and unto the Greeks foolishness; But unto them which are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God, and the wisdom of God. Because the foolishness of God is wiser than men; and the weakness of God is stronger than men." Finally Paul turns the lens on the congregation itself as the standing evidence of his case: "ye see your calling, brethren, how that not many wise men after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, are called: But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty; And base things of the world, and things which are despised, hath God chosen, yea, and things which are not, to bring to nought things that are." The purpose is stated without softening — "That no flesh should glory in his presence" — and the only permitted alternative is Christ himself, "who of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption: That, according as it is written, He that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord." Paul thanks God for the Corinthians before he corrects them, and what he thanks God for is exactly what they have abused. They are "enriched by him, in all utterance, and in all knowledge" and "come behind in no gift," yet the whole letter will show a church that is gifted and immature at the same time. The chapter therefore refuses the assumption that spiritual endowment is spiritual maturity: eloquence, knowledge, and charism are real gifts of grace and are no proof at all that the people holding them are walking rightly. Correction begins by acknowledging what God has genuinely given, not by denying it. The security Paul offers is placed entirely outside the Corinthians themselves. It is God "Who shall also confirm you unto the end, that ye may be blameless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ," and the ground of that confidence is stated as a bare fact about God rather than about them: "God is faithful, by whom ye were called unto the fellowship of his Son Jesus Christ our Lord." A church that has just been described as full of contentions is told that its future blamelessness rests on divine fidelity, which is both the strongest possible comfort and the strongest possible rebuke to factional self-confidence. The party slogans are treated as a single disease rather than three good options and one bad one. "I am of Paul; and I of Apollos; and I of Cephas; and I of Christ" — and the fourth slogan, which sounds unimpeachable, is listed alongside the others as one more banner in a fight. The three questions that follow expose what a party spirit actually claims: "Is Christ divided? was Paul crucified for you? or were ye baptized in the name of Paul?" No teacher was crucified for the church and no one was baptized into a teacher's name, so attaching one's identity to a human leader is a quiet theft of what belongs to Christ alone. "For Christ sent me not to baptize, but to preach the gospel" is a statement about Paul's particular commission, not a ranking of baptism as unimportant, and the sentence itself proves it, since Paul carefully recalls whom he did baptize and why he is glad the number was small: "Lest any should say that I had baptized in mine own name." His concern is that the rite not become a personal loyalty badge. The reason given for preaching "not with wisdom of words" is likewise practical rather than anti-intellectual: rhetorical brilliance can so absorb the hearer's admiration that "the cross of Christ should be made of none effect," the message swallowed by the medium. The cross divides humanity by what it looks like to them: "the preaching of the cross is to them that perish foolishness; but unto us which are saved it is the power of God." Paul names the two standing objections of his world with precision — "the Jews require a sign, and the Greeks seek after wisdom" — and answers both with the same offensive content, "Christ crucified, unto the Jews a stumblingblock, and unto the Greeks foolishness." He does not soften the offense but relocates it, because to "them which are called" that identical crucified Christ is "the power of God, and the wisdom of God." The gospel is not a sign for the sign-seekers and a philosophy for the philosophers; it is one scandal that becomes power in those who are called. The Corinthian membership roll is itself the argument: "not many wise men after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, are called: But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise... and things which are not, to bring to nought things that are." God's choosing runs deliberately against every metric of status, and the stated purpose is the elimination of boasting — "That no flesh should glory in his presence." The chapter then closes by naming what replaces the boast, since Christ "of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption." Everything the factions were competing over is already given in one person, which is why the only remaining option is that "He that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord." Paul, called to be an apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God, and Sosthenes our brother, Unto the church of God which is at Corinth, to them that are sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints, with all that in every place call upon the name of Jesus Christ our Lord, both theirs and ours: Grace be unto you, and peace, from God our Father, and from the Lord Jesus Christ. I thank my God always on your behalf, for the grace of God which is given you by Jesus Christ; That in every thing ye are enriched by him, in all utterance, and in all knowledge; Even as the testimony of Christ was confirmed in you: So that ye come behind in no gift; waiting for the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ: Who shall also confirm you unto the end, that ye may be blameless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. God is faithful, by whom ye were called unto the fellowship of his Son Jesus Christ our Lord. Now I beseech you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you; but that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment. For it hath been declared unto me of you, my brethren, by them which are of the house of Chloe, that there are contentions among you. Now this I say, that every one of you saith, I am of Paul; and I of Apollos; and I of Cephas; and I of Christ. Is Christ divided? was Paul crucified for you? or were ye baptized in the name of Paul? I thank God that I baptized none of you, but Crispus and Gaius; Lest any should say that I had baptized in mine own name. And I baptized also the household of Stephanas: besides, I know not whether I baptized any other. For Christ sent me not to baptize, but to preach the gospel: not with wisdom of words, lest the cross of Christ should be made of none effect. For the preaching of the cross is to them that perish foolishness; but unto us which are saved it is the power of God. For it is written, I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and will bring to nothing the understanding of the prudent. Where is the wise? where is the scribe? where is the disputer of this world? hath not God made foolish the wisdom of this world? For after that in the wisdom of God the world by wisdom knew not God, it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe. For the Jews require a sign, and the Greeks seek after wisdom: But we preach Christ crucified, unto the Jews a stumblingblock, and unto the Greeks foolishness; But unto them which are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God, and the wisdom of God. Because the foolishness of God is wiser than men; and the weakness of God is stronger than men. For ye see your calling, brethren, how that not many wise men after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, are called: But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty; And base things of the world, and things which are despised, hath God chosen, yea, and things which are not, to bring to nought things that are: That no flesh should glory in his presence. But of him are ye in Christ Jesus, who of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption: That, according as it is written, He that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord.

label: 1 Corinthians 2
text: Having just argued that God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise, Paul turns the argument on himself and offers his own arrival at Corinth as the proof. "And I, brethren, when I came to you, came not with excellency of speech or of wisdom, declaring unto you the testimony of God." In a city that priced rhetoric and paid well for it, he came with a deliberately narrowed subject — "For I determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified" — and by his own account he was no impressive figure while he did it: "And I was with you in weakness, and in fear, and in much trembling." The manner matched the message. His "speech and my preaching was not with enticing words of man’s wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power," and he names the reason without hedging: "That your faith should not stand in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God." A faith produced by a persuasive speaker rests on that speaker, and falls when he is outargued. Then Paul guards himself against being misheard as despising thought altogether. "Howbeit we speak wisdom among them that are perfect: yet not the wisdom of this world, nor of the princes of this world, that come to nought." There is a wisdom, but it belongs to another order: "we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, even the hidden wisdom, which God ordained before the world unto our glory." Its hiddenness is proved by the crucifixion itself — "Which none of the princes of this world knew: for had they known it, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory" — so that the powers who arranged the cross were, in that very act, walking into the plan they meant to defeat. What no eye discovered, God disclosed: "Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared for them that love him. But God hath revealed them unto us by his Spirit." The last third grounds all of this in the Spirit’s own competence. "The Spirit searcheth all things, yea, the deep things of God," and Paul argues from the analogy of self-knowledge: as "the things of a man" are known only by "the spirit of man which is in him," so "the things of God knoweth no man, but the Spirit of God." Believers have "received, not the spirit of the world, but the spirit which is of God; that we might know the things that are freely given to us of God," and the teaching that carries this gift is in kind with it, "not in the words which man’s wisdom teacheth, but which the Holy Ghost teacheth; comparing spiritual things with spiritual." Hence the impasse the whole chapter has been circling: "the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned." Paul ends with a prophet’s unanswerable question and an answer that should not exist: "For who hath known the mind of the Lord, that he may instruct him? But we have the mind of Christ." Paul handicaps his own presentation on purpose, and he tells us why. He "came not with excellency of speech or of wisdom" and refused "enticing words of man’s wisdom" so "that your faith should not stand in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God." The reasoning is pastoral rather than aesthetic: whatever wins a hearer is what holds him, so a faith argued into place by brilliance is only as durable as the next, more brilliant argument. By stripping the delivery, Paul makes the foundation visible, and the question he forces on every preacher and teacher after him is not whether their case is compelling but what their hearers will finally be resting on. "For I determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified" is a decision about content, not a boast about ignorance. It is also not a beginner’s topic later outgrown, because when Paul goes on to speak "wisdom among them that are perfect," the wisdom he names is "the wisdom of God in a mystery, even the hidden wisdom, which God ordained before the world unto our glory" — the same crucified Lord seen at depth. Christian maturity in this chapter is not moving on from the cross to something more advanced; it is being taken further into what was there from the beginning. The chapter sets Paul’s condition and the effect of his preaching side by side without embarrassment: he was "in weakness, and in fear, and in much trembling," and yet his preaching was "in demonstration of the Spirit and of power." The juxtaposition is the argument. Had the speaker been formidable, the power could plausibly have been credited to him; because he was not, the demonstration had to be attributed elsewhere. This is why weakness in ministry is treated here as evidence rather than as an obstacle to be apologized for or engineered away. The most chilling line in the chapter is a claim about competence: "Which none of the princes of this world knew: for had they known it, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory." Worldly power at its most decisive was at its most blind, and it executed the plan it was trying to stop. Paul has already said such wisdom and such rulers "come to nought," so the verdict is not that the world’s expertise is merely second-rate but that it is on a trajectory toward nothing. Every confident judgment made without the Spirit stands under the possibility of being that catastrophically wrong. "Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man" is often quoted as a sigh about how little we can know, but Paul’s next word overturns it: "But God hath revealed them unto us by his Spirit." The three avenues named — sight, hearing, imagination — cover the whole range of human discovery, and all three come up empty; the knowledge arrives instead as self-disclosure, because only "the Spirit of God" knows "the things of God" the way a man’s own spirit knows "the things of a man." Revelation here is not humanity climbing to a conclusion but God opening his own interior life to those he loves. "The natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned" explains why the same gospel lands as power on one hearer and absurdity on another, and it removes any grounds for smugness in those who believe, since what they have is something "freely given to us of God." Note also the grammar of the conclusion: it is "we have the mind of Christ," not I. The discernment Paul claims, and the statement that "he that is spiritual judgeth all things," is spoken in the plural to a congregation he is in the middle of correcting — a possession of the body, not a private trump card to be played against it. And I, brethren, when I came to you, came not with excellency of speech or of wisdom, declaring unto you the testimony of God. For I determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified. And I was with you in weakness, and in fear, and in much trembling. And my speech and my preaching was not with enticing words of man’s wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power: That your faith should not stand in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God. Howbeit we speak wisdom among them that are perfect: yet not the wisdom of this world, nor of the princes of this world, that come to nought: But we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, even the hidden wisdom, which God ordained before the world unto our glory: Which none of the princes of this world knew: for had they known it, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory. But as it is written, Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared for them that love him. But God hath revealed them unto us by his Spirit: for the Spirit searcheth all things, yea, the deep things of God. For what man knoweth the things of a man, save the spirit of man which is in him? even so the things of God knoweth no man, but the Spirit of God. Now we have received, not the spirit of the world, but the spirit which is of God; that we might know the things that are freely given to us of God. Which things also we speak, not in the words which man’s wisdom teacheth, but which the Holy Ghost teacheth; comparing spiritual things with spiritual. But the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned. But he that is spiritual judgeth all things, yet he himself is judged of no man. For who hath known the mind of the Lord, that he may instruct him? But we have the mind of Christ.

label: 1 Corinthians 3
text: Paul has already named the Corinthian factions; here he diagnoses them. He tells them he "could not speak unto you as unto spiritual, but as unto carnal, even as unto babes in Christ," having fed them "with milk, and not with meat" because they were not able to bear it — "neither yet now are ye able." The proof of their infancy is not ignorance of doctrine but the temper of their common life: "whereas there is among you envying, and strife, and divisions, are ye not carnal, and walk as men?" Party slogans are the symptom, and Paul takes the first of them as his own indictment: "while one saith, I am of Paul; and another, I am of Apollos; are ye not carnal?" His answer deflates both names at once — "Who then is Paul, and who is Apollos, but ministers by whom ye believed, even as the Lord gave to every man?" — and then supplies the image that governs the rest of the chapter: "I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase." Because growth belongs to God, "neither is he that planteth any thing, neither he that watereth," yet the workers are not thereby erased; they "are one," and "every man shall receive his own reward according to his own labour." The field turns into a construction site: "ye are God’s husbandry, ye are God’s building." Paul describes himself as "a wise masterbuilder" who has "laid the foundation, and another buildeth thereon," with a warning attached — "let every man take heed how he buildeth thereupon" — since "other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ." What is built on that foundation will be sorted by fire: some raise "gold, silver, precious stones," others "wood, hay, stubble," and "the day shall declare it, because it shall be revealed by fire; and the fire shall try every man’s work of what sort it is." Work that abides earns "a reward"; work that burns means real loss, "but he himself shall be saved; yet so as by fire." The building then proves to be a sanctuary: "Know ye not that ye are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwelleth in you?" — and the party spirit tearing at that community is no small matter, for "if any man defile the temple of God, him shall God destroy; for the temple of God is holy, which temple ye are." Paul closes by inverting the very thing the factions were competing over. "Let no man deceive himself. If any man among you seemeth to be wise in this world, let him become a fool, that he may be wise," because "the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God," as the scriptures testify: "He taketh the wise in their own craftiness," and "The Lord knoweth the thoughts of the wise, that they are vain." The conclusion turns their arithmetic inside out — they had been dividing themselves up among teachers, when in fact "all things are yours; Whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, or the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come; all are yours; And ye are Christ’s; and Christ is God’s." Spiritual maturity is measured here by how a community behaves, not by how much it knows. Paul calls the Corinthians "carnal" and "babes in Christ" and names the evidence plainly: "envying, and strife, and divisions." They are not accused of heresy or immorality at this point, only of factionalism — which turns out to be enough. To "walk as men" is to run a church by the ordinary logic of rival loyalties and personalities, and Paul treats that as a diet problem: people still on "milk, and not with meat" cannot digest the deeper teaching, and the reason is moral rather than intellectual. The chapter dismantles celebrity ministry without dismissing ministers. "Who then is Paul, and who is Apollos, but ministers by whom ye believed" strips the names of any claim to be sources; "I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase" locates all fruitfulness in God alone. Yet the same passage refuses to make the workers irrelevant: they "are one," not competitors, they are "labourers together with God," and "every man shall receive his own reward according to his own labour." Genuine human effort is real and will be genuinely rewarded, precisely because it is not the cause of the growth and therefore has nothing to protect. There is exactly one foundation and unlimited responsibility for what is raised on it. "Other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ" closes the question of the church’s basis permanently, but that settled foundation makes the next sentence more urgent rather than less: "let every man take heed how he buildeth thereupon." The contrast between "gold, silver, precious stones" and "wood, hay, stubble" is not a contrast between true and false religion — all of it is built on Christ — but between work that survives testing and work that does not. Being on the right foundation is no guarantee of building well. Judgment is described as revelation before it is described as punishment. "Every man’s work shall be made manifest: for the day shall declare it, because it shall be revealed by fire; and the fire shall try every man’s work of what sort it is." The fire is an assayer, not primarily an executioner; its function is to show "of what sort" the work is. And the outcome for the builder whose work fails is stated with striking restraint — "he shall suffer loss: but he himself shall be saved; yet so as by fire." Real loss and real salvation are held together in a single verse, which is why this text has carried so much weight in later argument about what happens to a saved person’s unworthy work. The community itself is the sanctuary, and damaging it is sacrilege. "Know ye not that ye are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwelleth in you?" is addressed to a whole congregation in the plural, so the temple in view is the assembled church before it is the individual believer. That is what raises the stakes of mere partisanship to "If any man defile the temple of God, him shall God destroy." Faction-building is not a matter of poor manners in a voluntary society; it is defacing a holy place, and the reason given is simply what the place is: "the temple of God is holy, which temple ye are." The remedy for competitive wisdom is a deliberate self-emptying. "If any man among you seemeth to be wise in this world, let him become a fool, that he may be wise" asks for a real surrender of standing, not a rhetorical pose, and it is grounded in a verdict already rendered: "the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God." The chapter’s final turn then exposes how small the factions had made themselves. In claiming a teacher they had been dividing an inheritance that was already entirely theirs — "all things are yours; Whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, or the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come" — and the whole chain is anchored where boasting cannot reach: "ye are Christ’s; and Christ is God’s." And I, brethren, could not speak unto you as unto spiritual, but as unto carnal, even as unto babes in Christ. I have fed you with milk, and not with meat: for hitherto ye were not able to bear it, neither yet now are ye able. For ye are yet carnal: for whereas there is among you envying, and strife, and divisions, are ye not carnal, and walk as men? For while one saith, I am of Paul; and another, I am of Apollos; are ye not carnal? Who then is Paul, and who is Apollos, but ministers by whom ye believed, even as the Lord gave to every man? I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase. So then neither is he that planteth any thing, neither he that watereth; but God that giveth the increase. Now he that planteth and he that watereth are one: and every man shall receive his own reward according to his own labour. For we are labourers together with God: ye are God’s husbandry, ye are God’s building. According to the grace of God which is given unto me, as a wise masterbuilder, I have laid the foundation, and another buildeth thereon. But let every man take heed how he buildeth thereupon. For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ. Now if any man build upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, stubble; Every man’s work shall be made manifest: for the day shall declare it, because it shall be revealed by fire; and the fire shall try every man’s work of what sort it is. If any man’s work abide which he hath built thereupon, he shall receive a reward. If any man’s work shall be burned, he shall suffer loss: but he himself shall be saved; yet so as by fire. Know ye not that ye are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwelleth in you? If any man defile the temple of God, him shall God destroy; for the temple of God is holy, which temple ye are. Let no man deceive himself. If any man among you seemeth to be wise in this world, let him become a fool, that he may be wise. For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. For it is written, He taketh the wise in their own craftiness. And again, The Lord knoweth the thoughts of the wise, that they are vain. Therefore let no man glory in men. For all things are yours; Whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, or the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come; all are yours; And ye are Christ’s; and Christ is God’s.

label: 1 Corinthians 4
text: Paul closes his argument against the Corinthian party spirit by fixing the apostles in their proper place: "Let a man so account of us, as of the ministers of Christ, and stewards of the mysteries of God." A steward owns nothing and answers to his master, so only one demand is made of him — "Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful." That single standard dissolves the habit of ranking teachers, and Paul refuses the Corinthians' verdict and even his own: "with me it is a very small thing that I should be judged of you, or of man’s judgment: yea, I judge not mine own self." A clean conscience settles nothing, since "I know nothing by myself; yet am I not hereby justified: but he that judgeth me is the Lord." The real verdict waits — "judge nothing before the time, until the Lord come, who both will bring to light the hidden things of darkness, and will make manifest the counsels of the hearts: and then shall every man have praise of God." Paul then names his method, that "these things, brethren, I have in a figure transferred to myself and to Apollos for your sakes; that ye might learn in us not to think of men above that which is written, that no one of you be puffed up for one against another," and drives at the root of the factions with three questions: "who maketh thee to differ from another? and what hast thou that thou didst not receive? now if thou didst receive it, why dost thou glory, as if thou hadst not received it?" Everything they boast in arrived as a gift, so the boasting is incoherent. Irony follows — "Now ye are full, now ye are rich, ye have reigned as kings without us: and I would to God ye did reign, that we also might reign with you" — and against that imagined enthronement Paul sets the apostles' actual position, "last, as it were appointed to death: for we are made a spectacle unto the world, and to angels, and to men." The contrast is laid out in pairs: "We are fools for Christ’s sake, but ye are wise in Christ; we are weak, but ye are strong; ye are honourable, but we are despised." The catalogue that follows is physical and unglamorous — they "hunger, and thirst, and are naked, and are buffeted, and have no certain dwellingplace," they "labour, working with our own hands," and their response to hostility reverses it: "being reviled, we bless; being persecuted, we suffer it: Being defamed, we intreat," until they are "made as the filth of the world, and are the offscouring of all things unto this day." Then the tone turns paternal. "I write not these things to shame you, but as my beloved sons I warn you. For though ye have ten thousand instructers in Christ, yet have ye not many fathers: for in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the gospel." On that ground alone he can say "be ye followers of me," and he sends Timotheus, "my beloved son, and faithful in the Lord," to "bring you into remembrance of my ways which be in Christ, as I teach every where in every church." To those "puffed up, as though I would not come to you," he promises a visit that will test substance rather than rhetoric: "I will come to you shortly, if the Lord will, and will know, not the speech of them which are puffed up, but the power. For the kingdom of God is not in word, but in power." The chapter ends by handing them the choice: "What will ye? shall I come unto you with a rod, or in love, and in the spirit of meekness?" Ministry is defined here by stewardship rather than by ownership or celebrity. Paul asks only that he be accounted one of "the ministers of Christ, and stewards of the mysteries of God," and a steward is by definition handling what belongs to someone else. That is why the measure applied to him is not eloquence, results, or popularity but a single quality — "it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful." The Corinthians were grading their teachers like patrons grading orators; Paul answers that the goods were never his to be praised for, and that the only relevant question about a steward is whether he was true to the master's intent with the master's property. The chapter installs a deliberate reserve about verdicts, including verdicts on oneself. Paul treats the church's opinion of him as "a very small thing," and then goes further: "yea, I judge not mine own self. For I know nothing by myself; yet am I not hereby justified." A quiet conscience is evidence, not acquittal, because self-knowledge is partial and the court is not one's own. The instruction that follows — "judge nothing before the time, until the Lord come" — is not a ban on discernment, since Paul issues sharp judgments a chapter later, but a ban on premature final verdicts about persons whose hidden motives only God can read. Notably, the outcome he expects from that disclosure is generous: "then shall every man have praise of God." The three questions of verse seven cut the nerve of every rivalry in the letter: "who maketh thee to differ from another? and what hast thou that thou didst not receive? now if thou didst receive it, why dost thou glory, as if thou hadst not received it?" Paul does not deny that the Corinthians have real gifts, real teachers, and real knowledge. He denies that any of it originated with them. Boasting in a gift is a category error, treating a received thing as an achievement, and once that is seen, being "puffed up for one against another" collapses on its own without needing any further argument. Paul's irony exposes a church that thinks it has already arrived. "Now ye are full, now ye are rich, ye have reigned as kings without us" describes a community living as though the age of glory had come early, and his wistful reply — "I would to God ye did reign, that we also might reign with you" — concedes the hope while denying the timing. The apostolic reality is the opposite shape: "last, as it were appointed to death," a "spectacle unto the world, and to angels, and to men," hungry, homeless, "the offscouring of all things." The pattern of authentic ministry is cruciform, and the sign of it is the reversal in their conduct — "being reviled, we bless; being persecuted, we suffer it: Being defamed, we intreat." Against a market of teachers Paul asserts a relationship that cannot be duplicated: "though ye have ten thousand instructers in Christ, yet have ye not many fathers: for in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the gospel." Instruction can be shopped for, but the one through whom the gospel first gave them life stands in a different relation entirely, which is why he can follow it with "be ye followers of me" without arrogance. The fatherhood is exercised as warning rather than shaming — "I write not these things to shame you, but as my beloved sons I warn you" — and it is handed on through a person, Timotheus, who will "bring you into remembrance of my ways which be in Christ, as I teach every where in every church." The content taught at Corinth is not a local variant but the same teaching given everywhere. The closing test is between talk and reality: "I will come to you shortly, if the Lord will, and will know, not the speech of them which are puffed up, but the power. For the kingdom of God is not in word, but in power." In a city that prized rhetorical display, Paul says the kingdom will be audited by what it actually effects, not by how impressively it is described. The final question leaves the outcome with the Corinthians rather than with him — "shall I come unto you with a rod, or in love, and in the spirit of meekness?" — so that even apostolic discipline is presented as something their own response determines. Let a man so account of us, as of the ministers of Christ, and stewards of the mysteries of God. Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful. But with me it is a very small thing that I should be judged of you, or of man’s judgment: yea, I judge not mine own self. For I know nothing by myself; yet am I not hereby justified: but he that judgeth me is the Lord. Therefore judge nothing before the time, until the Lord come, who both will bring to light the hidden things of darkness, and will make manifest the counsels of the hearts: and then shall every man have praise of God. And these things, brethren, I have in a figure transferred to myself and to Apollos for your sakes; that ye might learn in us not to think of men above that which is written, that no one of you be puffed up for one against another. For who maketh thee to differ from another? and what hast thou that thou didst not receive? now if thou didst receive it, why dost thou glory, as if thou hadst not received it? Now ye are full, now ye are rich, ye have reigned as kings without us: and I would to God ye did reign, that we also might reign with you. For I think that God hath set forth us the apostles last, as it were appointed to death: for we are made a spectacle unto the world, and to angels, and to men. We are fools for Christ’s sake, but ye are wise in Christ; we are weak, but ye are strong; ye are honourable, but we are despised. Even unto this present hour we both hunger, and thirst, and are naked, and are buffeted, and have no certain dwellingplace; And labour, working with our own hands: being reviled, we bless; being persecuted, we suffer it: Being defamed, we intreat: we are made as the filth of the world, and are the offscouring of all things unto this day. I write not these things to shame you, but as my beloved sons I warn you. For though ye have ten thousand instructers in Christ, yet have ye not many fathers: for in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the gospel. Wherefore I beseech you, be ye followers of me. For this cause have I sent unto you Timotheus, who is my beloved son, and faithful in the Lord, who shall bring you into remembrance of my ways which be in Christ, as I teach every where in every church. Now some are puffed up, as though I would not come to you. But I will come to you shortly, if the Lord will, and will know, not the speech of them which are puffed up, but the power. For the kingdom of God is not in word, but in power. What will ye? shall I come unto you with a rod, or in love, and in the spirit of meekness?

label: 1 Corinthians 5
text: Paul turns from the parties and personalities of the first four chapters to a scandal that had become public knowledge: "It is reported commonly that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as is not so much as named among the Gentiles, that one should have his father’s wife." The offense is measured against pagan Corinth itself and found to exceed it. What appalls Paul as much as the deed is the congregation's posture toward it — "And ye are puffed up, and have not rather mourned, that he that hath done this deed might be taken away from among you." A community that should be in grief is instead inflated, and their self-satisfaction is treated as the deeper disease. Paul then renders a verdict at a distance: "For I verily, as absent in body, but present in spirit, have judged already, as though I were present, concerning him that hath so done this deed," and directs an action to be carried out "In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, when ye are gathered together, and my spirit, with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ, To deliver such an one unto Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus." The sentence is severe and its stated aim is rescue. He then reaches for a proverb and a feast: "Your glorying is not good. Know ye not that a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump? Purge out therefore the old leaven, that ye may be a new lump, as ye are unleavened. For even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us: Therefore let us keep the feast, not with old leaven, neither with the leaven of malice and wickedness; but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth." A previous letter had evidently been misread, and Paul corrects it: "I wrote unto you in an epistle not to company with fornicators: Yet not altogether with the fornicators of this world, or with the covetous, or extortioners, or with idolaters; for then must ye needs go out of the world." The line he is drawing runs inside the community, not around it: "But now I have written unto you not to keep company, if any man that is called a brother be a fornicator, or covetous, or an idolater, or a railer, or a drunkard, or an extortioner; with such an one no not to eat." The principle of jurisdiction follows — "For what have I to do to judge them also that are without? do not ye judge them that are within? But them that are without God judgeth" — and the chapter closes by putting an old command from Israel's law into the mouth of the church: "Therefore put away from among yourselves that wicked person." The chapter's sharpest rebuke is aimed at the congregation rather than at the offender. Paul states the sin in a single sentence and then spends the rest of the chapter on the church's reaction to it: "And ye are puffed up, and have not rather mourned." Tolerance here is not presented as generosity but as a species of pride, a community so pleased with its own broad-mindedness that it cannot feel the injury done in its midst. The prescribed emotion is grief — the man "might be taken away from among you" is stated as the thing they should have been mourning toward, not a punishment they should have been eager to inflict. Discipline that does not begin in mourning has already gone wrong. The severity of the sentence is bounded by its purpose. "To deliver such an one unto Satan for the destruction of the flesh" is as harsh a phrase as Paul writes anywhere, and it is immediately given a redemptive end: "that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus." Exclusion is aimed at the man's salvation, not at the community's comfort or its reputation. This makes the measure medicinal rather than merely punitive, and it supplies the test by which any later act of the same kind must be judged: a discipline that has stopped hoping for the offender's restoration is no longer doing what Paul is doing here. "Know ye not that a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump?" refuses the notion that serious sin can be a private matter within a body. The image is not of contagion by proximity but of a small quantity working invisibly through everything it touches, so that the question is never whether one man's conduct affects the whole but only how long the working takes. The corporate framing runs through the whole chapter — the church is a "lump," a "feast," a body that eats together — and it is why the remedy is corporate too, carried out "when ye are gathered together." The Passover imagery grounds the command in something already accomplished rather than in something to be achieved. "Purge out therefore the old leaven, that ye may be a new lump, as ye are unleavened" holds an imperative and an indicative in the same breath: become what you already are. The reason given is not the community's effort but a completed sacrifice — "For even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us" — and the resulting life is described as an ongoing festival: "Therefore let us keep the feast... with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth." Holiness is presented as feasting rather than as fasting, the natural conduct of people for whom the deliverance has already happened. Paul's correction of his earlier letter dismantles the instinct to withdraw from the world. He had written "not to company with fornicators," and someone had taken this as a program of separation from ordinary society; his answer is almost impatient — "for then must ye needs go out of the world." The boundary he is drawing runs through the church, not around it, applying to "any man that is called a brother." The claim to the name is precisely what makes the conduct a matter for the community, and its absence is precisely what puts the outsider beyond its reach. The list of disqualifying sins quietly widens the scope past the scandal that prompted it. Alongside the fornicator stand "the covetous, or an idolater, or a railer, or a drunkard, or an extortioner" — greed, abusive speech, and drunkenness placed in the same sentence as a sexual sin so notorious that pagans would not name it. A church willing to act on the spectacular offense and untroubled by the covetous man or the railer in good standing has not learned this chapter. Paul's final principle guards the other flank as well: "what have I to do to judge them also that are without? do not ye judge them that are within? But them that are without God judgeth." The community's competence is over its own members, and outsiders are left to a judgment that is not the church's to pronounce. It is reported commonly that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as is not so much as named among the Gentiles, that one should have his father’s wife. And ye are puffed up, and have not rather mourned, that he that hath done this deed might be taken away from among you. For I verily, as absent in body, but present in spirit, have judged already, as though I were present, concerning him that hath so done this deed, In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, when ye are gathered together, and my spirit, with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ, To deliver such an one unto Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus. Your glorying is not good. Know ye not that a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump? Purge out therefore the old leaven, that ye may be a new lump, as ye are unleavened. For even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us: Therefore let us keep the feast, not with old leaven, neither with the leaven of malice and wickedness; but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. I wrote unto you in an epistle not to company with fornicators: Yet not altogether with the fornicators of this world, or with the covetous, or extortioners, or with idolaters; for then must ye needs go out of the world. But now I have written unto you not to keep company, if any man that is called a brother be a fornicator, or covetous, or an idolater, or a railer, or a drunkard, or an extortioner; with such an one no not to eat. For what have I to do to judge them also that are without? do not ye judge them that are within? But them that are without God judgeth. Therefore put away from among yourselves that wicked person.

label: 1 Corinthians 6
text: Paul moves from the scandal of the previous chapter to two further failures that expose the same underlying problem: a congregation that has forgotten what it is. First the lawsuits. “Dare any of you, having a matter against another, go to law before the unjust, and not before the saints?” The issue is not that the Corinthians have grievances but where they are carrying them. Paul argues backward from the end of history to the present quarrel — “Do ye not know that the saints shall judge the world?” and “Know ye not that we shall judge angels?” — so that a people appointed to share in the final judgment are asked why they are “unworthy to judge the smallest matters” and “things that pertain to this life.” The sarcasm is deliberate: rather than drag the family quarrel before pagan magistrates, better to “set them to judge who are least esteemed in the church,” because “I speak to your shame. Is it so, that there is not a wise man among you? no, not one that shall be able to judge between his brethren?” Then Paul steps past the procedural question to the spiritual one, and the verdict falls on winner and loser alike: “Now therefore there is utterly a fault among you, because ye go to law one with another. Why do ye not rather take wrong? why do ye not rather suffer yourselves to be defrauded?” The lawsuits are not merely undignified; they are the visible edge of something worse — “Nay, ye do wrong, and defraud, and that your brethren.” That charge opens into a catalogue of the life the Corinthians have supposedly left behind: “Know ye not that the unrighteous shall not inherit the kingdom of God? Be not deceived,” and then the list of fornicators, idolaters, adulterers, thieves, covetous, drunkards, revilers, and extortioners, none of whom “shall inherit the kingdom of God.” The sentence that follows is the hinge of the chapter: “And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God.” From that new identity Paul answers a Corinthian slogan he quotes back at them twice: “All things are lawful unto me, but all things are not expedient: all things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of any.” Their argument seems to have run from appetite to appetite — “Meats for the belly, and the belly for meats” — as though the body were a temporary instrument whose use is morally weightless. Paul cuts the analogy: “the body is not for fornication, but for the Lord; and the Lord for the body,” and he anchors that claim in the resurrection, since “God hath both raised up the Lord, and will also raise up us by his own power.” The body has a future, so it has a meaning. What follows is startlingly concrete: “Know ye not that your bodies are the members of Christ? shall I then take the members of Christ, and make them the members of an harlot? God forbid.” Union is the category, and Paul reaches back to Eden for it — “he which is joined to an harlot is one body? for two, saith he, shall be one flesh” — set against its opposite, “But he that is joined unto the Lord is one spirit.” Hence the single imperative of the section: “Flee fornication. Every sin that a man doeth is without the body; but he that committeth fornication sinneth against his own body.” The chapter closes by naming what the body actually is and to whom it belongs: “know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own? For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God’s.” Paul settles the lawsuit question by an appeal to identity rather than to procedure. He never says the Corinthians' grievances are imaginary or that justice does not matter; he says they have misjudged who they are. A community told that “the saints shall judge the world” and even that “we shall judge angels” has been handed an astonishing eschatological vocation, and it is precisely that vocation which makes the current spectacle absurd — people destined for the assize of the world confessing themselves “unworthy to judge the smallest matters.” The withering suggestion to “set them to judge who are least esteemed in the church” is not contempt for the humble but a measure of how low the bar is: the least member of a Spirit-indwelt body should outstrip a pagan tribunal for the purpose at hand. What the church is in Christ ought to determine how it handles its own disputes. The deepest indictment in the first half of the chapter is aimed at the litigant who is in the right. “Now therefore there is utterly a fault among you, because ye go to law one with another” means that the mere existence of the suit is already the defeat, whatever the verdict. Then come two questions that cut against every instinct of self-protection: “Why do ye not rather take wrong? why do ye not rather suffer yourselves to be defrauded?” Paul is not abolishing justice but describing a freedom that can afford to absorb a loss, because the one who was defrauded of everything is the pattern. And he refuses to let the injured party feel comfortable for long, since the very next line turns the accusation around — “Nay, ye do wrong, and defraud, and that your brethren” — a reminder that in most church conflicts the roles of victim and offender are not as cleanly distributed as either side believes. The vice list is framed by two safeguards that must be held together. On one side stands a plain warning — “Know ye not that the unrighteous shall not inherit the kingdom of God? Be not deceived” — addressed not to outsiders but to baptized members of a church, which means Paul thinks self-deception on this point is a live danger inside the assembly. On the other side stands the most gracious sentence in the chapter: “And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God.” The tense matters. Those categories are the Corinthians' past, not their name, and the three verbs pile up as accomplished facts done to them rather than achievements produced by them. Moral seriousness and assurance are not rivals here; the warning has force only because something real has already happened. “All things are lawful unto me, but all things are not expedient: all things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of any.” Paul quotes the Corinthian slogan and then fences it twice, and the two fences are different. The first is about benefit: liberty is measured by what it builds, not by what it permits. The second is about mastery: a freedom that ends in being owned by the thing you were free to take has already stopped being freedom. This is the practical answer to every argument that begins with “I am allowed.” Permission is the lowest possible standard for a Christian decision, and a person who can only ask whether something is forbidden has already surrendered the initiative to whatever appetite is doing the asking. The Corinthian argument appears to have run through the stomach — “Meats for the belly, and the belly for meats” — treating physical acts as morally indifferent because the flesh is passing away. Paul concedes the transience and denies the conclusion: “God shall destroy both it and them. Now the body is not for fornication, but for the Lord; and the Lord for the body.” The reason the analogy fails is the resurrection: “God hath both raised up the Lord, and will also raise up us by his own power.” Because the body is destined to be raised rather than discarded, it is not a neutral container for a soul that alone matters. This is the sharpest possible rebuke to every spirituality, ancient or modern, that treats what is done in the body as irrelevant to what is happening to the person. The chapter's last movement makes sexual union a question of belonging rather than of rules. “Know ye not that your bodies are the members of Christ?” makes the believer's body already spoken for, so that joining it to a harlot is not merely a private transaction but a wrenching of what belongs to Christ — and Paul's “God forbid” is the reaction of someone describing sacrilege, not impropriety. He grounds it in the creation account, since “he which is joined to an harlot is one body? for two, saith he, shall be one flesh,” which means the act performs a union whether or not the participants intend one. Against that stands “But he that is joined unto the Lord is one spirit,” and from the contrast comes the only strategy offered: “Flee fornication” — not resist, not manage, but leave. The final ground is ownership and indwelling together: “your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own? For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God’s.” The body is consecrated ground and purchased property, and the conclusion is positive rather than merely prohibitive — glorify God with it. Dare any of you, having a matter against another, go to law before the unjust, and not before the saints? Do ye not know that the saints shall judge the world? and if the world shall be judged by you, are ye unworthy to judge the smallest matters? Know ye not that we shall judge angels? how much more things that pertain to this life? If then ye have judgments of things pertaining to this life, set them to judge who are least esteemed in the church. I speak to your shame. Is it so, that there is not a wise man among you? no, not one that shall be able to judge between his brethren? But brother goeth to law with brother, and that before the unbelievers.
