Let all things be done decently and in order." One criterion runs through the entire chapter and settles every question in it: does the assembly understand, and is it built up. Paul states it as a command — "seek that ye may excel to the edifying of the church" — and repeats it as the rule over the whole gathering, "Let all things be done unto edifying." Intelligibility is not a concession to the slow or the unspiritual; it is the criterion by which a genuine gift is evaluated in public. The trumpet image makes the stakes plain, since "if the trumpet give an uncertain sound, who shall prepare himself to the battle?" A signal nobody can read is not a superior signal but a failed one. Paul never prohibits tongues; he ranks and regulates them, and he is scrupulous about saying so at both ends of the argument. He opens with "I would that ye all spake with tongues," claims "I thank my God, I speak with tongues more than ye all," and closes with the direct command "forbid not to speak with tongues." What he denies is that a private benefit is automatically a public one, since "he that speaketh in an unknown tongue edifieth himself; but he that prophesieth edifieth the church." His own arithmetic is the sharpest statement of the ratio: "five words with my understanding" in the assembly are worth more than "ten thousand words in an unknown tongue." Corporate worship is assessed by how it lands on the person who does not yet belong. Paul introduces two outsiders — the "unlearned" who cannot "say Amen at thy giving of thanks, seeing he understandeth not what thou sayest," and the unbeliever who walks in off the street — and the two outcomes he sketches could not be further apart. Untranslated ecstasy produces the verdict "ye are mad"; comprehensible prophecy produces conviction so exact that "the secrets of his heart made manifest," ending with a man "falling down on his face" to "worship God, and report that God is in you of a truth." A church's meeting is therefore a public act with evangelistic consequences, and self-absorbed worship forfeits them. Inspiration, in Paul's account, does not suspend the speaker's responsibility. His rule that "the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets" means the gift is under the control of the person who has it, which is why he can command a prophet mid-flow to "hold his peace" when "any thing be revealed to another that sitteth by," cap tongues at "two, or at the most by three," and impose silence where there is no interpreter. This removes the standard excuse for disorder. Nobody at Corinth could plead that the Spirit had overridden them, because the Spirit does not produce what "God is not the author of" — namely "confusion." Prophecy is also placed under judgement rather than accepted uncritically: "Let the prophets speak two or three, and let the other judge." A word claimed as revelation is to be weighed by the assembly, not received simply because it was delivered with confidence. Paired with the discerning of spirits named in the previous chapter, this establishes that the New Testament expects inspired speech to be tested in public, which is as much a protection of the congregation as it is a discipline on the speaker. The order Paul imposes is theological rather than merely administrative, and it is deliberately not a demand for silence. He grounds it in God's own character, "God is not the author of confusion, but of peace," appeals beyond Corinth to the practice of "all churches of the saints," and punctures their sense of being a special case with "came the word of God out from you? or came it unto you only?" Yet the same passage envisions a meeting where "every one of you hath a psalm, hath a doctrine, hath a tongue, hath a revelation" and where "ye may all prophesy one by one, that all may learn, and all may be comforted." The final rule, "Let all things be done decently and in order," is stated positively for that reason: the regulation exists to make broad participation possible, not to shut it down. Follow after charity, and desire spiritual gifts, but rather that ye may prophesy. For he that speaketh in an unknown tongue speaketh not unto men, but unto God: for no man understandeth him; howbeit in the spirit he speaketh mysteries. But he that prophesieth speaketh unto men to edification, and exhortation, and comfort. He that speaketh in an unknown tongue edifieth himself; but he that prophesieth edifieth the church. I would that ye all spake with tongues, but rather that ye prophesied: for greater is he that prophesieth than he that speaketh with tongues, except he interpret, that the church may receive edifying. Now, brethren, if I come unto you speaking with tongues, what shall I profit you, except I shall speak to you either by revelation, or by knowledge, or by prophesying, or by doctrine? And even things without life giving sound, whether pipe or harp, except they give a distinction in the sounds, how shall it be known what is piped or harped? For if the trumpet give an uncertain sound, who shall prepare himself to the battle? So likewise ye, except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken? for ye shall speak into the air. There are, it may be, so many kinds of voices in the world, and none of them is without signification. Therefore if I know not the meaning of the voice, I shall be unto him that speaketh a barbarian, and he that speaketh shall be a barbarian unto me. Even so ye, forasmuch as ye are zealous of spiritual gifts, seek that ye may excel to the edifying of the church. Wherefore let him that speaketh in an unknown tongue pray that he may interpret. For if I pray in an unknown tongue, my spirit prayeth, but my understanding is unfruitful. What is it then? I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the understanding also: I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the understanding also. Else when thou shalt bless with the spirit, how shall he that occupieth the room of the unlearned say Amen at thy giving of thanks, seeing he understandeth not what thou sayest? For thou verily givest thanks well, but the other is not edified. I thank my God, I speak with tongues more than ye all: Yet in the church I had rather speak five words with my understanding, that by my voice I might teach others also, than ten thousand words in an unknown tongue. Brethren, be not children in understanding: howbeit in malice be ye children, but in understanding be men. In the law it is written, With men of other tongues and other lips will I speak unto this people; and yet for all that will they not hear me, saith the Lord. Wherefore tongues are for a sign, not to them that believe, but to them that believe not: but prophesying serveth not for them that believe not, but for them which believe. If therefore the whole church be come together into one place, and all speak with tongues, and there come in those that are unlearned, or unbelievers, will they not say that ye are mad? But if all prophesy, and there come in one that believeth not, or one unlearned, he is convinced of all, he is judged of all: And thus are the secrets of his heart made manifest; and so falling down on his face he will worship God, and report that God is in you of a truth. How is it then, brethren? when ye come together, every one of you hath a psalm, hath a doctrine, hath a tongue, hath a revelation, hath an interpretation. Let all things be done unto edifying. If any man speak in an unknown tongue, let it be by two, or at the most by three, and that by course; and let one interpret. But if there be no interpreter, let him keep silence in the church; and let him speak to himself, and to God. Let the prophets speak two or three, and let the other judge. If any thing be revealed to another that sitteth by, let the first hold his peace. For ye may all prophesy one by one, that all may learn, and all may be comforted. And the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets. For God is not the author of confusion, but of peace, as in all churches of the saints. Let your women keep silence in the churches: for it is not permitted unto them to speak; but they are commanded to be under obedience, as also saith the law. And if they will learn any thing, let them ask their husbands at home: for it is a shame for women to speak in the church. What? came the word of God out from you? or came it unto you only? If any man think himself to be a prophet, or spiritual, let him acknowledge that the things that I write unto you are the commandments of the Lord. But if any man be ignorant, let him be ignorant. Wherefore, brethren, covet to prophesy, and forbid not to speak with tongues. Let all things be done decently and in order.

label: 1 Corinthians 15
text: Paul turns from disorder in the assembly to the foundation underneath everything he has argued, reminding the Corinthians of “the gospel which I preached unto you, which also ye have received, and wherein ye stand,” by which they are saved “if ye keep in memory what I preached unto you, unless ye have believed in vain.” What he hands on he first received: “how that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures; And that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures.” Then the witnesses are counted out one after another — “seen of Cephas, then of the twelve,” “of above five hundred brethren at once; of whom the greater part remain unto this present,” “of James; then of all the apostles,” and “last of all he was seen of me also, as of one born out of due time,” by a man who calls himself “the least of the apostles” because “I persecuted the church of God,” yet who can say “by the grace of God I am what I am.” Only then does the problem surface: “how say some among you that there is no resurrection of the dead?” Paul runs that denial to its end without softening it. “If there be no resurrection of the dead, then is Christ not risen”; preaching is vain and faith is vain; the apostles are “found false witnesses of God”; “ye are yet in your sins”; those “fallen asleep in Christ are perished”; and “if in this life only we have hope in Christ, we are of all men most miserable.” Against that ruin he sets one sentence: “But now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept.” Two men are set head to head — “for as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive” — and an order is laid out: “Christ the firstfruits; afterward they that are Christ’s at his coming,” then “the end,” when the kingdom is delivered up and “all rule and all authority and power” put down, for “he must reign, till he hath put all enemies under his feet,” and “the last enemy that shall be destroyed is death,” until at last “God may be all in all.” Practical arguments follow in quick succession: the much-disputed “what shall they do which are baptized for the dead, if the dead rise not at all?”; Paul’s own exposure, “why stand we in jeopardy every hour?” and “I die daily”; his fight “with beasts at Ephesus”; and the only honest alternative if the grave is final, “let us eat and drink; for to morrow we die.” He breaks off into warning — “evil communications corrupt good manners” — and summons: “Awake to righteousness, and sin not; for some have not the knowledge of God: I speak this to your shame.” To the sceptic’s question, “How are the dead raised up? and with what body do they come?”, he answers with seed and starlight. What is sown “is not quickened, except it die,” and “thou sowest not that body that shall be, but bare grain,” while “God giveth it a body as it hath pleased him, and to every seed his own body.” As “one star differeth from another star in glory,” so the risen body differs from the buried one: “it is sown in corruption; it is raised in incorruption: It is sown in dishonour; it is raised in glory: it is sown in weakness; it is raised in power: It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body.” The two Adams frame the whole — “the first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam was made a quickening spirit,” “the first man is of the earth, earthy: the second man is the Lord from heaven” — and the promise is that “as we have borne the image of the earthy, we shall also bear the image of the heavenly.” The chapter ends in mystery and trumpet. “Flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God; neither doth corruption inherit incorruption,” yet “we shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed, In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump,” when “this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality,” and the old word comes true: “Death is swallowed up in victory. O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?” Because “the sting of death is sin; and the strength of sin is the law,” the thanks belong wholly to God “which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” — and the argument lands, characteristically, as a command to keep working: “be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.” Paul introduces the resurrection not as his insight but as a delivery: “I delivered unto you first of all that which I also received.” He presents himself as a link in a chain rather than an origin, and the content he passes on is already fixed and confessional in shape — died for our sins, was buried, rose the third day, was seen. That handing-on is what makes the gospel checkable: he can name Cephas, the twelve, James, “above five hundred brethren at once; of whom the greater part remain unto this present,” effectively inviting anyone who doubts to go and ask them. And it is not merely informational, since salvation is bound to holding it fast: they are saved “if ye keep in memory what I preached unto you, unless ye have believed in vain.” The chain of consequences in verses 13-19 refuses to let the resurrection be an optional appendix to Christian faith. If the dead are not raised, then Christ is not raised; if Christ is not raised, “then is our preaching vain, and your faith is also vain”; worse, the apostles are “found false witnesses of God,” not merely mistaken but slanderers of him. Most striking is what Paul says collapses next: “ye are yet in your sins.” Forgiveness is not something the cross secures independently of Easter and to which the resurrection merely adds confirmation. And the honest conclusion, if it were all untrue, is not a diminished but still admirable religion — it is that “we are of all men most miserable.” “Firstfruits” is a harvest word, and Paul leans on everything it implies: “now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept.” The first sheaf is not a different crop from the rest but the same crop arriving early, so Christ’s risen body is a specimen of what is promised rather than a unique exception to the rule of death. From this comes both a sequence — “Christ the firstfruits; afterward they that are Christ’s at his coming” — and a destination, since “the last enemy that shall be destroyed is death” and the reign of the Son ends not in his own aggrandizement but “that God may be all in all.” Christian hope here is not escape from embodiment but the abolition of the thing that ends embodied life. Asked “with what body do they come?” Paul neither retreats into a bodiless afterlife nor promises a mere resuscitation of the corpse. The seed answers both errors at once: “that which thou sowest is not quickened, except it die,” and “thou sowest not that body that shall be, but bare grain.” There is real continuity — the same seed, “to every seed his own body” — and real transformation, hammered out in four matched pairs: “sown in corruption... raised in incorruption... sown in dishonour... raised in glory... sown in weakness... raised in power... sown a natural body... raised a spiritual body.” The “spiritual body” is not a body made of spirit but a body wholly answerable to the Spirit, which is why “flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God” denies the survival of mortality, not of matter. The chapter’s anthropology is corporate before it is individual. Every human being is described as wearing a likeness received from another: “the first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam was made a quickening spirit,” and “as is the earthy, such are they also that are earthy: and as is the heavenly, such are they also that are heavenly.” Death is therefore not a private biological fact but an inheritance — “since by man came death, by man came also the resurrection of the dead” — and glory is likewise received rather than achieved: “as we have borne the image of the earthy, we shall also bear the image of the heavenly.” Solidarity with Adam is unchosen; solidarity with Christ is offered. The most abstract chapter Paul ever wrote ends with a work order. “Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.” The word “vain” has been the chapter’s refrain — preaching vain, faith vain, believing in vain — and it is now decisively negated on the other side. If the body has a future, then what is done in the body is not wasted motion, and the contrary slogan Paul quoted, “let us eat and drink; for to morrow we die,” is exposed as the only rational ethic for people with no resurrection. Doctrine here is not the opposite of practicality; it is what makes endurance reasonable. Moreover, brethren, I declare unto you the gospel which I preached unto you, which also ye have received, and wherein ye stand; By which also ye are saved, if ye keep in memory what I preached unto you, unless ye have believed in vain. For I delivered unto you first of all that which I also received, how that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures; And that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures: And that he was seen of Cephas, then of the twelve: After that, he was seen of above five hundred brethren at once; of whom the greater part remain unto this present, but some are fallen asleep. After that, he was seen of James; then of all the apostles. And last of all he was seen of me also, as of one born out of due time. For I am the least of the apostles, that am not meet to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God. But by the grace of God I am what I am: and his grace which was bestowed upon me was not in vain; but I laboured more abundantly than they all: yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me. Therefore whether it were I or they, so we preach, and so ye believed. Now if Christ be preached that he rose from the dead, how say some among you that there is no resurrection of the dead? But if there be no resurrection of the dead, then is Christ not risen: And if Christ be not risen, then is our preaching vain, and your faith is also vain. Yea, and we are found false witnesses of God; because we have testified of God that he raised up Christ: whom he raised not up, if so be that the dead rise not. For if the dead rise not, then is not Christ raised: And if Christ be not raised, your faith is vain; ye are yet in your sins. Then they also which are fallen asleep in Christ are perished. If in this life only we have hope in Christ, we are of all men most miserable. But now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept. For since by man came death, by man came also the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive. But every man in his own order: Christ the firstfruits; afterward they that are Christ’s at his coming. Then cometh the end, when he shall have delivered up the kingdom to God, even the Father; when he shall have put down all rule and all authority and power. For he must reign, till he hath put all enemies under his feet. The last enemy that shall be destroyed is death. For he hath put all things under his feet. But when he saith all things are put under him, it is manifest that he is excepted, which did put all things under him. And when all things shall be subdued unto him, then shall the Son also himself be subject unto him that put all things under him, that God may be all in all. Else what shall they do which are baptized for the dead, if the dead rise not at all? why are they then baptized for the dead? And why stand we in jeopardy every hour? I protest by your rejoicing which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord, I die daily. If after the manner of men I have fought with beasts at Ephesus, what advantageth it me, if the dead rise not? let us eat and drink; for to morrow we die. Be not deceived: evil communications corrupt good manners. Awake to righteousness, and sin not; for some have not the knowledge of God: I speak this to your shame. But some man will say, How are the dead raised up? and with what body do they come? Thou fool, that which thou sowest is not quickened, except it die: And that which thou sowest, thou sowest not that body that shall be, but bare grain, it may chance of wheat, or of some other grain: But God giveth it a body as it hath pleased him, and to every seed his own body. All flesh is not the same flesh: but there is one kind of flesh of men, another flesh of beasts, another of fishes, and another of birds. There are also celestial bodies, and bodies terrestrial: but the glory of the celestial is one, and the glory of the terrestrial is another. There is one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars: for one star differeth from another star in glory. So also is the resurrection of the dead. It is sown in corruption; it is raised in incorruption: It is sown in dishonour; it is raised in glory: it is sown in weakness; it is raised in power: It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. There is a natural body, and there is a spiritual body. And so it is written, The first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam was made a quickening spirit. Howbeit that was not first which is spiritual, but that which is natural; and afterward that which is spiritual. The first man is of the earth, earthy: the second man is the Lord from heaven. As is the earthy, such are they also that are earthy: and as is the heavenly, such are they also that are heavenly. And as we have borne the image of the earthy, we shall also bear the image of the heavenly. Now this I say, brethren, that flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God; neither doth corruption inherit incorruption. Behold, I shew you a mystery; We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed, In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump: for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed. For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality. So when this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and this mortal shall have put on immortality, then shall be brought to pass the saying that is written, Death is swallowed up in victory. O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory? The sting of death is sin; and the strength of sin is the law. But thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.

label: 1 Corinthians 16
text: One verse after the last trumpet, Paul is talking about money. “Now concerning the collection for the saints, as I have given order to the churches of Galatia, even so do ye” — and the order is unglamorously concrete: “Upon the first day of the week let every one of you lay by him in store, as God hath prospered him, that there be no gatherings when I come.” Everyone gives, the amount is proportioned to what each has received, the habit is weekly rather than impulsive, and the point of the discipline is that nothing be scrambled together at the last moment under the pressure of an apostle’s presence. Nor will Paul touch it alone: the Corinthians themselves will choose the couriers, “whomsoever ye shall approve by your letters,” to carry “your liberality unto Jerusalem,” and he will accompany them only “if it be meet that I go also.” Travel plans follow, held with open hands. He will come “when I shall pass through Macedonia”; he may “abide, yea, and winter with you”; he hopes “to tarry a while with you, if the Lord permit”; but for now “I will tarry at Ephesus until Pentecost,” and the reason he gives is both invitation and hazard in one breath: “For a great door and effectual is opened unto me, and there are many adversaries.” Then people. Timothy is commended to a congregation Paul evidently fears may bruise him — “see that he may be with you without fear: for he worketh the work of the Lord, as I also do. Let no man therefore despise him: but conduct him forth in peace” — and Apollos, whose name had been made a party banner at Corinth, is reported as freely declining: “I greatly desired him to come unto you with the brethren: but his will was not at all to come at this time.” Sixteen chapters of correction then compress into five short imperatives and one governing qualifier: “Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong. Let all your things be done with charity.” The household of Stephanas is held up as the pattern of the leadership the church actually needs, “the firstfruits of Achaia” who “have addicted themselves to the ministry of the saints,” and the congregation is told, “That ye submit yourselves unto such, and to every one that helpeth with us, and laboureth.” Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus have arrived and “refreshed my spirit and yours: therefore acknowledge ye them that are such.” Greetings come from “the churches of Asia” and from “Aquila and Priscilla... with the church that is in their house,” with the charge to “greet ye one another with an holy kiss.” Paul then takes the pen from the scribe — “the salutation of me Paul with mine own hand” — and in his own writing sets down a line of startling severity beside a word of longing: “If any man love not the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be Anathema Maranatha.” The letter that opened by rebuking a church split into factions closes without a single condition attached: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. My love be with you all in Christ Jesus. Amen.” The collection is administered with a care that borders on the bureaucratic, and that is deliberate. “Upon the first day of the week let every one of you lay by him in store, as God hath prospered him” makes giving universal, regular, and proportional rather than exceptional and emotional, while “that there be no gatherings when I come” removes the apostle’s personal pressure from the moment of giving. Most telling is the handling of the funds: the Corinthians choose the carriers, “whomsoever ye shall approve by your letters,” and Paul travels with them only if it seems fitting. A man who could have claimed unquestioned authority over the money instead builds a structure in which he is never alone with it. The day named is not incidental. Immediately after a chapter arguing that everything rests on Christ having “rose again the third day,” Paul assumes without explanation that “the first day of the week” is the natural rhythm of the Corinthians’ common life. The resurrection is not merely something they believe; it has already reshaped their calendar, so that the day the tomb was found empty is the day on which their charity is organized. Doctrine and habit are the same fabric here, which is why the transition from the last trumpet to a weekly envelope is not a change of subject. Paul’s plans are stated firmly and held loosely at once. He intends to winter at Corinth and to stay until Pentecost at Ephesus, yet everything is subordinated to “if the Lord permit.” And his reason for staying is a sentence that refuses the usual logic of guidance: “for a great door and effectual is opened unto me, and there are many adversaries.” The opposition is not evidence that the door is shut; the two arrive together, and the second clause is offered as part of the case for remaining rather than as a reason to leave. Two co-workers are handled in ways that quietly undo the party spirit the letter opened by attacking. Timothy, younger and evidently vulnerable at Corinth, is given apostolic cover — “see that he may be with you without fear... Let no man therefore despise him” — with the ground being simply that “he worketh the work of the Lord, as I also do.” Apollos, whose name some Corinthians had adopted as a faction label, is shown declining Paul’s own urging: “his will was not at all to come at this time.” Paul neither commands him nor resents him. The men the Corinthians were setting against each other are visibly not competing. The whole letter is compressed into five imperatives and then immediately qualified: “Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong. Let all your things be done with charity.” The four commands before it are vigilant, immovable, courageous, and strong — the vocabulary of a garrison — and the Corinthians were a church quite capable of being all four in the service of their own quarrels. The last sentence governs the rest. Not some of your things and not chiefly your religious things, but “all your things,” done in the manner set out earlier in the letter, where charity is what makes every gift worth having. Authority in the closing paragraph is grounded entirely in labour freely undertaken. The household of Stephanas “have addicted themselves to the ministry of the saints,” and precisely because of that the congregation is told to “submit yourselves unto such, and to every one that helpeth with us, and laboureth.” No title is mentioned, no appointment recounted; the claim rests on having given themselves away and having “refreshed my spirit and yours.” The instruction “acknowledge ye them that are such” makes recognition a duty owed by the church, not a favour granted — the exact inverse of a community that had been choosing its leaders by eloquence and preference. Now concerning the collection for the saints, as I have given order to the churches of Galatia, even so do ye. Upon the first day of the week let every one of you lay by him in store, as God hath prospered him, that there be no gatherings when I come. And when I come, whomsoever ye shall approve by your letters, them will I send to bring your liberality unto Jerusalem. And if it be meet that I go also, they shall go with me. Now I will come unto you, when I shall pass through Macedonia: for I do pass through Macedonia. And it may be that I will abide, yea, and winter with you, that ye may bring me on my journey whithersoever I go. For I will not see you now by the way; but I trust to tarry a while with you, if the Lord permit. But I will tarry at Ephesus until Pentecost. For a great door and effectual is opened unto me, and there are many adversaries. Now if Timotheus come, see that he may be with you without fear: for he worketh the work of the Lord, as I also do. Let no man therefore despise him: but conduct him forth in peace, that he may come unto me: for I look for him with the brethren. As touching our brother Apollos, I greatly desired him to come unto you with the brethren: but his will was not at all to come at this time; but he will come when he shall have convenient time. Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong. Let all your things be done with charity. I beseech you, brethren, (ye know the house of Stephanas, that it is the firstfruits of Achaia, and that they have addicted themselves to the ministry of the saints,) That ye submit yourselves unto such, and to every one that helpeth with us, and laboureth. I am glad of the coming of Stephanas and Fortunatus and Achaicus: for that which was lacking on your part they have supplied. For they have refreshed my spirit and yours: therefore acknowledge ye them that are such. The churches of Asia salute you. Aquila and Priscilla salute you much in the Lord, with the church that is in their house. All the brethren greet you. Greet ye one another with an holy kiss. The salutation of me Paul with mine own hand. If any man love not the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be Anathema Maranatha. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. My love be with you all in Christ Jesus. Amen.

label: 2 Corinthians 1
text: Paul writes as "an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, and Timothy our brother, unto the church of God which is at Corinth, with all the saints which are in all Achaia," and then does something he does not do in the first letter: instead of thanking God for his readers he blesses God outright — "Blessed be God, even the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies, and the God of all comfort." The word comfort then dominates the paragraph, and it moves in a circuit rather than a straight line, since God "comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God." Affliction and consolation are yoked in fixed proportion — "as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so our consolation also aboundeth by Christ" — and both are turned outward toward the congregation, so that "whether we be afflicted, it is for your consolation and salvation, which is effectual in the enduring of the same sufferings which we also suffer: or whether we be comforted, it is for your consolation and salvation." On that basis he can say "our hope of you is stedfast, knowing, that as ye are partakers of the sufferings, so shall ye be also of the consolation." Only then does he name the concrete crisis he has been generalizing from: "our trouble which came to us in Asia, that we were pressed out of measure, above strength, insomuch that we despaired even of life." He does not soften the account, and he assigns it a purpose — "we had the sentence of death in ourselves, that we should not trust in ourselves, but in God which raiseth the dead" — before laying out deliverance in three tenses, past, present, and future: "Who delivered us from so great a death, and doth deliver: in whom we trust that he will yet deliver us." The Corinthians are given a share in that outcome, "Ye also helping together by prayer for us, that for the gift bestowed upon us by the means of many persons thanks may be given by many on our behalf." From here the letter turns defensive. Paul's boast is not achievement but integrity: "our rejoicing is this, the testimony of our conscience, that in simplicity and godly sincerity, not with fleshly wisdom, but by the grace of God, we have had our conversation in the world, and more abundantly to you-ward," and his letters carry no hidden layer, "for we write none other things unto you, than what ye read or acknowledge." He recalls the itinerary he had promised — "I was minded to come unto you before, that ye might have a second benefit; And to pass by you into Macedonia, and to come again out of Macedonia unto you" — and confronts the accusation the change produced: "did I use lightness? or the things that I purpose, do I purpose according to the flesh, that with me there should be yea yea, and nay nay?" The answer escalates a complaint about travel plans into christology. "But as God is true, our word toward you was not yea and nay. For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was preached among you by us, even by me and Silvanus and Timotheus, was not yea and nay, but in him was yea. For all the promises of God in him are yea, and in him Amen, unto the glory of God by us." The guarantee behind both the message and the messengers is God's own action in four verbs: "he which stablisheth us with you in Christ, and hath anointed us, is God; Who hath also sealed us, and given the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts." Paul closes the chapter under oath, giving the real reason for the delay — "I call God for a record upon my soul, that to spare you I came not as yet unto Corinth" — and immediately disowns the very leverage he has just exercised: "Not for that we have dominion over your faith, but are helpers of your joy: for by faith ye stand." The opening is a blessing rather than a thanksgiving, and the difference matters. Where the first letter begins "I thank my God always on your behalf," this one begins "Blessed be God, even the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies, and the God of all comfort" — praise directed at God's character rather than at anything currently visible in the Corinthians. After a painful visit, a severe letter, and a congregation that has been questioning his motives, Paul has less to say about them and everything to say about the God who is "the Father of mercies." A relationship under strain is not repaired here by flattery or by a truce; it is reopened by naming what God is, so that whatever is said afterward about grievances stands inside that frame. Comfort in this chapter is not a private consolation but a transferable good, and the sentence that says so is deliberately circular: God "comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God." The purpose clause is the point. What is received is not stored, and the qualification to console is not natural sympathy or good technique but having actually been consoled by God in one's own tribulation. This makes affliction the training ground of usefulness rather than an interruption of it, and it means the comfort a sufferer receives already belongs, in part, to someone he has not yet met. The proportion Paul states is exact and unsentimental: "as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so our consolation also aboundeth by Christ." Consolation does not arrive as the cancellation of suffering but as its companion, scaled to it, and both come through the same person. He then refuses to let either half be private property — "whether we be afflicted, it is for your consolation and salvation... or whether we be comforted, it is for your consolation and salvation" — so that every state he can possibly be in is already ordered toward the church. The logic also runs forward: "as ye are partakers of the sufferings, so shall ye be also of the consolation," which makes shared suffering the ground of a confident hope about people who have been treating him badly. Paul's report of the crisis in Asia is remarkable for how little he protects his own reputation. He was "pressed out of measure, above strength, insomuch that we despaired even of life," and "we had the sentence of death in ourselves" — no claim to serene faith under pressure, and no suggestion that despair was a failure to be hidden. The purpose clause reframes it without denying it: the sentence of death came "that we should not trust in ourselves, but in God which raiseth the dead." Resurrection is invoked not as a doctrine about the last day but as the only adequate object of trust for a man who has run out of resources, and the deliverance is then held in three tenses at once — "Who delivered us from so great a death, and doth deliver: in whom we trust that he will yet deliver us" — so that a single past rescue becomes the pattern for the present and the pledge for the future. The apostle who has just described himself as the church's comforter immediately makes himself the church's debtor: "Ye also helping together by prayer for us, that for the gift bestowed upon us by the means of many persons thanks may be given by many on our behalf." His deliverance is described as coming "by the means of many persons," which credits the prayers of a congregation that had been quarrelling with him, and the intended result is not merely his survival but a widened chorus of thanksgiving. The traffic in this chapter runs both directions, and the same instinct surfaces again in the four verbs of the closing paragraph, where Paul cannot even describe his own standing without including them: it is God "which stablisheth us with you in Christ." A dispute about a changed itinerary is answered with the character of God rather than with an alibi. Accused of "lightness" and of purposing "according to the flesh," Paul does not chiefly argue that his reasons were good; he argues that his message admits no double-mindedness, since "the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was preached among you by us... was not yea and nay, but in him was yea. For all the promises of God in him are yea, and in him Amen." The claim is that a preacher whose subject is God's unqualified Yes cannot conduct his affairs as a series of qualified maybes — his reliability is derivative, borrowed from the content he carries. The mention of the Amen also gathers up the congregation's own liturgical response, so that the church's assent in worship is itself evidence of the argument. The last two verses hold an unusual tension. Paul swears an oath — "I call God for a record upon my soul" — and uses it to reveal that his absence was mercy: "to spare you I came not as yet unto Corinth." The silence they read as unreliability was restraint, which means he has been exercising authority precisely by not showing up. And in the same breath he disowns the category: "Not for that we have dominion over your faith, but are helpers of your joy: for by faith ye stand." The disclaimer arrives at the exact moment his power is most evident, and it names both the limit and the aim of pastoral office — faith is not something a minister can command, joy is what he exists to serve, and the church's standing rests on faith rather than on him. Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, and Timothy our brother, unto the church of God which is at Corinth, with all the saints which are in all Achaia: Grace be to you and peace from God our Father, and from the Lord Jesus Christ. Blessed be God, even the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies, and the God of all comfort; Who comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God. For as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so our consolation also aboundeth by Christ. And whether we be afflicted, it is for your consolation and salvation, which is effectual in the enduring of the same sufferings which we also suffer: or whether we be comforted, it is for your consolation and salvation. And our hope of you is stedfast, knowing, that as ye are partakers of the sufferings, so shall ye be also of the consolation. For we would not, brethren, have you ignorant of our trouble which came to us in Asia, that we were pressed out of measure, above strength, insomuch that we despaired even of life: But we had the sentence of death in ourselves, that we should not trust in ourselves, but in God which raiseth the dead: Who delivered us from so great a death, and doth deliver: in whom we trust that he will yet deliver us; Ye also helping together by prayer for us, that for the gift bestowed upon us by the means of many persons thanks may be given by many on our behalf. For our rejoicing is this, the testimony of our conscience, that in simplicity and godly sincerity, not with fleshly wisdom, but by the grace of God, we have had our conversation in the world, and more abundantly to you-ward. For we write none other things unto you, than what ye read or acknowledge; and I trust ye shall acknowledge even to the end; As also ye have acknowledged us in part, that we are your rejoicing, even as ye also are ours in the day of the Lord Jesus. And in this confidence I was minded to come unto you before, that ye might have a second benefit; And to pass by you into Macedonia, and to come again out of Macedonia unto you, and of you to be brought on my way toward Judaea. When I therefore was thus minded, did I use lightness? or the things that I purpose, do I purpose according to the flesh, that with me there should be yea yea, and nay nay? But as God is true, our word toward you was not yea and nay. For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was preached among you by us, even by me and Silvanus and Timotheus, was not yea and nay, but in him was yea. For all the promises of God in him are yea, and in him Amen, unto the glory of God by us. Now he which stablisheth us with you in Christ, and hath anointed us, is God; Who hath also sealed us, and given the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts. Moreover I call God for a record upon my soul, that to spare you I came not as yet unto Corinth. Not for that we have dominion over your faith, but are helpers of your joy: for by faith ye stand.

label: 2 Corinthians 2
text: The chapter opens with a decision already taken and now explained: "But I determined this with myself, that I would not come again to you in heaviness." Paul had made a painful visit and has chosen not to repeat it, and the reason he gives is not self-protection but a strange kind of mutual dependence — "For if I make you sorry, who is he then that maketh me glad, but the same which is made sorry by me?" The only people who could gladden him are the very people he would have had to wound, so a second grieving visit would have cost him his own joy. He therefore wrote instead of coming: "And I wrote this same unto you, lest, when I came, I should have sorrow from them of whom I ought to rejoice; having confidence in you all, that my joy is the joy of you all." The letter itself he now describes from the inside, and the description is unusually exposed for an apostle defending his authority: "For out of much affliction and anguish of heart I wrote unto you with many tears; not that ye should be grieved, but that ye might know the love which I have more abundantly unto you." Severity is claimed as an act of love, and the tears are offered as evidence. Paul then turns to the man who caused the trouble, and immediately refuses to stand at the centre of the injury: "But if any have caused grief, he hath not grieved me, but in part: that I may not overcharge you all." The offence was against the church, not chiefly against Paul, and Paul will not let the congregation be over-blamed for it either. What follows is the chapter's pastoral hinge. "Sufficient to such a man is this punishment, which was inflicted of many" — the censure the community imposed has done its work and is now to stop. "So that contrariwise ye ought rather to forgive him, and comfort him, lest perhaps such a one should be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow. Wherefore I beseech you that ye would confirm your love toward him." Forgiveness here is not a private feeling but a corporate act that must be made visible, and the danger Paul fears is no longer laxity but a repentant man drowned by the discipline meant to save him. He explains why he had pressed so hard: "For to this end also did I write, that I might know the proof of you, whether ye be obedient in all things." Then he binds his own act of pardon to theirs: "To whom ye forgive any thing, I forgive also: for if I forgave any thing, to whom I forgave it, for your sakes forgave I it in the person of Christ;" and he names the stake with a soldier's clarity — "Lest Satan should get an advantage of us: for we are not ignorant of his devices." The narrative then resumes where the letter's opening had left it: "Furthermore, when I came to Troas to preach Christ’s gospel, and a door was opened unto me of the Lord, I had no rest in my spirit, because I found not Titus my brother: but taking my leave of them, I went from thence into Macedonia." An open door is left unentered because a friend is missing and news of Corinth has not come. From that raw admission Paul breaks without transition into one of his great doxologies: "Now thanks be unto God, which always causeth us to triumph in Christ, and maketh manifest the savour of his knowledge by us in every place." The image is a triumphal procession trailing incense, and the incense is read differently by different noses: "For we are unto God a sweet savour of Christ, in them that are saved, and in them that perish: To the one we are the savour of death unto death; and to the other the savour of life unto life." The weight of that double effect produces the chapter's last question, "And who is sufficient for these things?", and its immediate answer is negative and moral rather than a boast of competence: "For we are not as many, which corrupt the word of God: but as of sincerity, but as of God, in the sight of God speak we in Christ." Paul grounds his change of travel plans in a piece of pastoral logic that is easy to skip over: "if I make you sorry, who is he then that maketh me glad, but the same which is made sorry by me?" He has no reservoir of joy independent of the people he must correct, and he says so plainly — "my joy is the joy of you all." This makes the chapter's severity structurally different from mere discipline administered from above. A pastor whose gladness is not bound up with his people can wound them at no cost to himself; Paul cannot, and the whole tone of the chapter, including the tears, follows from that. The severe letter is defended by disclosing the state of the man who wrote it: "out of much affliction and anguish of heart I wrote unto you with many tears; not that ye should be grieved, but that ye might know the love which I have more abundantly unto you." Paul distinguishes the intended effect of correction from its felt effect. Grief was the unavoidable instrument, not the goal; the goal was that they should know a love they had begun to doubt. The verse quietly rules out two failures at once — correction delivered without anguish, and love that will not risk causing pain. "But if any have caused grief, he hath not grieved me, but in part" is a deliberate act of self-removal. Paul had every ground to treat the offence as a personal wound, since his authority had been publicly resisted, yet he insists the injury was primarily the community's and adds "that I may not overcharge you all" so that the church is not made to carry more blame than it owes. Two temptations are refused in a single sentence: making oneself the aggrieved party, and letting a whole congregation be indicted for one man's act. The chapter establishes that church discipline has a terminus built into it. "Sufficient to such a man is this punishment, which was inflicted of many" declares the censure adequate and therefore finished, and "contrariwise ye ought rather to forgive him, and comfort him" turns the same authority that imposed it toward release. The stated danger is now the opposite of the original one — "lest perhaps such a one should be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow" — and the remedy is not merely lifting a penalty but an active, visible gesture: "confirm your love toward him." A community can sin by refusing to end a punishment as truly as by refusing to begin one. "Lest Satan should get an advantage of us: for we are not ignorant of his devices" places the whole discipline episode on a battlefield, and reverses the expected direction of the threat. Elsewhere the offender is handed over to Satan; here Satan's opening is the church's own unrelenting rigour, which could destroy through despair the man that discipline was meant to recover. The plural is pointed — the advantage would be gained "of us," over the community, not merely over the sinner. Paul treats unforgiveness as a strategy the enemy is known to use, which is why refusing to forgive is not caution but defeat. The Troas episode is one of the most humanly transparent moments in Paul's correspondence: "a door was opened unto me of the Lord, I had no rest in my spirit, because I found not Titus my brother: but taking my leave of them, I went from thence into Macedonia." An acknowledged providential opening is left behind because anxiety over a church and a missing colleague made him unable to work. Paul does not present this as failure or as obedience to a special leading; he simply reports it. Placed immediately before "thanks be unto God, which always causeth us to triumph in Christ," it defines what the triumph is not — it is not the absence of restlessness, dead ends, or abandoned opportunities. The savour imagery makes the preacher's effect independent of the preacher's intent. The same aroma rises from the same ministry, yet "To the one we are the savour of death unto death; and to the other the savour of life unto life," and both are described as being "unto God a sweet savour of Christ" — the offering is acceptable regardless of how it is received. This is why the question "who is sufficient for these things?" is not rhetorical modesty. Nothing in a minister's competence controls the outcome, so the only thing left within his power is integrity, which is exactly where Paul goes next: not to corrupt the word of God, but to speak "as of sincerity, but as of God, in the sight of God." But I determined this with myself, that I would not come again to you in heaviness. For if I make you sorry, who is he then that maketh me glad, but the same which is made sorry by me? And I wrote this same unto you, lest, when I came, I should have sorrow from them of whom I ought to rejoice; having confidence in you all, that my joy is the joy of you all. For out of much affliction and anguish of heart I wrote unto you with many tears; not that ye should be grieved, but that ye might know the love which I have more abundantly unto you. But if any have caused grief, he hath not grieved me, but in part: that I may not overcharge you all. Sufficient to such a man is this punishment, which was inflicted of many. So that contrariwise ye ought rather to forgive him, and comfort him, lest perhaps such a one should be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow. Wherefore I beseech you that ye would confirm your love toward him. For to this end also did I write, that I might know the proof of you, whether ye be obedient in all things. To whom ye forgive any thing, I forgive also: for if I forgave any thing, to whom I forgave it, for your sakes forgave I it in the person of Christ; Lest Satan should get an advantage of us: for we are not ignorant of his devices. Furthermore, when I came to Troas to preach Christ’s gospel, and a door was opened unto me of the Lord, I had no rest in my spirit, because I found not Titus my brother: but taking my leave of them, I went from thence into Macedonia. Now thanks be unto God, which always causeth us to triumph in Christ, and maketh manifest the savour of his knowledge by us in every place. For we are unto God a sweet savour of Christ, in them that are saved, and in them that perish: To the one we are the savour of death unto death; and to the other the savour of life unto life. And who is sufficient for these things? For we are not as many, which corrupt the word of God: but as of sincerity, but as of God, in the sight of God speak we in Christ.

label: 2 Corinthians 3
text: Paul resumes a self-defence he finds faintly absurd and says so at once: "Do we begin again to commend ourselves? or need we, as some others, epistles of commendation to you, or letters of commendation from you?" Rivals at Corinth evidently arrived carrying written credentials, and Paul answers by pointing at the congregation itself — "Ye are our epistle written in our hearts, known and read of all men" — then presses the metaphor until it stops being a compliment and becomes a covenant claim: they are "manifestly declared to be the epistle of Christ ministered by us, written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God; not in tables of stone, but in fleshy tables of the heart." Every term in that sentence is chosen: Christ is the author and Paul only the one through whom the writing was ministered, the ink is the Spirit of the living God, and the writing surface is the human heart rather than the stone of Sinai, which is the prophetic promise of a law written inwardly and a heart of flesh given in place of a heart of stone. The confidence this yields is immediately stripped of any personal claim: "And such trust have we through Christ to God-ward: Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think any thing as of ourselves; but our sufficiency is of God; Who also hath made us able ministers of the new testament; not of the letter, but of the spirit: for the letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life." From that antithesis the chapter becomes a sustained argument from the lesser to the greater, and the lesser is conceded in full: "But if the ministration of death, written and engraven in stones, was glorious, so that the children of Israel could not stedfastly behold the face of Moses for the glory of his countenance; which glory was to be done away: How shall not the ministration of the spirit be rather glorious? For if the ministration of condemnation be glory, much more doth the ministration of righteousness exceed in glory." Paul never says Sinai lacked glory; he says it is outshone — "even that which was made glorious had no glory in this respect, by reason of the glory that excelleth" — and that the contrast is finally one of permanence, "for if that which is done away was glorious, much more that which remaineth is glorious." The comparison then turns pastoral and personal: "Seeing then that we have such hope, we use great plainness of speech: And not as Moses, which put a vail over his face, that the children of Israel could not stedfastly look to the end of that which is abolished." At this point the veil migrates from the face of the mediator to the hearing of his people: "But their minds were blinded: for until this day remaineth the same vail untaken away in the reading of the old testament; which vail is done away in Christ. But even unto this day, when Moses is read, the vail is upon their heart." Its removal is not a matter of technique or cleverness but of direction — "Nevertheless when it shall turn to the Lord, the vail shall be taken away. Now the Lord is that Spirit: and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty" — and the chapter closes by setting the whole church where only one man had stood on the mountain, and doing to them what merely looking never did to him: "But we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord." Paul's refusal of "epistles of commendation" is not a rejection of accountability but a claim about what finally authenticates a ministry. Against rivals who carried paperwork, he offers people: "Ye are our epistle written in our hearts, known and read of all men." The letter has two locations at once — inward, in the affection of the apostle who cannot produce it on demand, and public, legible to anyone who cares to look at the changed lives in Corinth. And crucially the authorship is not his. They are "the epistle of Christ ministered by us," so the minister is the one through whom the writing was delivered, never the one whose name is signed. That is what makes the boast safe: Paul is pointing at handwriting that is demonstrably not his own. The chapter states confidence and disowns competence in the same breath. "Such trust have we through Christ to God-ward" is followed instantly by "Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think any thing as of ourselves," and the disclaimer is pushed further than expected — not merely to do anything, but to think any thing. What is left is a conferred fitness: "our sufficiency is of God; Who also hath made us able ministers of the new testament." New covenant ministry is therefore an office one is made able for, not a capacity one brings; the same God who wrote the letter also equipped the courier, which is why the assurance is total and the self-regard is nil. "For the letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life" is not a verdict against Scripture or against law as such, and Paul immediately proves it by calling the very thing he has just called deadly "glorious." The letter in view is the commandment "written and engraven in stones" — holy, God-given, radiant enough that Israel "could not stedfastly behold the face of Moses." The problem is not the standard but its effect on flesh that cannot meet it: a written requirement can specify righteousness and expose failure, but it has no power to produce what it demands. Hence "the ministration of death" and "the ministration of condemnation" are descriptions of an outcome, not insults to Sinai, and the contrast is between two economies, one that inscribes on stone and one that writes with "the Spirit of the living God" on "fleshy tables of the heart." The argument is concessive rather than polemical, and its logic runs entirely upward. Three times Paul builds the same ladder — if the ministration of death was glorious, "how shall not the ministration of the spirit be rather glorious"; if condemnation had glory, "much more doth the ministration of righteousness exceed in glory"; if what is done away was glorious, "much more that which remaineth is glorious." He never argues that the old was worthless; he argues that it was real and temporary. Verse ten makes the point with unusual delicacy: "even that which was made glorious had no glory in this respect, by reason of the glory that excelleth." Something can be genuinely luminous and still be unable to be seen once a greater light is in the room, and the decisive difference is finally durability — one glory "was to be done away," the other "remaineth." The veil moves, and where it lands is the chapter's sharpest observation. Moses covers his own face so that Israel "could not stedfastly look to the end of that which is abolished"; now Paul says the same covering has relocated onto the audience, "for until this day remaineth the same vail untaken away in the reading of the old testament," and more bluntly, "when Moses is read, the vail is upon their heart." The difficulty in reading the older Scriptures is therefore not primarily textual obscurity but something over the perceiver, which is why the cure is not scholarship or decoding but a change of orientation: "when it shall turn to the Lord, the vail shall be taken away." Paul's own "great plainness of speech" follows from this — a minister of a covenant with nothing fading to conceal has no motive to veil anything. The final verse takes the most exclusive scene in Israel's history and hands it to everyone. Moses alone went up, and what he brought back had to be hidden; now "we all, with open face" behold "the glory of the Lord," and the beholding is not merely permitted but effective — "changed into the same image from glory to glory." The verbs matter: Israel "could not stedfastly behold," while the church gazes and is transformed by gazing, and the transformation happens to them rather than being achieved by them, "even as by the Spirit of the Lord." This also defines the liberty of verse seventeen. "Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty" is not freedom from obligation but freedom from the veil and from the condemnation of a law that could only accuse — the unhindered access of people who no longer have to look away, and who are being made to resemble what they are finally allowed to see. The whole chapter quietly answers the question it opened with. Paul was asked, in effect, for his credentials; he ends by describing a ministry whose evidence is a congregation being visibly rewritten by the Spirit and progressively conformed to the image of the Lord. The credential and the theology are the same thing. If the new covenant really writes on hearts rather than stone, then the only proof a minister of it can offer is hearts, and the only proper boast is that the handwriting belongs to someone else. Do we begin again to commend ourselves? or need we, as some others, epistles of commendation to you, or letters of commendation from you? Ye are our epistle written in our hearts, known and read of all men: Forasmuch as ye are manifestly declared to be the epistle of Christ ministered by us, written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God; not in tables of stone, but in fleshy tables of the heart. And such trust have we through Christ to God-ward: Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think any thing as of ourselves; but our sufficiency is of God; Who also hath made us able ministers of the new testament; not of the letter, but of the spirit: for the letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life. But if the ministration of death, written and engraven in stones, was glorious, so that the children of Israel could not stedfastly behold the face of Moses for the glory of his countenance; which glory was to be done away: How shall not the ministration of the spirit be rather glorious? For if the ministration of condemnation be glory, much more doth the ministration of righteousness exceed in glory. For even that which was made glorious had no glory in this respect, by reason of the glory that excelleth. For if that which is done away was glorious, much more that which remaineth is glorious. Seeing then that we have such hope, we use great plainness of speech: And not as Moses, which put a vail over his face, that the children of Israel could not stedfastly look to the end of that which is abolished: But their minds were blinded: for until this day remaineth the same vail untaken away in the reading of the old testament; which vail is done away in Christ. But even unto this day, when Moses is read, the vail is upon their heart. Nevertheless when it shall turn to the Lord, the vail shall be taken away. Now the Lord is that Spirit: and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty. But we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord.

label: 2 Corinthians 4
text: The chapter opens by drawing a conclusion from the glorious ministry just described, and the conclusion is endurance grounded in something other than stamina: "Therefore seeing we have this ministry, as we have received mercy, we faint not." Paul then defines that ministry first by what he has refused — he has "renounced the hidden things of dishonesty, not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully" — and then by his one permitted method, "by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man’s conscience in the sight of God." No technique is left; only the truth set plainly before another person's conscience, with God watching. That confession forces him to account for failure without blaming his own methods: "But if our gospel be hid, it is hid to them that are lost: In whom the god of this world hath blinded the minds of them which believe not, lest the light of the glorious gospel of Christ, who is the image of God, should shine unto them." The obstacle is neither the message's obscurity nor the preacher's incompetence but an active hostile blinding, which is also why the preacher must be careful never to occupy the frame: "For we preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus the Lord; and ourselves your servants for Jesus’ sake." What breaks the blindness is a second act of creation, described in the language of the first: "For God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ." Against that blaze Paul immediately sets the fragility of the people carrying it — "But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us" — and the reason is stated as purpose, not accident: the cheapness of the container is what makes the source of the power unmistakable. Four antitheses then trace the cracks in the vessel and the treasure holding it together: "We are troubled on every side, yet not distressed; we are perplexed, but not in despair; Persecuted, but not forsaken; cast down, but not destroyed." Paul reads his own battered body as an exhibition of the Passion and the Resurrection at once, "Always bearing about in the body the dying of the Lord Jesus, that the life also of Jesus might be made manifest in our body," and repeats it to be sure it is not missed: "For we which live are alway delivered unto death for Jesus’ sake, that the life also of Jesus might be made manifest in our mortal flesh." The exchange is then stated with unnerving brevity — "So then death worketh in us, but life in you" — an apostolic ministry that costs the minister and pays the church. Speech continues because faith does, and Paul claims continuity with the psalmist: "We having the same spirit of faith, according as it is written, I believed, and therefore have I spoken; we also believe, and therefore speak." The content of that faith is resurrection and reunion, "Knowing that he which raised up the Lord Jesus shall raise up us also by Jesus, and shall present us with you," and its purpose runs outward and then upward, "For all things are for your sakes, that the abundant grace might through the thanksgiving of many redound to the glory of God." The chapter closes by repeating its opening refusal and explaining it: "For which cause we faint not; but though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day." Two things are happening in the same body at the same time, one visible decay and one invisible renewal, and the weighing of them yields the chapter's most audacious sentence: "For our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory." This is possible only under a particular discipline of attention, which the final verse names: "While we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen: for the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal." "We faint not" frames the chapter twice, at verse one and again at verse sixteen, and each time Paul gives a reason that has nothing to do with his own resilience. The first is backward-looking — "as we have received mercy" — and the second is forward-looking, the eternal weight of glory being produced. Between those two bookends stands a catalogue of trouble, perplexity, persecution, and being cast down, so the refusal to faint is plainly not a claim to feel fine. Paul is perplexed; he simply is not in despair. The chapter therefore separates endurance from emotional buoyancy: what keeps the minister going is mercy already received and glory already guaranteed, neither of which fluctuates with how the week has gone. The ministry Paul describes has been stripped of every instrument except transparency. He has "renounced the hidden things of dishonesty, not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully," which rules out not only lying but the subtler professional arts — the managed impression, the selectively edited message, the text bent toward the effect one wants. What remains is "by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man’s conscience in the sight of God," an appeal aimed at the hearer's conscience rather than at his admiration, and audited by God rather than by results. It is a deliberately defenseless way to work, and the rest of the chapter explains why a man who has renounced all leverage does not thereby become desperate. Verses three and four remove a temptation that haunts anyone whose message is refused: the assumption that rejection is a verdict on the presentation. "If our gospel be hid, it is hid to them that are lost: In whom the god of this world hath blinded the minds of them which believe not." The hiding is not in the gospel, which by definition is a manifestation, and not in Paul, who has just renounced craftiness; it is an active blinding with a stated aim, "lest the light of the glorious gospel of Christ, who is the image of God, should shine unto them." Unbelief is here treated as something inflicted as well as chosen, which both dignifies the unbeliever's condition as a genuine bondage and removes the preacher's power to fix it by cleverness. The remedy Paul names for that blindness is not argument but creation. "For God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ." The allusion is to the first day of the world, and the parallel is exact in its unilaterality: darkness contributes nothing to the arrival of light, and the same God who spoke then speaks now. Two further things follow from the verse's wording. The light is given as knowledge, not as sensation — it illuminates rather than merely warms — and its location is a human face, so that the glory once sought on a mountain or behind a veil is now met in a person. "But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us" is a statement of design, not of regret. Paul does not apologize for the pottery or promise that it will improve; the fragility is the point, because a container this obviously cheap makes it impossible to confuse the shine with the shell. The four antitheses that follow keep the same structure — troubled but not distressed, perplexed but not in despair, persecuted but not forsaken, cast down but not destroyed — and each pairs a real, unminimized affliction with a limit it cannot cross. The vessel is genuinely cracking, and every crack is where the argument for God's power is actually made. The most confronting sentence in the chapter is its shortest: "So then death worketh in us, but life in you." Paul has just described himself as "always bearing about in the body the dying of the Lord Jesus" so that "the life also of Jesus might be made manifest in our body," and he now applies that pattern to the transaction between apostle and congregation. His suffering is not merely private discipline; it is fruitful for other people, which is why he can immediately add that "all things are for your sakes." Ministry is thereby described as participation in the shape of the cross — costly at the point of delivery, life-giving at the point of reception — and the whole exchange terminates not in the minister's reputation but in "the thanksgiving of many" redounding "to the glory of God." The final weighing is deliberately outrageous, and its terms should not be softened. "Our light affliction, which is but for a moment" is written by a man being killed by inches; "a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory" is the counterweight, and the verb between them is active — affliction "worketh" the glory rather than merely preceding it. Two clocks are running simultaneously in the same person, since "though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day," and only one of them is visible. That is why the chapter ends with a rule of attention rather than a rule of feeling: "While we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen." The visible is not denied; it is dated. "The things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal." Therefore seeing we have this ministry, as we have received mercy, we faint not; But have renounced the hidden things of dishonesty, not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully; but by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man’s conscience in the sight of God. But if our gospel be hid, it is hid to them that are lost: In whom the god of this world hath blinded the minds of them which believe not, lest the light of the glorious gospel of Christ, who is the image of God, should shine unto them. For we preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus the Lord; and ourselves your servants for Jesus’ sake. For God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ. But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us. We are troubled on every side, yet not distressed; we are perplexed, but not in despair; Persecuted, but not forsaken; cast down, but not destroyed; Always bearing about in the body the dying of the Lord Jesus, that the life also of Jesus might be made manifest in our body. For we which live are alway delivered unto death for Jesus’ sake, that the life also of Jesus might be made manifest in our mortal flesh. So then death worketh in us, but life in you. We having the same spirit of faith, according as it is written, I believed, and therefore have I spoken; we also believe, and therefore speak; Knowing that he which raised up the Lord Jesus shall raise up us also by Jesus, and shall present us with you. For all things are for your sakes, that the abundant grace might through the thanksgiving of many redound to the glory of God. For which cause we faint not; but though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day. For our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory; While we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen: for the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal.

label: 2 Corinthians 5
text: Paul begins not with a hope but with a claim to knowledge: "For we know that if our earthly house of this tabernacle were dissolved, we have a building of God, an house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens." The metaphors shift under his hand — the body is first a tent that can be struck and then a garment, since "in this we groan, earnestly desiring to be clothed upon with our house which is from heaven: If so be that being clothed we shall not be found naked." He is careful to say what the groaning is and is not: "we that are in this tabernacle do groan, being burdened: not for that we would be unclothed, but clothed upon, that mortality might be swallowed up of life." The longing is for more embodiment rather than for escape from it, and its guarantee is neither temperament nor argument but a divine deposit already paid: "he that hath wrought us for the selfsame thing is God, who also hath given unto us the earnest of the Spirit." From that pledge follows a settled disposition — "Therefore we are always confident, knowing that, whilst we are at home in the body, we are absent from the Lord" — qualified by a parenthesis that governs the whole chapter, "( For we walk by faith, not by sight:)." Paul then states the preference plainly: "We are confident, I say, and willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord." Confidence does not dissolve responsibility, because the very next clause is ambition: "Wherefore we labour, that, whether present or absent, we may be accepted of him. For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ; that every one may receive the things done in his body, according to that he hath done, whether it be good or bad." Judgment is what makes his preaching urgent — "Knowing therefore the terror of the Lord, we persuade men" — and also what makes self-defence unnecessary, since "we are made manifest unto God; and I trust also are made manifest in your consciences."
