He insists the point is not self-promotion: "we commend not ourselves again unto you, but give you occasion to glory on our behalf, that ye may have somewhat to answer them which glory in appearance, and not in heart," and he hands both extremes of his reputation over to God and to the church — "whether we be beside ourselves, it is to God: or whether we be sober, it is for your cause." Then he names the engine of the whole ministry: "For the love of Christ constraineth us; because we thus judge, that if one died for all, then were all dead: And that he died for all, that they which live should not henceforth live unto themselves, but unto him which died for them, and rose again." A death that comprehensive resets perception itself — "Wherefore henceforth know we no man after the flesh: yea, though we have known Christ after the flesh, yet now henceforth know we him no more" — and issues in the chapter's most quoted sentence: "Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new." The initiative is God's from beginning to end, for "all things are of God, who hath reconciled us to himself by Jesus Christ, and hath given to us the ministry of reconciliation; To wit, that God was in Christ, reconciling the world unto himself, not imputing their trespasses unto them; and hath committed unto us the word of reconciliation." That commission gives Paul his standing and his tone at once: "Now then we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God did beseech you by us: we pray you in Christ's stead, be ye reconciled to God." And the ground of the whole appeal is set down in a single sentence of exchange that the chapter does not explain but simply states: "For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him." Paul's imagery is deliberately unstable and the instability is the argument. A tent "dissolved" would leave a person exposed, so he switches to clothing and then refuses the natural conclusion of his own metaphor: "not for that we would be unclothed, but clothed upon, that mortality might be swallowed up of life." The hope is not that the soul should shed the body but that the mortal body should be overwhelmed by life, the way a garment is put on over another rather than stripped away. This is why the anxiety of being "found naked" appears at all — Paul is not describing liberation from matter but the dread of an unfinished state, and he answers it with a fuller embodiment rather than with a purer spirituality. The confidence of this chapter is not a mood but an inference from a deposit. "He that hath wrought us for the selfsame thing is God, who also hath given unto us the earnest of the Spirit" — the word describes a first instalment that both guarantees and partially constitutes what is still owed. God has already manufactured the believer for this very outcome and has already paid something down. The parenthesis "( For we walk by faith, not by sight:)" then tells us what kind of knowing sustains the "we know" of the first verse: nothing in the present situation looks like an eternal house, and the certainty does not come from looking. Assurance and accountability are stated in consecutive breaths without any sense of contradiction. The same apostle who is "always confident" and "willing rather to be absent from the body" says in the next line, "Wherefore we labour, that, whether present or absent, we may be accepted of him. For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ." The judgment is universal ("we must all"), individual ("every one"), embodied ("the things done in his body"), and two-sided ("whether it be good or bad"). Paul draws no comfort from vagueness here; instead the prospect fuels his work — "Knowing therefore the terror of the Lord, we persuade men" — so that fear of God becomes evangelistic energy rather than paralysis. The chapter contains a quiet theory of how people should be evaluated. Paul's rivals "glory in appearance, and not in heart," and his defence is not a better display but an appeal to what is already visible to God and, he hopes, to conscience: "we are made manifest unto God; and I trust also are made manifest in your consciences." He then generalizes the principle to the point of scandal — "henceforth know we no man after the flesh: yea, though we have known Christ after the flesh, yet now henceforth know we him no more." If even Christ is no longer assessed by outward impressiveness, then no apostle, and no member of the congregation, may be ranked that way either. "For the love of Christ constraineth us" is followed immediately by a piece of reasoning, not by a sentiment: "because we thus judge, that if one died for all, then were all dead." The death of the one is read backwards as a diagnosis of the condition of the many; the scope of the remedy discloses the scope of the disease. And the stated purpose of that death is not merely acquittal but a reversal of the direction of a life: "that they which live should not henceforth live unto themselves, but unto him which died for them, and rose again." The verb "constraineth" carries the sense of being hemmed in and pressed forward at once, which is exactly how Paul describes a ministry he did not choose and cannot lay down. The reconciliation passage keeps the initiative entirely with God while ending in a plea. "All things are of God, who hath reconciled us to himself by Jesus Christ" — the offended party acts, the offender is acted upon, and "God was in Christ, reconciling the world unto himself, not imputing their trespasses unto them." Yet what God has accomplished is then "committed unto us" as a "word," and delivered by "ambassadors for Christ" who speak "in Christ's stead," so that the divine appeal reaches people through human speech. Most striking of all, the plea "be ye reconciled to God" is addressed to a baptized congregation, which means Paul does not treat reconciliation as a transaction filed away in the past but as something a church can drift out of and must keep entering. For we know that if our earthly house of this tabernacle were dissolved, we have a building of God, an house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. For in this we groan, earnestly desiring to be clothed upon with our house which is from heaven: If so be that being clothed we shall not be found naked. For we that are in this tabernacle do groan, being burdened: not for that we would be unclothed, but clothed upon, that mortality might be swallowed up of life. Now he that hath wrought us for the selfsame thing is God, who also hath given unto us the earnest of the Spirit. Therefore we are always confident, knowing that, whilst we are at home in the body, we are absent from the Lord: ( For we walk by faith, not by sight:) We are confident, I say, and willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord. Wherefore we labour, that, whether present or absent, we may be accepted of him. For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ; that every one may receive the things done in his body, according to that he hath done, whether it be good or bad. Knowing therefore the terror of the Lord, we persuade men; but we are made manifest unto God; and I trust also are made manifest in your consciences. For we commend not ourselves again unto you, but give you occasion to glory on our behalf, that ye may have somewhat to answer them which glory in appearance, and not in heart. For whether we be beside ourselves, it is to God: or whether we be sober, it is for your cause. For the love of Christ constraineth us; because we thus judge, that if one died for all, then were all dead: And that he died for all, that they which live should not henceforth live unto themselves, but unto him which died for them, and rose again. Wherefore henceforth know we no man after the flesh: yea, though we have known Christ after the flesh, yet now henceforth know we him no more. Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new. And all things are of God, who hath reconciled us to himself by Jesus Christ, and hath given to us the ministry of reconciliation; To wit, that God was in Christ, reconciling the world unto himself, not imputing their trespasses unto them; and hath committed unto us the word of reconciliation. Now then we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God did beseech you by us: we pray you in Christ’s stead, be ye reconciled to God. For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.

label: 2 Corinthians 6
text: Having just described himself as an ambassador begging on Christ's behalf, Paul now names the partnership and the peril together: "We then, as workers together with him, beseech you also that ye receive not the grace of God in vain." The warning is addressed not to outsiders but to a congregation that has already received grace, and it assumes that grace can be received and still come to nothing. To press the urgency he reaches for an oracle of divine answer — "For he saith, I have heard thee in a time accepted, and in the day of salvation have I succoured thee" — and then breaks in with his own doubled exclamation, transposing the prophecy into the present: "behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation." What follows is Paul's defence of his own ministry, offered not as self-praise but as evidence, and it begins with a negative concern for the office rather than the man: "Giving no offence in any thing, that the ministry be not blamed: But in all things approving ourselves as the ministers of God." The credentials come in a long, accelerating list that shifts preposition twice. First the circumstances endured — "in much patience, in afflictions, in necessities, in distresses, In stripes, in imprisonments, in tumults, in labours, in watchings, in fastings" — nine hardships, three of them inflicted by hostile power and three of them self-imposed. Then the resources by which they are borne: "By pureness, by knowledge, by longsuffering, by kindness, by the Holy Ghost, by love unfeigned, By the word of truth, by the power of God, by the armour of righteousness on the right hand and on the left." Then the reception, which is double-edged from the start — "By honour and dishonour, by evil report and good report" — and this tips the list into a series of paradoxes in which the world's verdict and God's are set side by side: "as deceivers, and yet true; As unknown, and yet well known; as dying, and, behold, we live; as chastened, and not killed; As sorrowful, yet alway rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things." The argument then turns suddenly personal, and Paul does something he does nowhere else in this letter — he calls them by name. "O ye Corinthians, our mouth is open unto you, our heart is enlarged." The diagnosis that follows locates the blockage precisely: "Ye are not straitened in us, but ye are straitened in your own bowels," and the only payment he asks for is symmetry of affection, requested in a father's voice: "Now for a recompence in the same, (I speak as unto my children,) be ye also enlarged." From that plea for an opened heart Paul moves without transition to a demand for a closed door: "Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers." Five rhetorical questions follow, each pairing two things that cannot be made one — "what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness? And what concord hath Christ with Belial? or what part hath he that believeth with an infidel? And what agreement hath the temple of God with idols?" — and the fifth question does not end in a prohibition but in an identity: "for ye are the temple of the living God." That identity is then established out of Scripture itself, a chain of promises stitched into one divine speech: "I will dwell in them, and walk in them; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people. Wherefore come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing; and I will receive you, And will be a Father unto you, and ye shall be my sons and daughters, saith the Lord Almighty." The chapter that opened with a warning about grace received in vain closes with the reason such grace must not be squandered: the people warned are the dwelling place of God and the adopted children of the Almighty. The chapter opens by holding two things together that are often separated: God's initiative and the real possibility of human waste. Paul and his colleagues are "workers together with him," and the very next clause is the fear that the Corinthians might "receive not the grace of God in vain." The warning presupposes that grace has already been given — this is not an appeal to the unconverted — and that a gift genuinely received can still be rendered fruitless by the one who holds it. Paul then refuses to let the matter be postponed. He takes a prophetic word spoken to God's servant in the past tense, "I have heard thee in a time accepted," and cracks it open with a twice-repeated "behold" that drags it into the present: "now is the accepted time; now is the day of salvation." Prophecy is not treated as a prediction awaiting fulfilment somewhere ahead, but as a window that has opened onto the hearer's own morning. The credential list is built with a deliberate grammatical architecture that most readings flatten. The first movement is governed by "in" and names circumstances suffered — "in afflictions, in necessities, in distresses, In stripes, in imprisonments, in tumults" — with the last three, "in labours, in watchings, in fastings," quietly shifting from what was done to Paul to what Paul did to himself. The second movement is governed by "by" and names the equipment: moral qualities first, "pureness, knowledge, longsuffering, kindness," then the divine agents, "the Holy Ghost," "the word of truth," "the power of God." The third movement collapses into paradox. Read in sequence, the list argues that a ministry is authenticated neither by its comfort nor by its results but by the coherence of endurance, character, and divine power under conditions that would expose a fraud. "By honour and dishonour, by evil report and good report" is the hinge on which the whole catalogue turns, because it concedes that Paul's reputation is genuinely mixed and then declines to treat that as a problem. The paradoxes that follow are not consolations offered to a defeated man; they are a systematic refusal of the Corinthian habit of judging ministers by appearance. "As deceivers, and yet true" grants the accusation as a perception while denying it as a fact. "As dying, and, behold, we live" places the same "behold" here that announced the day of salvation, so that the apostle's survival is itself a sign of the accepted time. And "as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things" describes a wealth that can only be measured by what it transfers to others, which is precisely the wealth a status-conscious congregation was least equipped to recognize. The three verses at the centre are the emotional pivot of the letter, and they are unusually raw. Paul names the church directly — "O ye Corinthians" — something he does only when the pressure is greatest, and describes an openness that is both verbal and affective: "our mouth is open unto you, our heart is enlarged." Then he places the fault where it belongs: "Ye are not straitened in us, but ye are straitened in your own bowels." The constriction is theirs, not his. What he asks in return is not money, not obedience, not an apology, but the same enlargement, and he asks it in the register of family rather than authority: "(I speak as unto my children,) be ye also enlarged." A heart narrowed toward a faithful pastor and a heart wide open to compromising alliances are, in the argument that follows, the same disorder viewed from two sides. The command "Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers" is argued rather than merely imposed, and its argument is a cascade of five questions that each ask the same thing in a rising key — righteousness and unrighteousness, light and darkness, Christ and Belial, believer and infidel, temple and idols. The progression moves from abstract moral qualities to cosmic opposites to named persons to concrete cultic objects, tightening from principle to practice. Crucially, the series does not terminate in a rule. The fifth question is answered by a declaration of who the Corinthians already are: "for ye are the temple of the living God." Separation is therefore grounded in indwelling rather than in contempt. The reason a Christian cannot be harnessed to idolatry is not that unbelievers are disgusting but that the believer is occupied territory, and God does not share a sanctuary with what displaces him. The closing promises are a mosaic of Scripture rather than a single quotation, and the seams are where the theology happens. The tabernacle pledge that God would dwell and walk among his people, the summons to leave an unclean land and touch no unclean thing, and the covenant with the house of David are welded into one continuous speech of "the Lord Almighty" and applied to a largely Gentile congregation in a Greek port city. Two moves in that mosaic are striking. First, the dwelling promise is made interior — "I will dwell in them, and walk in them" — so that the temple is the people rather than a building they visit. Second, a promise of sonship originally spoken to one royal heir is pluralized and widened to "my sons and daughters," explicitly including women in an adoption that the older text had reserved to a king. A chapter that began by warning against wasting grace ends by describing how much has actually been given. We then, as workers together with him, beseech you also that ye receive not the grace of God in vain. ( For he saith, I have heard thee in a time accepted, and in the day of salvation have I succoured thee: behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation.) Giving no offence in any thing, that the ministry be not blamed: But in all things approving ourselves as the ministers of God, in much patience, in afflictions, in necessities, in distresses, In stripes, in imprisonments, in tumults, in labours, in watchings, in fastings; By pureness, by knowledge, by longsuffering, by kindness, by the Holy Ghost, by love unfeigned, By the word of truth, by the power of God, by the armour of righteousness on the right hand and on the left, By honour and dishonour, by evil report and good report: as deceivers, and yet true; As unknown, and yet well known; as dying, and, behold, we live; as chastened, and not killed; As sorrowful, yet alway rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things. O ye Corinthians, our mouth is open unto you, our heart is enlarged. Ye are not straitened in us, but ye are straitened in your own bowels. Now for a recompence in the same, (I speak as unto my children,) be ye also enlarged. Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers: for what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness? And what concord hath Christ with Belial? or what part hath he that believeth with an infidel? And what agreement hath the temple of God with idols? for ye are the temple of the living God; as God hath said, I will dwell in them, and walk in them; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people. Wherefore come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing; and I will receive you, And will be a Father unto you, and ye shall be my sons and daughters, saith the Lord Almighty.

label: 2 Corinthians 7
text: The chapter opens by gathering the promises just cited into a single imperative: "Having therefore these promises, dearly beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from all filthiness of the flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God" — a command whose ground is a gift already given, and whose reach runs past outward behaviour into the interior life. Paul then turns back to the strained relationship that dominates the letter, first with a threefold protest of innocence, "Receive us; we have wronged no man, we have corrupted no man, we have defrauded no man," then immediately blunting it so it cannot be heard as a countercharge — "I speak not this to condemn you: for I have said before, that ye are in our hearts to die and live with you" — and finally letting affection overflow into something close to extravagance: "Great is my boldness of speech toward you, great is my glorying of you: I am filled with comfort, I am exceeding joyful in all our tribulation." At verse five the travel narrative Paul had broken off earlier resumes without warning: "when we were come into Macedonia, our flesh had no rest, but we were troubled on every side; without were fightings, within were fears." The relief that comes is not a vision or a rescue but a friend arriving with news — "Nevertheless God, that comforteth those that are cast down, comforted us by the coming of Titus; And not by his coming only, but by the consolation wherewith he was comforted in you, when he told us your earnest desire, your mourning, your fervent mind toward me; so that I rejoiced the more." Paul then reopens the painful letter he had sent them and admits, remarkably, that he had second thoughts about sending it: "though I made you sorry with a letter, I do not repent, though I did repent: for I perceive that the same epistle hath made you sorry, though it were but for a season." What vindicates the letter is not the pain it inflicted but what the pain produced: "Now I rejoice, not that ye were made sorry, but that ye sorrowed to repentance: for ye were made sorry after a godly manner, that ye might receive damage by us in nothing." Out of this comes the chapter's most quoted sentence and its sharpest distinction — "For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death" — immediately tested against the evidence, a rush of seven results piled one on another: "what carefulness it wrought in you, yea, what clearing of yourselves, yea, what indignation, yea, what fear, yea, what vehement desire, yea, what zeal, yea, what revenge! In all things ye have approved yourselves to be clear in this matter." Paul then names the aim behind the whole painful exchange, and it turns out to be neither of the two parties in the original offence: "I did it not for his cause that had done the wrong, nor for his cause that suffered wrong, but that our care for you in the sight of God might appear unto you." The chapter closes in shared relief, with comfort travelling in a circle between the apostle, his messenger, and the church: "Therefore we were comforted in your comfort: yea, and exceedingly the more joyed we for the joy of Titus, because his spirit was refreshed by you all." The confidence Paul had staked on them in public has held — "if I have boasted any thing to him of you, I am not ashamed; but as we spake all things to you in truth, even so our boasting, which I made before Titus, is found a truth" — and Titus himself is now bound to them, since "his inward affection is more abundant toward you, whilst he remembereth the obedience of you all, how with fear and trembling ye received him." The last line of the chapter is not a doctrine but a restored relationship: "I rejoice therefore that I have confidence in you in all things." The opening word is "therefore," and everything in the sentence hangs on it. "Having therefore these promises, dearly beloved, let us cleanse ourselves" places the command downstream of a gift: the promises come first, the cleansing follows, and the effort is a response to what God has already pledged rather than a bid to secure it. Yet Paul does not therefore make the believer passive. The verb is active and reflexive — "let us cleanse ourselves" — and the goal is stated as an ongoing work, "perfecting holiness in the fear of God." The chapter thus refuses both halves of a familiar false choice: holiness is not something we manufacture to win God's favour, and it is not something that happens to us while we watch. The "fear of God" named here is the reverence appropriate to people whom God has promised to indwell, not the terror of people uncertain whether he will. "All filthiness of the flesh and spirit" quietly dismantles the instinct that locates real impurity in the body alone. Paul has just been writing to a city with a reputation for bodily vice, and he could easily have aimed the exhortation there; instead he doubles the target, so that the defilements of the spirit — resentment, contempt, partisanship, the sins that leave no visible mark — are placed on exactly the same footing as the defilements of the flesh. This is a harder standard, not a softer one, because sins of the spirit are the ones a respectable congregation can carry indefinitely without ever noticing them. It also means that "perfecting holiness" cannot be reduced to a program of physical restraint; the whole person, inward and outward, is the field of the work. Verse five resumes a story Paul dropped several chapters earlier, and the seam is worth noticing because of what he lets slip when he picks it up: "our flesh had no rest, but we were troubled on every side; without were fightings, within were fears." An apostle in the middle of a letter defending his apostleship admits to fear, and admits it in the same breath as external opposition, as though the two were of a piece. Then comes the relief, and it is strikingly ordinary: God "comforteth those that are cast down," and the comfort arrives "by the coming of Titus." Not by a vision, not by a deliverance, but by a colleague walking into Macedonia with good news. Paul is content to describe a human arrival as the very instrument of divine consolation, which sets a pattern for how God's comfort usually reaches people. "I do not repent, though I did repent" is one of the most humanly honest sentences Paul ever wrote. He sent a letter that hurt them, then wished he had not, and now, seeing the result, is glad he did. He does not pretend to a serenity he lacked, and he does not defend the letter on the grounds that hard truth is always justified. He defends it only by its fruit — "not that ye were made sorry, but that ye sorrowed to repentance" — and he is careful to say the wound was temporary, "though it were but for a season." Sorrow, in this account, is never the objective. It is an instrument, deliberately brief, and anyone who inflicts it on others as an end in itself, or who prolongs it, has misread what Paul is doing here. The distinction between the two sorrows is not drawn by how they feel but by what they do: "godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death." Both kinds hurt, and the text gives no way to tell them apart by intensity of remorse. The test is directional — whether grief drives a person toward God and out into changed action, or curves back on itself into despair, self-protection, and ruin. Paul then supplies the evidence in a piling-up of results that reads almost breathlessly: "what carefulness it wrought in you, yea, what clearing of yourselves, yea, what indignation, yea, what fear, yea, what vehement desire, yea, what zeal, yea, what revenge!" Repentance here is energetic and public and costly, not a private mood. It has a visible shape, and Paul can point at that shape and say the sorrow was genuine. The stated purpose of the severe letter is the chapter's real surprise: "I did it not for his cause that had done the wrong, nor for his cause that suffered wrong, but that our care for you in the sight of God might appear unto you." Neither the offender nor the victim was the primary object. The letter was written so that the whole community would discover how much it was loved, which reframes church discipline as an act of pastoral affection aimed at a body rather than a legal proceeding aimed at an individual. That reframing is confirmed by how the chapter ends. Comfort circulates — Paul comforted by Titus, Titus refreshed by the Corinthians, Paul rejoicing again in Titus's joy — and the final note is not a verdict but restored trust: "I rejoice therefore that I have confidence in you in all things." The most quoted teaching on repentance in the New Testament is embedded, not in a treatise, but in the account of a friendship being repaired. Having therefore these promises, dearly beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from all filthiness of the flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God. Receive us; we have wronged no man, we have corrupted no man, we have defrauded no man. I speak not this to condemn you: for I have said before, that ye are in our hearts to die and live with you. Great is my boldness of speech toward you, great is my glorying of you: I am filled with comfort, I am exceeding joyful in all our tribulation. For, when we were come into Macedonia, our flesh had no rest, but we were troubled on every side; without were fightings, within were fears. Nevertheless God, that comforteth those that are cast down, comforted us by the coming of Titus; And not by his coming only, but by the consolation wherewith he was comforted in you, when he told us your earnest desire, your mourning, your fervent mind toward me; so that I rejoiced the more. For though I made you sorry with a letter, I do not repent, though I did repent: for I perceive that the same epistle hath made you sorry, though it were but for a season. Now I rejoice, not that ye were made sorry, but that ye sorrowed to repentance: for ye were made sorry after a godly manner, that ye might receive damage by us in nothing. For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death. For behold this selfsame thing, that ye sorrowed after a godly sort, what carefulness it wrought in you, yea, what clearing of yourselves, yea, what indignation, yea, what fear, yea, what vehement desire, yea, what zeal, yea, what revenge! In all things ye have approved yourselves to be clear in this matter. Wherefore, though I wrote unto you, I did it not for his cause that had done the wrong, nor for his cause that suffered wrong, but that our care for you in the sight of God might appear unto you. Therefore we were comforted in your comfort: yea, and exceedingly the more joyed we for the joy of Titus, because his spirit was refreshed by you all. For if I have boasted any thing to him of you, I am not ashamed; but as we spake all things to you in truth, even so our boasting, which I made before Titus, is found a truth. And his inward affection is more abundant toward you, whilst he remembereth the obedience of you all, how with fear and trembling ye received him. I rejoice therefore that I have confidence in you in all things.

label: 2 Corinthians 8
text: Having finished the long defence of his ministry and the joy of his reconciliation with Corinth, Paul turns to money, and he begins not with a request but with a report about somebody else: "we do you to wit of the grace of God bestowed on the churches of Macedonia." The word he uses for their collection is grace, and everything in the chapter follows from that naming. What the Macedonians did is described as a compound impossibility: "in a great trial of affliction the abundance of their joy and their deep poverty abounded unto the riches of their liberality." Affliction and poverty are the soil, joy and riches the harvest, and Paul piles the vocabulary of wealth onto churches that had none. He testifies as an eyewitness that "to their power, I bear record, yea, and beyond their power they were willing of themselves," and that they were not solicited but had to solicit him, "Praying us with much intreaty that we would receive the gift, and take upon us the fellowship of the ministering to the saints" — begging for the privilege of paying. The explanation Paul offers is the hinge of the whole appeal: "this they did, not as we hoped, but first gave their own selves to the Lord, and unto us by the will of God." The money followed a prior surrender; it was not a substitute for one. That example is then turned, gently, toward Corinth. Titus, who "had begun," is sent back to "finish in you the same grace also," and Paul frames the request as the completion of a set: "as ye abound in every thing, in faith, and utterance, and knowledge, and in all diligence, and in your love to us, see that ye abound in this grace also." He immediately disclaims coercion — "I speak not by commandment, but by occasion of the forwardness of others, and to prove the sincerity of your love" — and then supplies the only motive he finally trusts, a single sentence of theology dropped into the middle of a fundraising letter: "For ye know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that, though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich." From there the practical counsel is almost embarrassed in its tact. "Herein I give my advice: for this is expedient for you, who have begun before, not only to do, but also to be forward a year ago" — the Corinthians had been first to volunteer and last to deliver, so "Now therefore perform the doing of it; that as there was a readiness to will, so there may be a performance also out of that which ye have." The measure is deliberately relative and merciful: "if there be first a willing mind, it is accepted according to that a man hath, and not according to that he hath not." Paul then forestalls the obvious fear of being drained: "I mean not that other men be eased, and ye burdened: But by an equality, that now at this time your abundance may be a supply for their want, that their abundance also may be a supply for your want: that there may be equality," and he anchors this in the wilderness, "As it is written, He that had gathered much had nothing over; and he that had gathered little had no lack." The chapter's last third is logistics, and Paul treats logistics as a moral matter. He thanks God "which put the same earnest care into the heart of Titus for you," notes that Titus needed no persuading since "being more forward, of his own accord he went unto you," and adds two companions: one "whose praise is in the gospel throughout all the churches" who "was also chosen of the churches to travel with us with this grace," and another "whom we have oftentimes proved diligent in many things." The reason for the committee is stated bluntly — "Avoiding this, that no man should blame us in this abundance which is administered by us: Providing for honest things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men" — and the men themselves are honoured as "the messengers of the churches, and the glory of Christ," while Corinth is asked to give them, and the watching congregations, "the proof of your love, and of our boasting on your behalf." Paul never calls this collection a donation, a duty, or a tax; he calls it grace, and he uses the same word five times for five different things — what God bestowed on the Macedonians, what they gave, what Titus is to finish at Corinth, what the Corinthians are to abound in, and what Christ did in becoming poor. The effect is to make the money a visible extension of a single divine movement rather than a human transaction bolted onto it. The Macedonians are not praised as generous people; they are exhibited as evidence of "the grace of God bestowed on the churches of Macedonia." This reframing means that a church's giving is diagnostic rather than meritorious in the ordinary sense: it shows what grace has actually done in them, which is exactly why Paul can offer it as proof "of the sincerity of your love." The order in verse five governs everything else: "first gave their own selves to the Lord, and unto us by the will of God." Paul explicitly says this exceeded his expectation — "not as we hoped" — meaning he had hoped for money and received persons. Giving that runs "beyond their power" is not explained by unusual willpower or by unusual resources, since they had neither, but by a prior self-donation that made the money a small afterthought. The pastoral implication is severe and freeing at once: a contribution offered instead of oneself is a lesser thing than Paul is asking for, and once the self is given the question of amount has already largely answered itself. Verse nine is the shortest and most complete statement of the Incarnation in the letter, and Paul deploys it as a fundraising argument. "Though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich" presumes a wealth Christ possessed before he was poor, a real and voluntary descent, and an exchange in which his loss becomes the reader's gain. What is striking is the sheer economy of the move: Paul does not argue from the doctrine, he simply names it and expects the Corinthians to feel the shape of it pressing on their own accounts. Christian giving in this chapter is not imitation of a moral example so much as participation in a pattern the giver has already been enriched by, which is why the transfer of money between two provinces can be described as the same kind of act as the descent of God. Paul's handling of the Corinthians' delay is a study in refusing leverage while applying pressure. He says he speaks "not by commandment," calls what follows "my advice," bases the appeal on "the forwardness of others" rather than on his apostolic office, and sets the standard at what a person actually has: "it is accepted according to that a man hath, and not according to that he hath not." Yet the same paragraph presses hard on the gap between intention and act — they were first to be "forward a year ago" and have not finished — and insists that "as there was a readiness to will, so there may be a performance also." Willingness that never becomes a performance is treated as an unfinished thing rather than a completed inward virtue, and the remedy offered is not more feeling but delivery. The principle of verse fourteen is neither a demand for uniform poverty nor a merely optional kindness. Paul rejects the first explicitly — "I mean not that other men be eased, and ye burdened" — and then twice names the goal as equality, made concrete and temporal: "now at this time your abundance may be a supply for their want, that their abundance also may be a supply for your want." The relationship is reciprocal and expected to reverse, so the giver is not a patron and the recipient is not a dependent; both are members whose surpluses and shortfalls are held in common over time. The manna citation, "He that had gathered much had nothing over; and he that had gathered little had no lack," pushes further still, since in the wilderness the leveling was God's own doing and the effort of the strong gatherer produced no private advantage. Surplus, in this reading, is not primarily a possession but a temporary assignment. Nearly a third of the chapter is devoted to who will carry the bag, and Paul makes no apology for the space. He sends three men rather than one, one of them not his own appointee but "chosen of the churches to travel with us with this grace," and states the reason without piety or evasion: "Avoiding this, that no man should blame us in this abundance which is administered by us." The governing sentence, "Providing for honest things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men," refuses the excuse that a clear conscience before God is sufficient in the handling of other people's money. Paul, who has spent seven chapters insisting that he does not answer to human judgment, here submits his accounts to it, because the reputation at risk is not finally his own but the collection's and the gospel's. Moreover, brethren, we do you to wit of the grace of God bestowed on the churches of Macedonia; How that in a great trial of affliction the abundance of their joy and their deep poverty abounded unto the riches of their liberality. For to their power, I bear record, yea, and beyond their power they were willing of themselves; Praying us with much intreaty that we would receive the gift, and take upon us the fellowship of the ministering to the saints. And this they did, not as we hoped, but first gave their own selves to the Lord, and unto us by the will of God. Insomuch that we desired Titus, that as he had begun, so he would also finish in you the same grace also. Therefore, as ye abound in every thing, in faith, and utterance, and knowledge, and in all diligence, and in your love to us, see that ye abound in this grace also. I speak not by commandment, but by occasion of the forwardness of others, and to prove the sincerity of your love. For ye know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that, though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich. And herein I give my advice: for this is expedient for you, who have begun before, not only to do, but also to be forward a year ago. Now therefore perform the doing of it; that as there was a readiness to will, so there may be a performance also out of that which ye have. For if there be first a willing mind, it is accepted according to that a man hath, and not according to that he hath not. For I mean not that other men be eased, and ye burdened: But by an equality, that now at this time your abundance may be a supply for their want, that their abundance also may be a supply for your want: that there may be equality: As it is written, He that had gathered much had nothing over; and he that had gathered little had no lack. But thanks be to God, which put the same earnest care into the heart of Titus for you. For indeed he accepted the exhortation; but being more forward, of his own accord he went unto you. And we have sent with him the brother, whose praise is in the gospel throughout all the churches; And not that only, but who was also chosen of the churches to travel with us with this grace, which is administered by us to the glory of the same Lord, and declaration of your ready mind: Avoiding this, that no man should blame us in this abundance which is administered by us: Providing for honest things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men. And we have sent with them our brother, whom we have oftentimes proved diligent in many things, but now much more diligent, upon the great confidence which I have in you. Whether any do enquire of Titus, he is my partner and fellowhelper concerning you: or our brethren be enquired of, they are the messengers of the churches, and the glory of Christ. Wherefore shew ye to them, and before the churches, the proof of your love, and of our boasting on your behalf.

label: 2 Corinthians 9
text: Paul opens with a disclaimer that immediately contradicts itself: "as touching the ministering to the saints, it is superfluous for me to write to you," and then writes at length. The apparent redundancy is deliberate, because he has already spent his credit on them — "I know the forwardness of your mind, for which I boast of you to them of Macedonia, that Achaia was ready a year ago; and your zeal hath provoked very many." Corinth's early enthusiasm has been used as fuel for other churches, which means Corinth's delay is now everybody's problem. The three brethren are therefore sent ahead "lest our boasting of you should be in vain in this behalf," and Paul sketches the scene he wants to avoid with unusual candour: "Lest haply if they of Macedonia come with me, and find you unprepared, we (that we say not, ye) should be ashamed in this same confident boasting." He puts the shame on himself first and lets the parenthesis do the rest. The purpose of the advance visit is stated in a phrase that governs the whole chapter's psychology: the fund is to be gathered beforehand "that the same might be ready, as a matter of bounty, and not as of covetousness" — money extracted under the pressure of a delegation standing in the room would be the same sum and a different act, and Paul would rather protect the quality of the gift than maximise it. From verse six he leaves logistics for the underlying principle, and it arrives as a proverb of the field: "He which soweth sparingly shall reap also sparingly; and he which soweth bountifully shall reap also bountifully." The image resets the accounting, since seed put into the ground is neither spent nor kept but planted, and no farmer calls sowing a loss. Then comes the sentence the chapter is remembered for, and it is a rule about the interior act rather than the amount: "Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." Two motives are excluded by name, the reluctant heart and the compelled hand, and what is left is a decision taken freely and in advance. The promise attached to it is not wealth but capacity — "God is able to make all grace abound toward you; that ye, always having all sufficiency in all things, may abound to every good work" — where the sufficiency is granted precisely so that the abundance can keep flowing outward. Paul then reaches for Scripture, quoting the psalm's portrait of the just man, "He hath dispersed abroad; he hath given to the poor: his righteousness remaineth for ever," and prays that the God "that ministereth seed to the sower" would "both minister bread for your food, and multiply your seed sown, and increase the fruits of your righteousness." Bread and seed are carefully distinguished: one is for the giver's table, the other for the ground. The result is described in verse eleven with a chain that runs past the recipients entirely — "Being enriched in every thing to all bountifulness, which causeth through us thanksgiving to God" — and the last movement of the chapter follows that chain upward. "The administration of this service not only supplieth the want of the saints, but is abundant also by many thanksgivings unto God," so the collection produces two harvests, one material in Jerusalem and one liturgical in heaven. The Jewish believers, watching "by the experiment of this ministration," will "glorify God for your professed subjection unto the gospel of Christ, and for your liberal distribution unto them, and unto all men," and the money will come back as intercession: "by their prayer for you, which long after you for the exceeding grace of God in you." Gentile cash purchases Jewish affection and Jewish prayers, which is the reconciliation Paul has been after all along. He ends not with a total or a deadline but with an exclamation that dwarfs the whole enterprise: "Thanks be unto God for his unspeakable gift." The chapter's practical anxiety is not that Corinth will give too little but that it will give under pressure. Paul sends the delegation ahead specifically so the collection can be "ready, as a matter of bounty, and not as of covetousness," which is to say that a gift squeezed out of embarrassment in front of visiting Macedonians would have been the wrong kind of act even at the right amount. He is willing to spend paragraphs, travel, and three men's time to protect the interior quality of the offering. This is a striking inversion of ordinary fundraising instinct, where the deadline and the audience are precisely the tools one would use; Paul treats them as contaminants and engineers them out. "God loveth a cheerful giver" is not sentiment but a rule with two exclusions built in. "Not grudgingly" rules out the gift given with an inward grievance still attached, and "or of necessity" rules out the gift given because someone applied leverage — and Paul has been at pains through two chapters to remove both. What remains is the phrase "according as he purposeth in his heart," which places the decisive act before the money moves: a deliberate, unhurried resolution rather than a reaction. The cheerfulness commended here is therefore the natural temperature of a freely chosen act, not an emotional performance required on top of the payment. The promise of verse eight is routinely misquoted as prosperity and is in fact a promise of adequacy for a purpose. "All sufficiency in all things" is granted so that the recipients "may abound to every good work," and verse ten separates the two streams with agricultural precision: God gives "bread for your food" and also multiplies "your seed sown." The giver is promised enough to live on and more to plant, never a barn to sit on. Read this way, an increase in means is an increase in assignment, and the language of harvest describes not the giver's enrichment but the widening of what passes through his hands. Verse nine borrows a psalm about the righteous man and hands his description to a congregation of Gentile converts in a Greek port. "He hath dispersed abroad; he hath given to the poor: his righteousness remaineth for ever" makes scattering, not accumulating, the thing that endures, and Paul then prays that God would "increase the fruits of your righteousness" — language of growth applied to something the readers are said already to possess. Whatever one makes of the theological weight of that increase, the rhetorical move is unmistakable: Paul is telling the Corinthians that the durable part of their lives is the part they have already let go of. The most surprising feature of the chapter is how little of it is about the poor of Jerusalem. From verse eleven onward the relief of want becomes almost a by-product: the gift "causeth through us thanksgiving to God," "supplieth the want of the saints, but is abundant also by many thanksgivings unto God," moves the recipients to "glorify God," and returns as "their prayer for you." Paul is describing a circuit in which material aid enters the Church at one point and exits as worship and intercession at another, so that a transfer of funds becomes a liturgical event. This is why he can end the appeal with a doxology rather than a receipt. Beneath the money lies a political problem Paul never names here: a Gentile church is sending relief to the Jewish mother church that has every reason to be suspicious of it. Verse thirteen gives the payoff — the recipients will glorify God "for your professed subjection unto the gospel of Christ, and for your liberal distribution unto them, and unto all men" — and verse fourteen has them "long after you." Cash is doing what argument could not, proving that the Gentile churches hold the same gospel and are not a rival movement. The collection is thus an instrument of unity before it is an instrument of relief, and Paul's willingness to risk his own reputation on it is proportionate to that stake. For as touching the ministering to the saints, it is superfluous for me to write to you: For I know the forwardness of your mind, for which I boast of you to them of Macedonia, that Achaia was ready a year ago; and your zeal hath provoked very many. Yet have I sent the brethren, lest our boasting of you should be in vain in this behalf; that, as I said, ye may be ready: Lest haply if they of Macedonia come with me, and find you unprepared, we ( that we say not, ye) should be ashamed in this same confident boasting. Therefore I thought it necessary to exhort the brethren, that they would go before unto you, and make up beforehand your bounty, whereof ye had notice before, that the same might be ready, as a matter of bounty, and not as of covetousness. But this I say, He which soweth sparingly shall reap also sparingly; and he which soweth bountifully shall reap also bountifully. Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver. And God is able to make all grace abound toward you; that ye, always having all sufficiency in all things, may abound to every good work: ( As it is written, He hath dispersed abroad; he hath given to the poor: his righteousness remaineth for ever. Now he that ministereth seed to the sower both minister bread for your food, and multiply your seed sown, and increase the fruits of your righteousness;) Being enriched in every thing to all bountifulness, which causeth through us thanksgiving to God. For the administration of this service not only supplieth the want of the saints, but is abundant also by many thanksgivings unto God; Whiles by the experiment of this ministration they glorify God for your professed subjection unto the gospel of Christ, and for your liberal distribution unto them, and unto all men; And by their prayer for you, which long after you for the exceeding grace of God in you. Thanks be unto God for his unspeakable gift.

label: 2 Corinthians 10
text: The tone changes abruptly, and Paul signals it by stepping forward under his own name: "Now I Paul myself beseech you." What follows is a defence, but he begins by disarming himself, appealing "by the meekness and gentleness of Christ" and quoting his critics' jibe in their own words — "who in presence am base among you, but being absent am bold toward you." He does not deny the description so much as ask that it not become necessary: "I beseech you, that I may not be bold when I am present with that confidence, wherewith I think to be bold against some, which think of us as if we walked according to the flesh." The charge is that his ministry runs on merely human resources, and he answers it with a distinction that concedes the first half and refuses the second: "though we walk in the flesh, we do not war after the flesh." The apostle is an ordinary man in an ordinary body; the campaign he is conducting is not. From there the language turns military and stays that way for three verses. "The weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds," and the strongholds turn out to be intellectual rather than territorial — he is "casting down imaginations, and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ." The siege ends not in destruction but in a captivity that is also an allegiance, and Paul adds the awkward corollary that a commander cannot avoid: he has "in a readiness to revenge all disobedience, when your obedience is fulfilled" — discipline held in reserve until the loyal majority has declared itself, so that the church is not punished along with its agitators. He then confronts the criterion his opponents are using: "Do ye look on things after the outward appearance?" Anyone confident of belonging to Christ should reason his way to the obvious conclusion, "that, as he is Christ’s, even so are we Christ’s." His authority he will name but not press hard, and he defines it by its purpose in the same breath — it was given "for edification, and not for your destruction" — adding wryly that he does not want to "seem as if I would terrify you by letters." The insult is then quoted verbatim, the only place in his correspondence where we hear what people actually said about him: "his letters, say they, are weighty and powerful; but his bodily presence is weak, and his speech contemptible." His reply is a promise rather than a rebuttal: "such as we are in word by letters when we are absent, such will we be also in deed when we are present." The last section takes apart the whole business of self-recommendation. With heavy irony he declines to join the competition — "we dare not make ourselves of the number, or compare ourselves with some that commend themselves" — and diagnoses the closed circuit such men inhabit: "they measuring themselves by themselves, and comparing themselves among themselves, are not wise." Against that he sets an assigned field, "the measure of the rule which God hath distributed to us, a measure to reach even unto you," and notes the plain historical fact that settles the question of jurisdiction: "we are come as far as to you also in preaching the gospel of Christ." He will not claim credit for "other men’s labours," and his ambition runs outward rather than inward, hoping that as their faith grows he may "preach the gospel in the regions beyond you, and not to boast in another man’s line of things made ready to our hand." The argument closes on a text from the prophets and a maxim that dismantles the entire contest: "he that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord. For not he that commendeth himself is approved, but whom the Lord commendeth." Paul's opening appeal "by the meekness and gentleness of Christ" is not a rhetorical softener but the standard by which he wants his own conduct judged. He is about to say hard things and stakes the whole passage on the claim that severity and gentleness are not opposites in Christ, whose meekness did not prevent him overturning tables. The critics have read the gap between his mild presence and his forceful letters as inconsistency or cowardice; Paul reads it as the ordinary discipline of a pastor who prefers not to use the sharper instrument and says so in advance. The whole chapter is written so that the visit will not require what the letter threatens. The distinction of verse three — walking in the flesh but not warring after the flesh — is the hinge on which Paul's entire self-defence turns, here and through the following chapters. He concedes everything his opponents can see: the unimpressive body, the unpolished speech, the manual labour, the beatings. He denies only that these are the instruments he is fighting with. Ministry conducted this way is permanently vulnerable to the charge of weakness, because its actual weaponry is invisible to the criterion being applied, and Paul refuses to resolve the tension by acquiring more impressive credentials. He will instead spend the next three chapters making his weakness the argument. The strongholds Paul besieges are ideas. "Casting down imaginations, and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God" describes a war fought at the level of reasoning and pretension, and the objective is stated as a captivity: "bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ." Two things follow. First, the intellect is treated as genuinely important, worth besieging rather than bypassing, which is why Paul argues rather than merely asserts. Second, the goal is not the destruction of thought but its subjection, so that thinking continues under a new allegiance — a formula that has funded both rigorous Christian intellectual work and, when read carelessly, the suppression of inquiry. Verse six is the sentence readers skip, and it shows Paul's pastoral sequencing. He holds discipline "in a readiness to revenge all disobedience, when your obedience is fulfilled" — that is, he will not act against the ringleaders while the congregation's own loyalty is still undecided, because premature discipline would divide the church rather than heal it. The order matters: the community is given every opportunity to align itself first, and only the residue is disciplined. It is a striking refusal of the efficient course, which would be to strike at once, and it treats the church's free assent as worth waiting for even at the cost of prolonging the crisis. The critics' taunt in verse ten is preserved with unusual fidelity — "his bodily presence is weak, and his speech contemptible" — and Paul neither denies it nor promises to improve. His answer concerns consistency rather than impressiveness: what the letters say, the visit will do. This quietly relocates the question of a minister's credibility from performance to correspondence between word and deed, a standard that an unimpressive man can meet and an eloquent one can fail. It also explains the strange rhetorical texture of the following chapters, in which Paul boasts by cataloguing precisely the things that make him look unimpressive. The final movement identifies the real disease at Corinth as a system of measurement. Those who "commend themselves" are "measuring themselves by themselves, and comparing themselves among themselves," a closed loop that can always be won because it supplies its own scale. Paul answers with two external references: an assignment given by God — "the measure of the rule which God hath distributed to us" — and a verdict rendered by God, "not he that commendeth himself is approved, but whom the Lord commendeth." Between them they abolish the comparison entirely, since a man measured by a field he did not choose and a judge he cannot lobby has nothing to gain by ranking himself against his neighbours. Now I Paul myself beseech you by the meekness and gentleness of Christ, who in presence am base among you, but being absent am bold toward you: But I beseech you, that I may not be bold when I am present with that confidence, wherewith I think to be bold against some, which think of us as if we walked according to the flesh. For though we walk in the flesh, we do not war after the flesh: ( For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds;) Casting down imaginations, and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ; And having in a readiness to revenge all disobedience, when your obedience is fulfilled. Do ye look on things after the outward appearance? If any man trust to himself that he is Christ’s, let him of himself think this again, that, as he is Christ’s, even so are we Christ’s. For though I should boast somewhat more of our authority, which the Lord hath given us for edification, and not for your destruction, I should not be ashamed: That I may not seem as if I would terrify you by letters. For his letters, say they, are weighty and powerful; but his bodily presence is weak, and his speech contemptible. Let such an one think this, that, such as we are in word by letters when we are absent, such will we be also in deed when we are present. For we dare not make ourselves of the number, or compare ourselves with some that commend themselves: but they measuring themselves by themselves, and comparing themselves among themselves, are not wise. But we will not boast of things without our measure, but according to the measure of the rule which God hath distributed to us, a measure to reach even unto you. For we stretch not ourselves beyond our measure, as though we reached not unto you: for we are come as far as to you also in preaching the gospel of Christ: Not boasting of things without our measure, that is, of other men’s labours; but having hope, when your faith is increased, that we shall be enlarged by you according to our rule abundantly, To preach the gospel in the regions beyond you, and not to boast in another man’s line of things made ready to our hand. But he that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord. For not he that commendeth himself is approved, but whom the Lord commendeth.

label: 2 Corinthians 11
text: Paul asks permission to do something he considers beneath him — "Would to God ye could bear with me a little in my folly: and indeed bear with me" — and then explains the anxiety that drives him to it. He is not defending a reputation but guarding a betrothal: "I am jealous over you with godly jealousy: for I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ." The apostle stands in the position of the go-between responsible for delivering the bride intact, and the danger is seduction rather than assault, "lest by any means, as the serpent beguiled Eve through his subtilty, so your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ." What is at stake is named with heavy sarcasm in verse four: if the newcomers preached "another Jesus," gave "another spirit," or brought "another gospel," then the Corinthians' hospitality would at least be intelligible — "ye might well bear with him." Since they do not, the tolerance is inexplicable. He then plants a marker he will return to: "I suppose I was not a whit behind the very chiefest apostles," conceding the one point his critics can prove — "though I be rude in speech, yet not in knowledge" — and appealing to their own long experience of him, "we have been throughly made manifest among you in all things." From verse seven the argument narrows to money, which is evidently the sore point. He asks with real bewilderment whether refusing payment was itself the crime: "Have I committed an offence in abasing myself that ye might be exalted, because I have preached to you the gospel of God freely?" The self-mockery is sharp — "I robbed other churches, taking wages of them, to do you service" — and the record is exact: when he ran short at Corinth "I was chargeable to no man," because "that which was lacking to me the brethren which came from Macedonia supplied." He swears to keep the policy, "As the truth of Christ is in me, no man shall stop me of this boasting in the regions of Achaia," anticipates the obvious misreading — "Wherefore? because I love you not? God knoweth" — and states the strategic purpose plainly: to "cut off occasion from them which desire occasion," so that the rivals who glory in being supported must either match his terms or be exposed. The verdict on them follows without softening: "such are false apostles, deceitful workers, transforming themselves into the apostles of Christ," and the disguise is traced to its origin, "for Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light," so that ministers appearing as "ministers of righteousness" is no surprise at all, though "whose end shall be according to their works." Then the fool's speech proper begins. Paul asks to be received "as a fool," admits "I speak it not after the Lord, but as it were foolishly," and justifies it only by the fact that "many glory after the flesh." His irony turns on the Corinthians themselves: "ye suffer fools gladly, seeing ye yourselves are wise" — and the list of abuses they have absorbed without complaint is brutal, since they tolerate a man who will "bring you into bondage," "devour you," "take of you," "exalt himself," and even "smite you on the face." Against that, his own gentleness has looked like weakness. The credentials come first and are matched item for item — "Are they Hebrews? so am I. Are they Israelites? so am I. Are they the seed of Abraham? so am I" — until the question "Are they ministers of Christ?" breaks the pattern, because here he claims superiority and then proves it with a catalogue no rival would want to win: "in labours more abundant, in stripes above measure, in prisons more frequent, in deaths oft." What follows is the fullest surviving account of what apostolic work cost — five Jewish scourgings of thirty-nine lashes, three beatings with rods, a stoning, three shipwrecks, "a night and a day I have been in the deep," and then the eightfold roll of perils, from rivers and robbers to "perils among false brethren," followed by hunger, thirst, cold and nakedness. The climax is not physical at all: "Beside those things that are without, that which cometh upon me daily, the care of all the churches," a pressure he describes as sympathy stretched to the point of pain — "Who is weak, and I am not weak? who is offended, and I burn not?" He states the principle the whole list has been demonstrating, "If I must needs glory, I will glory of the things which concern mine infirmities," swears to its truth by "The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, which is blessed for evermore," and then, instead of ending on a triumph, ends on the least heroic memory he owns: hunted in Damascus by the governor's garrison, "through a window in a basket was I let down by the wall, and escaped his hands." Paul's jealousy is presented as an imitation of God's own and is explicitly not a proprietary feeling about his converts. He is "jealous over you with godly jealousy" precisely because he is not the husband: he has "espoused you to one husband," and his whole office is to hand the bride over undamaged. This reframes what could look like wounded possessiveness as fiduciary responsibility, and it sets the terms for everything that follows — his fury at the intruders is not competitive but protective, and his refusal of their money is part of the same refusal to become the object of the church's attachment. The corruption Paul fears is of the mind and comes by persuasion rather than force: "as the serpent beguiled Eve through his subtilty, so your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ." The Genesis parallel is precise, because Eve was not compelled but talked into an improvement on what God had said. What is threatened is simplicity, singleness of attachment, which can be lost by addition as easily as by denial — an enriched gospel with more impressive credentials attached is still a different gospel. This is why Paul treats sophistication as a danger rather than an asset and cheerfully concedes that he is "rude in speech." The money dispute is the key to the whole quarrel and it inverted the Corinthians' expectations completely. In a culture where a teacher's fee signalled his worth and his patrons' status, Paul's refusal to be supported read as an insult and as evidence that he did not rate his own teaching. He answers on three levels at once: as fact — the Macedonians covered him; as affection — "because I love you not? God knoweth"; and as strategy — he keeps the policy in order to "cut off occasion from them which desire occasion." The last is the sharpest, because it makes his poverty a trap: the rivals must either work for nothing or admit the difference. Verse fourteen supplies the diagnostic principle that governs Paul's assessment of his opponents and, by extension, all religious impressiveness. "Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light" means that counterfeit ministry will not look sinister; it will look better than the real thing, more polished, more evidently anointed, more credentialed. The consequence Paul draws is that appearance is worthless as evidence in either direction, which is why he can neither be discredited by looking unimpressive nor his rivals credited by looking impressive. The only criterion left is the one he adds at the end of the sentence: "whose end shall be according to their works." The list of sufferings is constructed as a parody of an honours inscription, and its ordering is deliberate. Ancestry and office are matched item for item, but the moment ministry is mentioned Paul abandons parity for excess and then fills the excess with beatings, shipwrecks, hunger and cold — the exact contents that would disqualify a man in the eyes of anyone keeping score. What makes the passage more than rhetoric is its final term: after everything external comes "the care of all the churches," and after that a description of a man whose nerves are wired into other people's failures, "Who is weak, and I am not weak? who is offended, and I burn not?" The heaviest thing he carries is not what was done to him. Paul ends the catalogue with the Damascus basket, and the choice is pointed. Ancient military honour prized the man first over a besieged wall; Paul remembers going the other way, lowered through a window in a laundry basket by friends, escaping rather than conquering. Placed after the swearing of an oath by the everlasting God, it functions as the signature on the whole boast: the one episode he selects for the climax is the one with the least dignity in it. The rhetorical logic of the fool's speech is complete only when the boasting ends in something faintly ridiculous, which is exactly what "I will glory of the things which concern mine infirmities" was always going to require. Would to God ye could bear with me a little in my folly: and indeed bear with me. For I am jealous over you with godly jealousy: for I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ. But I fear, lest by any means, as the serpent beguiled Eve through his subtilty, so your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ. For if he that cometh preacheth another Jesus, whom we have not preached, or if ye receive another spirit, which ye have not received, or another gospel, which ye have not accepted, ye might well bear with him. For I suppose I was not a whit behind the very chiefest apostles. But though I be rude in speech, yet not in knowledge; but we have been throughly made manifest among you in all things. Have I committed an offence in abasing myself that ye might be exalted, because I have preached to you the gospel of God freely? I robbed other churches, taking wages of them, to do you service. And when I was present with you, and wanted, I was chargeable to no man: for that which was lacking to me the brethren which came from Macedonia supplied: and in all things I have kept myself from being burdensome unto you, and so will I keep myself. As the truth of Christ is in me, no man shall stop me of this boasting in the regions of Achaia. Wherefore? because I love you not? God knoweth. But what I do, that I will do, that I may cut off occasion from them which desire occasion; that wherein they glory, they may be found even as we. For such are false apostles, deceitful workers, transforming themselves into the apostles of Christ. And no marvel; for Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light. Therefore it is no great thing if his ministers also be transformed as the ministers of righteousness; whose end shall be according to their works. I say again, Let no man think me a fool; if otherwise, yet as a fool receive me, that I may boast myself a little. That which I speak, I speak it not after the Lord, but as it were foolishly, in this confidence of boasting. Seeing that many glory after the flesh, I will glory also. For ye suffer fools gladly, seeing ye yourselves are wise. For ye suffer, if a man bring you into bondage, if a man devour you, if a man take of you, if a man exalt himself, if a man smite you on the face. I speak as concerning reproach, as though we had been weak. Howbeit whereinsoever any is bold, (I speak foolishly,) I am bold also. Are they Hebrews? so am I. Are they Israelites? so am I. Are they the seed of Abraham? so am I. Are they ministers of Christ? ( I speak as a fool) I am more; in labours more abundant, in stripes above measure, in prisons more frequent, in deaths oft. Of the Jews five times received I forty stripes save one. Thrice was I beaten with rods, once was I stoned, thrice I suffered shipwreck, a night and a day I have been in the deep; In journeyings often, in perils of waters, in perils of robbers, in perils by mine own countrymen, in perils by the heathen, in perils in the city, in perils in the wilderness, in perils in the sea, in perils among false brethren; In weariness and painfulness, in watchings often, in hunger and thirst, in fastings often, in cold and nakedness. Beside those things that are without, that which cometh upon me daily, the care of all the churches. Who is weak, and I am not weak? who is offended, and I burn not? If I must needs glory, I will glory of the things which concern mine infirmities. The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, which is blessed for evermore, knoweth that I lie not. In Damascus the governor under Aretas the king kept the city of the Damascenes with a garrison, desirous to apprehend me: And through a window in a basket was I let down by the wall, and escaped his hands.

label: 2 Corinthians 12
text: Paul reaches the one credential his rivals cannot match and immediately spoils it: "It is not expedient for me doubtless to glory. I will come to visions and revelations of the Lord." What follows is told in the third person, at a distance of fourteen years, and with the crucial detail deliberately withheld. "I knew a man in Christ above fourteen years ago, (whether in the body, I cannot tell; or whether out of the body, I cannot tell: God knoweth;) such an one caught up to the third heaven," and again, "caught up into paradise, and heard unspeakable words, which it is not lawful for a man to utter." The one experience that would settle every argument about his standing is reported without content, without date beyond a vague reckoning, and without the admission that it happened to him — until verse five gives the game away in the act of refusing to play it: "Of such an one will I glory: yet of myself I will not glory, but in mine infirmities." He could press the point truthfully — "though I would desire to glory, I shall not be a fool; for I will say the truth" — and declines on a principle that governs his whole self-presentation: "but now I forbear, lest any man should think of me above that which he seeth me to be, or that he heareth of me." He will be judged on what is visible. Then comes the counterweight God himself attached to the vision. "Lest I should be exalted above measure through the abundance of the revelations, there was given to me a thorn in the flesh, the messenger of Satan to buffet me," and the purpose clause is repeated at both ends of the sentence as though Paul cannot say it often enough. The affliction is never identified; it is described only as given, as a thorn, as a messenger of Satan, and as a continual buffeting. "For this thing I besought the Lord thrice, that it might depart from me" — a threefold prayer that receives an answer and a refusal in the same breath: "My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness." The reply reverses the request rather than granting it, and Paul's response reverses his own instincts: "Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me. Therefore I take pleasure in infirmities, in reproaches, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ’s sake: for when I am weak, then am I strong." With that the fool's speech collapses, and he blames his audience for it: "I am become a fool in glorying; ye have compelled me: for I ought to have been commended of you," adding the claim already made once before and now with a devastating tail — "in nothing am I behind the very chiefest apostles, though I be nothing." The evidence he offers is not the vision but the record they watched: "the signs of an apostle were wrought among you in all patience, in signs, and wonders, and mighty deeds," with patience listed first among the signs. Then the money returns, in the bitterest irony of the letter: "what is it wherein ye were inferior to other churches, except it be that I myself was not burdensome to you? forgive me this wrong." He announces a third visit on the same unaltered terms — "I will not be burdensome to you: for I seek not yours, but you" — and grounds it in the household rather than the market, "for the children ought not to lay up for the parents, but the parents for the children," before making the offer total and unbalanced: "I will very gladly spend and be spent for you; though the more abundantly I love you, the less I be loved." The last accusation is that the free preaching was a front, and Paul quotes it in his opponents' voice — "being crafty, I caught you with guile" — before demolishing it with names and dates: "Did I make a gain of you by any of them whom I sent unto you?
