I desired Titus, and with him I sent a brother. Did Titus make a gain of you? walked we not in the same spirit? walked we not in the same steps?" He then refuses the whole posture of self-defence: "think ye that we excuse ourselves unto you? we speak before God in Christ: but we do all things, dearly beloved, for your edifying." The chapter ends in dread rather than vindication. He fears the visit will find "debates, envyings, wraths, strifes, backbitings, whisperings, swellings, tumults," and worse, that "my God will humble me among you, and that I shall bewail many which have sinned already, and have not repented of the uncleanness and fornication and lasciviousness which they have committed." The rhetorical construction of verses two to five is the most disciplined thing in the letter. Paul possesses an unanswerable credential and disposes of it by every available means: third person, fourteen years' distance, no location that can be checked, no content that may be repeated, and an explicit refusal to attach it to himself. The effect is not modesty as a tone but modesty as a method — he removes the experience from the argument while proving he has one. Behind it stands the principle of verse six, that no one should think of him above "that which he seeth me to be," which makes visible conduct the only admissible evidence and rules out spiritual experience as a basis for authority over others. The thorn is given, and Paul says so twice over in the same sentence. It arrives as "a messenger of Satan to buffet me" and yet its stated purpose is God's — that he not be "exalted above measure" — so the same affliction serves an enemy's malice and a divine intention without contradiction. This is a compressed statement of how the New Testament handles evil in a believer's life: not denied, not attributed to God's own hand, and not left outside his purpose. The refusal to identify the ailment has been read as tactful and as deliberate, but its effect is unmistakable, since a named illness would have narrowed the passage to fellow sufferers and an unnamed one leaves it open to everyone who has prayed three times and been refused. "My grace is sufficient for thee" is the only saying of the risen Christ that Paul quotes directly, and it is an answer that declines the request. He asked for removal and received a promise of adequacy instead, which means the sufficiency of grace is demonstrated inside the trouble rather than by its end. The second clause explains why the trouble stays: "my strength is made perfect in weakness" — not that weakness is good, but that it is the condition under which divine power becomes visible as divine rather than as personal capacity. Everything Paul says afterwards about taking pleasure in infirmities is an inference from that one sentence, not an independent taste for suffering. The list in verse ten is not a spiritual mood but a set of concrete disadvantages, and each item is a thing his rivals would count as disqualifying: infirmities, reproaches, necessities, persecutions, distresses. Paul says he takes pleasure in them, and then supplies the qualifier that keeps the statement from being masochism — they are "for Christ’s sake." The paradox he ends on, "when I am weak, then am I strong," is therefore not a claim that weakness is a hidden form of strength but that it is the space Christ's power occupies. The apostle's whole quarrel with Corinth turns on this: they want a minister whose strength is his own, and he insists that such a minister would be useless to them. Verse twelve names patience first among the signs of an apostle, ahead of "signs, and wonders, and mighty deeds." The ordering is easy to miss and is doing real work, since the Corinthians are evidently impressed by displays and Paul is insisting that the miracles were performed by a man who kept his temper for eighteen months in a difficult city. Read with verse six's insistence on what people can see, it produces a criterion of ministry that is stubbornly observable: not the intensity of a man's inner experience, but whether he stayed, endured, and did not exploit anyone. The signs were genuine, but they are listed as accompaniments to a character. The chapter's ending refuses every satisfaction the fool's speech might have delivered. Having proved his case, Paul does not anticipate vindication but fears humiliation: that God "will humble me among you" and that he will have to "bewail many which have sinned already, and have not repented." The list of what he expects to find — debates, envyings, wraths, strifes, backbitings, whisperings, swellings, tumults — is a portrait of a congregation tearing at itself, and the unrepented sins named at the end are the same moral failures the first letter had already addressed. His dread is not for his reputation but for what he will have to do and what it will cost him, which is the strongest possible answer to the charge that he has been defending himself all along. It is not expedient for me doubtless to glory. I will come to visions and revelations of the Lord. I knew a man in Christ above fourteen years ago, ( whether in the body, I cannot tell; or whether out of the body, I cannot tell: God knoweth;) such an one caught up to the third heaven. And I knew such a man, ( whether in the body, or out of the body, I cannot tell: God knoweth;) How that he was caught up into paradise, and heard unspeakable words, which it is not lawful for a man to utter. Of such an one will I glory: yet of myself I will not glory, but in mine infirmities. For though I would desire to glory, I shall not be a fool; for I will say the truth: but now I forbear, lest any man should think of me above that which he seeth me to be, or that he heareth of me. And lest I should be exalted above measure through the abundance of the revelations, there was given to me a thorn in the flesh, the messenger of Satan to buffet me, lest I should be exalted above measure. For this thing I besought the Lord thrice, that it might depart from me. And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me. Therefore I take pleasure in infirmities, in reproaches, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ’s sake: for when I am weak, then am I strong. I am become a fool in glorying; ye have compelled me: for I ought to have been commended of you: for in nothing am I behind the very chiefest apostles, though I be nothing. Truly the signs of an apostle were wrought among you in all patience, in signs, and wonders, and mighty deeds. For what is it wherein ye were inferior to other churches, except it be that I myself was not burdensome to you? forgive me this wrong. Behold, the third time I am ready to come to you; and I will not be burdensome to you: for I seek not yours, but you: for the children ought not to lay up for the parents, but the parents for the children. And I will very gladly spend and be spent for you; though the more abundantly I love you, the less I be loved. But be it so, I did not burden you: nevertheless, being crafty, I caught you with guile. Did I make a gain of you by any of them whom I sent unto you? I desired Titus, and with him I sent a brother. Did Titus make a gain of you? walked we not in the same spirit? walked we not in the same steps? Again, think ye that we excuse ourselves unto you? we speak before God in Christ: but we do all things, dearly beloved, for your edifying. For I fear, lest, when I come, I shall not find you such as I would, and that I shall be found unto you such as ye would not: lest there be debates, envyings, wraths, strifes, backbitings, whisperings, swellings, tumults: And lest, when I come again, my God will humble me among you, and that I shall bewail many which have sinned already, and have not repented of the uncleanness and fornication and lasciviousness which they have committed.

label: 2 Corinthians 13
text: The letter's last chapter opens as a legal notice. "This is the third time I am coming to you. In the mouth of two or three witnesses shall every word be established" — Paul cites the Mosaic rule of evidence, and whether he means his three visits or the witnesses he intends to summon, the effect is to announce that the coming visit will be a hearing rather than a reunion. The warning is repeated in the awkward tenses of a man who has already said this once and is saying it again in advance: "I told you before, and foretell you, as if I were present, the second time; and being absent now I write to them which heretofore have sinned, and to all other, that, if I come again, I will not spare." His reason for the severity is their own demand: "Since ye seek a proof of Christ speaking in me, which to you-ward is not weak, but is mighty in you." They have asked him to prove that Christ speaks through him, and he warns them that they may get the demonstration they asked for and not enjoy it. Then, in a single sentence, he grounds the entire quarrel about weakness and power in the cross itself: "though he was crucified through weakness, yet he liveth by the power of God. For we also are weak in him, but we shall live with him by the power of God toward you." The pattern of Christ is the pattern of his minister — weakness that is real, followed by power that is God's and directed toward this congregation. Having been ordered to submit to examination, Paul turns the instrument around: "Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves. Know ye not your own selves, how that Jesus Christ is in you, except ye be reprobates?" The logic is disarming, because the Corinthians are themselves the evidence of his apostleship, so that any test they pass vindicates him and any test they fail indicts them along with him. He expresses confidence in the outcome — "I trust that ye shall know that we are not reprobates" — and then, remarkably, offers to lose the argument if it would help: "I pray to God that ye do no evil; not that we should appear approved, but that ye should do that which is honest, though we be as reprobates." He would rather be thought a failure and have them do right than be vindicated by their misconduct, which is the practical form of the maxim that follows: "we can do nothing against the truth, but for the truth." The same reversal governs verse nine — "we are glad, when we are weak, and ye are strong" — and the goal is named plainly, "this also we wish, even your perfection," a word suggesting repair and completion, the mending of what has been torn. The purpose of the whole letter is then stated outright: "Therefore I write these things being absent, lest being present I should use sharpness, according to the power which the Lord hath given me to edification, and not to destruction." The severity in the pages is spent precisely so that it need not be spent in person, and the authority is defined once more by what it is for. The closing lines fall into a rapid series of imperatives — "Finally, brethren, farewell. Be perfect, be of good comfort, be of one mind, live in peace" — each answering a specific fracture in the church, with a promise attached: "the God of love and peace shall be with you." Then the ordinary greetings, "Greet one another with an holy kiss. All the saints salute you," and finally the fullest benediction in the Pauline letters, given to the most fractious congregation he ever wrote to: "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost, be with you all. Amen." Paul frames the visit with a rule of evidence rather than a threat of force. Invoking "two or three witnesses" places his coming inside a procedure the Corinthians can recognise and hold him to, which is a considerable concession from a man they have accused of ruling by intimidating letters. Discipline conducted under a known rule cannot be arbitrary, and the citation quietly answers the charge of verse ten in the previous chapter: the apostle who is said to terrify by post is committing himself in advance to the same standards of proof that protect any accused person under the Law. Severity and due process arrive in the same sentence. Verse four is the theological heart of the letter compressed into two clauses. "He was crucified through weakness, yet he liveth by the power of God" establishes that in the decisive event of the faith, weakness and power were not alternatives but sequence, and Paul then applies the sequence to himself: "we also are weak in him, but we shall live with him by the power of God toward you." This settles the argument that has run since chapter ten. The Corinthians' criterion — a minister should look strong — would have disqualified Christ on Good Friday, and the pattern of the crucified and risen Lord is not an exception to how God works but the template for how his servants are to be recognised. The reversal in verse five is one of Paul's sharpest moves and is easy to miss because the sentence has been so thoroughly detached from its setting. They have been auditing him; he tells them to audit themselves — "Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves" — and the question is not framed as a threat but as an appeal to something they already know, "Know ye not your own selves, how that Jesus Christ is in you." The apostle's credentials and the congregation's own standing turn out to be the same fact viewed from two sides, so a church that questions its founder's legitimacy is standing on a branch it is sawing through. Verse seven is the most generous sentence Paul ever wrote about his own reputation. He prays that they will do no evil "not that we should appear approved, but that ye should do that which is honest, though we be as reprobates" — accepting, hypothetically, permanent disgrace as the price of their integrity. Coming at the end of four chapters of self-defence, it retroactively reframes the whole apologia: he has argued for his standing not because he needs it but because their acceptance of the gospel is bound up with it, and the moment those two can be separated he abandons his own case without hesitation. The maxim that follows, "we can do nothing against the truth, but for the truth," is his explanation: an apostle has no power that can be used against reality. The word rendered "perfection" in verse nine and "be perfect" in verse eleven carries the sense of setting a broken thing right — mending a net, resetting a bone, restoring what has been dislocated. Read that way, the letter's closing wish is exactly matched to its subject: a congregation fractured by factions, damaged by a painful confrontation, and pulled apart by rival teachers is asked to be put back together. The imperatives that follow are correspondingly specific to the diagnosis — comfort for those wounded by the severe letter, one mind against the parties, peace against the debates and tumults he feared in the previous chapter — and the promise attached names God by the two qualities the church has been short of. The final benediction is remarkable for where it lands. Paul names Father, Son, and Spirit in one breath, assigning grace to Christ, love to God, and communion to the Holy Ghost, and he pronounces it over the congregation that has caused him more grief than any other. The order is worth noticing, since grace comes first as the point of access and communion last as the result, and the whole is given "to you all" — including, presumably, the party that has been attacking him. Whatever the visit will bring, the letter ends by placing the entire church, unresolved quarrels and all, inside the life of the God whose fellowship it has been failing to reflect. This is the third time I am coming to you. In the mouth of two or three witnesses shall every word be established. I told you before, and foretell you, as if I were present, the second time; and being absent now I write to them which heretofore have sinned, and to all other, that, if I come again, I will not spare: Since ye seek a proof of Christ speaking in me, which to you-ward is not weak, but is mighty in you. For though he was crucified through weakness, yet he liveth by the power of God. For we also are weak in him, but we shall live with him by the power of God toward you. Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves. Know ye not your own selves, how that Jesus Christ is in you, except ye be reprobates? But I trust that ye shall know that we are not reprobates. Now I pray to God that ye do no evil; not that we should appear approved, but that ye should do that which is honest, though we be as reprobates. For we can do nothing against the truth, but for the truth. For we are glad, when we are weak, and ye are strong: and this also we wish, even your perfection. Therefore I write these things being absent, lest being present I should use sharpness, according to the power which the Lord hath given me to edification, and not to destruction. Finally, brethren, farewell. Be perfect, be of good comfort, be of one mind, live in peace; and the God of love and peace shall be with you. Greet one another with an holy kiss. All the saints salute you. The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost, be with you all. Amen.

label: Galatians 1
text: The letter opens by arguing before it has finished introducing itself. Paul names himself "an apostle" and then interrupts his own salutation with a parenthesis that is really the thesis of the first two chapters: "not of men, neither by man, but by Jesus Christ, and God the Father, who raised him from the dead." Every other letter he writes can afford a quieter opening; this one cannot, because the question at Galatia is whether Paul's message has any standing that the Jerusalem-credentialed teachers now among them do not outrank. He adds "all the brethren which are with me" so that the letter cannot be dismissed as one man's grievance, addresses it flatly "unto the churches of Galatia" without a single word of commendation, and folds the whole gospel into the greeting: Christ "gave himself for our sins, that he might deliver us from this present evil world, according to the will of God and our Father." The rescue is from an age, not merely from a ledger of offences, and it was the Father's will, not a concession wrung out of him — two claims that will matter when the argument turns to law. Then comes the omission every ancient reader would have felt: where the thanksgiving belongs, Paul writes "I marvel." He does not say he marvels that they have left his teaching but that they "are so soon removed from him that called you into the grace of Christ," making the defection personal to God rather than to himself, and "so soon" registers both speed and shock. What they have turned to is "another gospel: Which is not another" — a rival that fails even to qualify as a rival, since a gospel that adds a requirement is not a variant good news but the abolition of good news. The agitators are described with deliberate vagueness, "some that trouble you," and their work with a strong verb, they "would pervert the gospel of Christ." Paul then pronounces the sentence twice, and the doubling is the point: "though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed," and again, "If any man preach any other gospel unto you than that ye have received, let him be accursed." He puts himself first in the list of possible offenders and an angel second, which removes the appeal from any authority whatever, including his own, and grounds it in the content already delivered and already received. The bitter question of verse ten — "do I now persuade men, or God? or do I seek to please men?" — is almost certainly quoting an accusation back at his accusers, who evidently said that Paul had dropped circumcision to make converts cheaply; his answer is that a man-pleaser is by definition not "the servant of Christ," and that a curse pronounced on oneself is poor evidence of flattery. From verse eleven the argument becomes autobiography, and the biography is offered as proof: "the gospel which was preached of me is not after man. For I neither received it of man, neither was I taught it, but by the revelation of Jesus Christ." He then narrates a life that could not possibly have produced this message by ordinary transmission. He was not a sympathetic outsider but the church's most effective enemy, who "beyond measure I persecuted the church of God, and wasted it," and no lukewarm adherent of the tradition he now relativizes: he "profited in the Jews’ religion above many my equals in mine own nation, being more exceedingly zealous of the traditions of my fathers." The turn is described entirely in the passive voice of divine initiative: "when it pleased God, who separated me from my mother’s womb, and called me by his grace, To reveal his Son in me." The purpose is given in the same breath as the call — "that I might preach him among the heathen" — so that the Gentile mission is not a later strategic decision but the content of the commission itself. What follows is a chronology assembled to close off every route by which he might have been catechized: "immediately I conferred not with flesh and blood: Neither went I up to Jerusalem to them which were apostles before me; but I went into Arabia, and returned again unto Damascus." Only "after three years" does he go to Jerusalem, and then the visit is small and private — fifteen days with Peter, no other apostle "save James the Lord’s brother" — after which he disappears into "the regions of Syria and Cilicia." Under oath he insists on the record, "behold, before God, I lie not," and then delivers the detail that finishes the argument: he "was unknown by face unto the churches of Judaea which were in Christ," who knew him only by report, "That he which persecuted us in times past now preacheth the faith which once he destroyed." The chapter ends not with Paul vindicated but with God praised: "And they glorified God in me." The one place where the churches of Judea and the apostle agree is that what happened to him was God's work, which is precisely what he needs the Galatians to concede. Paul refuses to let the dispute be framed as a quarrel between teachers, and the refusal shapes the whole chapter. He does not write that the Galatians have abandoned him, or his party, or his interpretation; he writes that they are "removed from him that called you into the grace of Christ." The agitators presumably presented themselves as supplementing Paul rather than replacing him — keep his gospel, add the mark of the covenant — and his answer is that there is no arithmetic in which a gospel can be added to. "Another gospel: Which is not another" is not a rhetorical flourish but a claim about the kind of thing the gospel is: an announcement of something completed, which a supplement contradicts rather than enriches. Once grace is one ingredient among two, it has already ceased to be grace, and the church that thought it was adding has in fact exchanged. The anathema of verses eight and nine is the least self-serving sentence Paul ever wrote, because he places himself inside its reach. "Though we, or an angel from heaven" makes the messenger irrelevant and the message decisive, and it means Paul is not asking Galatia to trust him. He is asking them to hold him, and any future claimant, to a standard they already possess — "that which we have preached unto you" and "that ye have received." This is the deep logic of the passage: the gospel is a deposit, publicly delivered and publicly received, and therefore something against which even apostolic and angelic voices can be measured. The doubling of the curse, unusual in Paul, signals that this is formal speech rather than temper; he is pronouncing a sentence, not venting. Verse ten is Paul quoting his opponents' charge and turning it inside out. The accusation was evidently that he softened the requirements to win a wider hearing, a preacher trimming his terms for the market. His reply concedes nothing about motives and instead points at the shape of his life: a man who wanted to please men would not curse his critics, would not have chosen a message that cost him his standing in the world where he had "profited" above his equals, and would not accept the persecution he will later say he still suffers precisely because he no longer preaches circumcision. The sentence "if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ" is not a proverb about boldness; it is an argument from consequences, and the word "yet" concedes that he once did seek that approval, in the years when zeal for the traditions of his fathers was the surest path to it. The autobiography is not a personal testimony in the devotional sense but a chain of evidence with a specific negative conclusion: there is no human channel through which Paul could have received what he preaches. He was formed in the opposite direction, "more exceedingly zealous of the traditions of my fathers," so the message cannot be explained by sympathy or drift; he did not confer with flesh and blood, did not go to Jerusalem, and left immediately for Arabia, so it cannot be explained by instruction; when he finally did go, he stayed fifteen days with one apostle and saw only one other, which is too little for a curriculum and too public to deny. Even the oath — "before God, I lie not" — belongs to the argument rather than to the emotion, because he is reciting dates and places that could be checked, and the checking is the point. The description of the call deliberately borrows the language used of the prophets. God "separated me from my mother’s womb, and called me by his grace," which places the decisive act before Paul existed, let alone before he behaved well or badly, and makes his persecuting years part of the story of a man already set apart rather than an obstacle overcome. The phrase "to reveal his Son in me" is stranger than the usual translation of a vision granted to him; the revelation is located within, and its stated purpose is outward — "that I might preach him among the heathen." Vocation and content arrive together. Paul does not receive a message and then look for an audience; the Gentile mission is inside the revelation, which is exactly why an added requirement of circumcision for Gentiles strikes him as an attack on the revelation itself and not as a difference in pastoral policy. The chapter's last four verses quietly undercut the assumption that independence means isolation. Paul insists he was "unknown by face unto the churches of Judaea," but he takes care to record that those churches, hearing of him, "glorified God in me." His gospel was not derived from Jerusalem, yet it was recognized there; he owes nothing to the mother church by way of instruction and is nevertheless in visible communion with it. The distinction he is drawing is between the source of the message and the fellowship of the messengers, and the whole force of the opening chapters depends on holding both. He will not surrender the first, and he will not do without the second, which is why the very next chapter takes him back to Jerusalem to have the matter settled in the open. Paul, an apostle, ( not of men, neither by man, but by Jesus Christ, and God the Father, who raised him from the dead;) And all the brethren which are with me, unto the churches of Galatia: Grace be to you and peace from God the Father, and from our Lord Jesus Christ, Who gave himself for our sins, that he might deliver us from this present evil world, according to the will of God and our Father: To whom be glory for ever and ever. Amen. I marvel that ye are so soon removed from him that called you into the grace of Christ unto another gospel: Which is not another; but there be some that trouble you, and would pervert the gospel of Christ. But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed. As we said before, so say I now again, If any man preach any other gospel unto you than that ye have received, let him be accursed. For do I now persuade men, or God? or do I seek to please men? for if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ. But I certify you, brethren, that the gospel which was preached of me is not after man. For I neither received it of man, neither was I taught it, but by the revelation of Jesus Christ. For ye have heard of my conversation in time past in the Jews’ religion, how that beyond measure I persecuted the church of God, and wasted it: And profited in the Jews’ religion above many my equals in mine own nation, being more exceedingly zealous of the traditions of my fathers. But when it pleased God, who separated me from my mother’s womb, and called me by his grace, To reveal his Son in me, that I might preach him among the heathen; immediately I conferred not with flesh and blood: Neither went I up to Jerusalem to them which were apostles before me; but I went into Arabia, and returned again unto Damascus. Then after three years I went up to Jerusalem to see Peter, and abode with him fifteen days. But other of the apostles saw I none, save James the Lord’s brother. Now the things which I write unto you, behold, before God, I lie not. Afterwards I came into the regions of Syria and Cilicia; And was unknown by face unto the churches of Judaea which were in Christ: But they had heard only, That he which persecuted us in times past now preacheth the faith which once he destroyed. And they glorified God in me.

label: Galatians 2
text: The chapter completes the chronology and then turns it into doctrine. "Fourteen years after" Paul goes up to Jerusalem again, and every detail of the sentence is chosen: he travels "with Barnabas," a man Jerusalem trusts, and he "took Titus with me also," an uncircumcised Greek carried into the capital of the circumcision as a living test case. He insists that he went "by revelation" and not by summons, so that even the journey is not an act of submission, and yet he did go, and he did lay the matter out — "communicated unto them that gospel which I preach among the Gentiles, but privately to them which were of reputation, lest by any means I should run, or had run, in vain." That last clause is startlingly candid: a man who has just denied receiving his gospel from men concedes that a rupture with Jerusalem would have wrecked the mission, not because the message would have become false but because a divided church could not have carried it. The outcome is stated as a fact rather than a concession: "neither Titus, who was with me, being a Greek, was compelled to be circumcised." Pressure was applied — Paul blames "false brethren unawares brought in, who came in privily to spy out our liberty which we have in Christ Jesus, that they might bring us into bondage" — and he records his refusal in a sentence that will not soften, "we gave place by subjection, no, not for an hour; that the truth of the gospel might continue with you." The reason is pastoral and forward-looking: had Titus been circumcised as a diplomatic gesture, the Galatians reading this letter would already have their answer. Toward the Jerusalem leadership Paul is respectful and pointedly unimpressed at the same time. He calls them "these who seemed to be somewhat," adds the almost brusque aside "whatsoever they were, it maketh no matter to me: God accepteth no man’s person," and reports the result as a negative: "they who seemed to be somewhat in conference added nothing to me." What they did instead was recognize what was already there — "when they saw that the gospel of the uncircumcision was committed unto me, as the gospel of the circumcision was unto Peter," and "he that wrought effectually in Peter to the apostleship of the circumcision, the same was mighty in me toward the Gentiles." The single gospel is not divided; the fields are. So "James, Cephas, and John, who seemed to be pillars, perceived the grace that was given unto me," and the settlement is sealed with a gesture rather than a document: "they gave to me and Barnabas the right hands of fellowship." One stipulation is attached, and it is not about circumcision: "Only they would that we should remember the poor; the same which I also was forward to do." The narrative then swings from agreement to confrontation without transition. "But when Peter was come to Antioch, I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed." The offence was not a doctrine but a movement of the body: Peter had been eating with Gentile believers, and "when certain came from James... he withdrew and separated himself, fearing them which were of the circumcision." Paul names the motive as fear, and he names the consequence as contagion — "the other Jews dissembled likewise with him; insomuch that Barnabas also was carried away with their dissimulation." That Barnabas, his own colleague and the man who had vouched for him in Jerusalem, was swept along is the measure of what a single withdrawal from a table could do. Paul's charge is that the practice contradicted the message: "they walked not uprightly according to the truth of the gospel," and so he spoke "unto Peter before them all," publicly because the act had been public. The rebuke is framed as an exposure of inconsistency rather than of heresy: "If thou, being a Jew, livest after the manner of Gentiles, and not as do the Jews, why compellest thou the Gentiles to live as do the Jews?" Peter's own table habits had already conceded the point his retreat now denied, and the pressure of that retreat was coercive even though no rule was announced, since Gentiles who wished to keep eating with the apostles would have to become Jews to do it. From verse fifteen the speech to Peter shades imperceptibly into the letter's argument, and it is impossible to say where one ends. Paul begins on the inside of the objection — "We who are Jews by nature, and not sinners of the Gentiles" — and then turns that birthright inside out: even we, who had the law, "knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ, even we have believed in Jesus Christ, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ, and not by the works of the law: for by the works of the law shall no flesh be justified." The threefold repetition in a single verse is not clumsiness; it is a nail driven three times. He then answers the predictable objection that this makes Christ an accomplice in sin — if seeking justification in Christ lands Jews in the same category as Gentile "sinners," then Christ has served sin — with a flat "God forbid," and reverses the logic: "if I build again the things which I destroyed, I make myself a transgressor." It is the rebuilding, not the demolition, that creates the offence, which is exactly what Peter's withdrawal amounted to. Then the argument becomes autobiography again, but of a different kind: "I through the law am dead to the law, that I might live unto God. I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me: and the life which I now live in the flesh I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself for me." The law itself brought him to a death it could not reverse, and what came out the other side is a life he can only describe by first denying that it is his. The chapter closes with a sentence that measures everything else in the letter: "I do not frustrate the grace of God: for if righteousness come by the law, then Christ is dead in vain." The Jerusalem episode is constructed to prove two things that pull in opposite directions, and Paul refuses to sacrifice either. He went "by revelation" and not under orders, submitted his gospel to no one's judgment, and reports that the pillars "added nothing to me" — his message is not derivative. Yet he also admits he sought the meeting "lest by any means I should run, or had run, in vain," which concedes that a gospel repudiated by Jerusalem would have produced a broken and unworkable church even while remaining true. The resolution is the handshake: the leaders do not authorize Paul, they recognize him, having "perceived the grace that was given unto me." Recognition presupposes that the thing recognized was already there and did not come from the recognizers, and it also presupposes that it mattered enormously whether they saw it. Titus is the argument in person, and the sentence about him is carefully negative: he "was not compelled to be circumcised." Paul does not say the question was never raised — the very next clause blames "false brethren" who "came in privily to spy out our liberty" — so the picture is of a real fight, real pressure, and a refusal held for the sake of people not in the room. "We gave place by subjection, no, not for an hour; that the truth of the gospel might continue with you" ties the outcome directly to the Galatians reading the letter. The stakes were not Titus's comfort but a precedent, since a single accommodation offered for peace would have established that Gentile believers are second-class until they submit. Paul's later willingness to circumcise Timothy, whose mother was Jewish, is not inconsistent with this; the difference is that nothing was being conceded there about who belongs. The Antioch confrontation is about behaviour rather than belief, and that is precisely why Paul treats it as a gospel crisis. Peter did not teach that Gentiles must be circumcised; he simply stopped eating with them, and Paul's charge is that they "walked not uprightly according to the truth of the gospel." A doctrine can be affirmed at a distance, but a table is a verdict, and a withdrawal from one says who is fully in and who is on probation more loudly than any statement. Paul also identifies the motive without euphemism — "fearing them which were of the circumcision" — and traces the damage: the other Jewish believers followed, and even Barnabas "was carried away with their dissimulation." The word for it is dissimulation, play-acting, because their conduct no longer matched what they knew, and the speed of the collapse shows how much a single leader's body language can teach. Paul's argument to Peter turns on an inconsistency rather than an error, and its logic is worth following closely. Peter, a Jew, had been living "after the manner of Gentiles" — he had already been persuaded that the old boundaries no longer determined fellowship, and he had eaten accordingly. His retreat did not merely revert to a private scruple; it silently imposed a condition on others, which is why Paul says he "compellest thou the Gentiles to live as do the Jews" though Peter had commanded nothing. Compulsion here is structural, not verbal: when the leading apostle will not eat with you unless you take on the law, the law has become the price of full membership whatever anyone says. That is the shape of the pressure Paul detects in Galatia too, where nobody had denied the sufficiency of Christ, only added a further step. Verse sixteen is the letter's hinge, and its rhetorical structure carries part of its meaning. Paul states the principle, applies it to himself and Peter as Jews who already had the law, and then restates it as a universal — "for by the works of the law shall no flesh be justified" — moving from a shared conviction to an unlimited one. He also frames the whole thing as something already "known" between them, not a novelty he is introducing, which is why the rebuke can be so direct. The word rendered "justified" belongs to the courtroom and to the covenant at once, and the passive keeps the acting subject offstage: no one justifies himself here. What Paul is dismantling is not moral effort but the idea that a person is brought into right standing with God by taking on the identity markers and obligations of the law, and his evidence is that Jews who had all of that turned to Christ anyway. The three sentences from verse nineteen to twenty-one refuse to let justification remain a transaction. "I through the law am dead to the law" says that the law itself, honestly followed, brought Paul to the end of what it could do; "I am crucified with Christ" says that the death he underwent was not merely the collapse of an old system but a participation in a particular death. Then the extraordinary correction: "nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me." Paul does not say he has been forgiven and is now trying harder, nor that he has been replaced; he asserts and denies his own agency in the same breath, and then locates the ongoing life in a relation — "the life which I now live in the flesh I live by the faith of the Son of God." The chapter's last line makes the whole argument a matter of honour rather than technique: to seek righteousness by the law is to say the cross was unnecessary, and Paul will not "frustrate the grace of God" by implying that Christ died for nothing. Then fourteen years after I went up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas, and took Titus with me also. And I went up by revelation, and communicated unto them that gospel which I preach among the Gentiles, but privately to them which were of reputation, lest by any means I should run, or had run, in vain. But neither Titus, who was with me, being a Greek, was compelled to be circumcised: And that because of false brethren unawares brought in, who came in privily to spy out our liberty which we have in Christ Jesus, that they might bring us into bondage: To whom we gave place by subjection, no, not for an hour; that the truth of the gospel might continue with you. But of these who seemed to be somewhat, ( whatsoever they were, it maketh no matter to me: God accepteth no man’s person:) for they who seemed to be somewhat in conference added nothing to me: But contrariwise, when they saw that the gospel of the uncircumcision was committed unto me, as the gospel of the circumcision was unto Peter; ( For he that wrought effectually in Peter to the apostleship of the circumcision, the same was mighty in me toward the Gentiles:) And when James, Cephas, and John, who seemed to be pillars, perceived the grace that was given unto me, they gave to me and Barnabas the right hands of fellowship; that we should go unto the heathen, and they unto the circumcision. Only they would that we should remember the poor; the same which I also was forward to do. But when Peter was come to Antioch, I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed. For before that certain came from James, he did eat with the Gentiles: but when they were come, he withdrew and separated himself, fearing them which were of the circumcision. And the other Jews dissembled likewise with him; insomuch that Barnabas also was carried away with their dissimulation. But when I saw that they walked not uprightly according to the truth of the gospel, I said unto Peter before them all, If thou, being a Jew, livest after the manner of Gentiles, and not as do the Jews, why compellest thou the Gentiles to live as do the Jews? We who are Jews by nature, and not sinners of the Gentiles, Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ, even we have believed in Jesus Christ, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ, and not by the works of the law: for by the works of the law shall no flesh be justified. But if, while we seek to be justified by Christ, we ourselves also are found sinners, is therefore Christ the minister of sin? God forbid. For if I build again the things which I destroyed, I make myself a transgressor. For I through the law am dead to the law, that I might live unto God. I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me: and the life which I now live in the flesh I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself for me. I do not frustrate the grace of God: for if righteousness come by the law, then Christ is dead in vain.

label: Galatians 3
text: Paul stops narrating and turns on his readers: "O foolish Galatians, who hath bewitched you, that ye should not obey the truth, before whose eyes Jesus Christ hath been evidently set forth, crucified among you?" The accusation of witchcraft is not decorative; it means their behaviour has no rational explanation, since the crucifixion was placarded before them in public preaching and they have somehow looked away from it. He then declines to argue from Scripture at first and argues from their own memory instead: "This only would I learn of you, Received ye the Spirit by the works of the law, or by the hearing of faith?" The question is unanswerable in the wrong direction, because they had no law when the Spirit came. The follow-up presses the absurdity of their trajectory — "having begun in the Spirit, are ye now made perfect by the flesh?" — and adds a note of real grief, "Have ye suffered so many things in vain?", immediately half-retracted by "if it be yet in vain," as though Paul cannot bring himself to close the door. He restates the question in the present tense, since the Spirit is still being ministered and miracles are still being worked "among you," and asks again whether this comes "by the works of the law, or by the hearing of faith." Only then does he go to Scripture, and he goes straight to the man his opponents were surely appealing to: "Even as Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness." From that single verse he draws a conclusion that would have startled his readers — "they which are of faith, the same are the children of Abraham" — redefining descent by faith rather than by flesh, and then reads the promise to Abraham as an anticipation of the Gentile mission: "the scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the heathen through faith, preached before the gospel unto Abraham, saying, In thee shall all nations be blessed." The blessing is therefore not a reward attached to law-keeping but a promise made before the law existed, and "they which be of faith are blessed with faithful Abraham." The other side of the ledger is a curse. "As many as are of the works of the law are under the curse," and the proof is drawn from the law's own sanctions: "Cursed is every one that continueth not in all things which are written in the book of the law to do them." The law demands totality, and Paul takes the demand seriously enough to treat partial compliance as no compliance at all. He then sets two texts against each other — "The just shall live by faith" and "The man that doeth them shall live in them" — and concludes that these describe two incompatible principles: "the law is not of faith." Into that impasse he places the cross in its most scandalous form: "Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us: for it is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree." The verse that the earliest opponents of the gospel would have quoted against a crucified messiah is turned into the mechanism of rescue, and the purpose is stated with the Gentiles in view — "That the blessing of Abraham might come on the Gentiles through Jesus Christ; that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith." Paul then argues from ordinary legal practice: "Though it be but a man’s covenant, yet if it be confirmed, no man disannulleth, or addeth thereto." If human agreements cannot be amended unilaterally after ratification, a divine promise certainly cannot, and "the law, which was four hundred and thirty years after, cannot disannul" a covenant already confirmed. Along the way he presses a single word to its limit: the promises were made to Abraham "and his seed," and "He saith not, And to seeds, as of many; but as of one, And to thy seed, which is Christ." The inheritance is therefore either promise or law and cannot be both — "if the inheritance be of the law, it is no more of promise: but God gave it to Abraham by promise." This raises the obvious objection, and Paul asks it himself: "Wherefore then serveth the law?" The answer is deliberately modest. It "was added because of transgressions," it had a term — "till the seed should come to whom the promise was made" — and it came at two removes, "ordained by angels in the hand of a mediator," whereas the promise was spoken by God to Abraham with no intermediary at all, which is the point of the cryptic remark that "a mediator is not a mediator of one, but God is one." Lest this sound like an attack, he asks the further question — "Is the law then against the promises of God?" — and answers "God forbid," with a concession that is also a diagnosis: had any law been capable of giving life, righteousness would indeed have come that way. Instead "the scripture hath concluded all under sin," locking everyone in so that the promise could be given on the only terms that could reach them, "by faith of Jesus Christ... to them that believe." The imprisonment is then described more gently: "before faith came, we were kept under the law, shut up unto the faith which should afterwards be revealed," and the law becomes "our schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ" — the household slave who escorted a child to his lessons, with real authority and a strictly temporary office — "But after that faith is come, we are no longer under a schoolmaster." The chapter ends by naming what the Galatians already are, in language that answers every anxiety the agitators had stirred: "ye are all the children of God by faith in Christ Jesus. For as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ. There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus." The final sentence closes the circle back to verse six: "And if ye be Christ’s, then are ye Abraham’s seed, and heirs according to the promise." They were being told they had to become Abraham's children; Paul tells them they already are, by belonging to the one Seed. Paul's first argument is not exegetical but experiential, and it is the more devastating for it. He asks the Galatians to remember an event they cannot dispute: the Spirit came upon them, with visible effects that are still occurring, at a time when they had no relationship to the law at all. "Received ye the Spirit by the works of the law, or by the hearing of faith?" cannot be answered wrongly, which is why he calls it the one thing he wishes to learn from them. The force of the question depends on the Spirit being something recognizable rather than a doctrine, and Paul plainly assumes it was — he speaks of miracles worked among them in the present tense. The argument is therefore that the Galatians are being asked to adopt a system that their own history has already bypassed, and that adding the law now would reverse the order of their entire Christian existence: "having begun in the Spirit, are ye now made perfect by the flesh?" By going to Abraham, Paul takes the fight onto his opponents' strongest ground. Anyone urging circumcision would have cited Abraham, who received circumcision as the sign of the covenant, and would have offered it to Gentiles as the way into his family. Paul's counter is chronological and textual at once: the verse that credits Abraham with righteousness records a moment of belief, and the promise that all nations would be blessed in him was spoken long before the law and even before the covenant sign. He therefore reads the promise as an anticipatory gospel — "the scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the heathen through faith, preached before the gospel unto Abraham" — which makes the Gentile mission the fulfilment of the Abrahamic covenant rather than an exception to it. The result is a redefinition of lineage: descent is by faith, so that Gentile believers are not admitted as guests to someone else's family but are children in it. The curse argument in verse ten is easy to misread as pessimism about human capacity, and it may be better read as an argument about the terms of the arrangement itself. Paul quotes the law's own conclusion — the curse falls on anyone who "continueth not in all things" — and treats the totality as decisive. To place oneself under law as the basis of standing is to accept an all-or-nothing arrangement in which any failure is fatal, and no provision inside that arrangement changes its terms. Against this he sets two scriptural principles that cannot be combined: "The just shall live by faith" and "The man that doeth them shall live in them." Both are in the sacred text, and Paul does not deny the second; he says the two describe different modes of life, and that only one of them is now operative for standing before God, because the first was always the deeper word. Verse thirteen is the letter's most compressed statement of the atonement, and its audacity is easy to miss. The text Paul quotes about a body hanging on a tree was the standard objection to a crucified messiah, since the manner of death appeared to place Jesus under God's own condemnation. Paul does not evade this; he affirms it and makes it the mechanism of rescue — "being made a curse for us" — so that the strongest argument against the gospel becomes its centre. Two things follow. The curse is real and is borne, not waived, which is why Paul can say the law's demand was satisfied rather than ignored. And the purpose is stated in terms that answer the Galatian crisis directly: the exchange happened so that "the blessing of Abraham might come on the Gentiles," which means the cross is the reason Gentiles need not enter through the law. Paul's treatment of the law is remarkably free of contempt, and the qualifications matter as much as the argument. He denies that it can justify, denies that it can give life, and dates it to a specific and limited term, yet he explicitly refuses the conclusion that it opposes God's promises — "Is the law then against the promises of God? God forbid" — and he assigns it real work: it was "added because of transgressions" and it kept its charges under guard until faith came. The image of the schoolmaster is precise: an escort with genuine authority over a child who is nonetheless the heir, whose whole function is to deliver him somewhere and then stop. To reintroduce that custodian after the destination has been reached is not stricter obedience but a refusal of the arrangement's own logic, which is why Paul treats the Galatian move as regression rather than as excess of zeal. The three couplets of verse twenty-eight are not a general manifesto detached from the argument but the conclusion of it, and their order is telling: the ethnic pair is the one actually in dispute, the social and sexual pairs are added because the same logic dissolves them. The claim is made about a specific location — "in Christ Jesus" — and about a specific new status, since the preceding verse says believers "have put on Christ" like a garment, so that what is seen is his identity rather than their categories. Paul does not say the distinctions have ceased to exist; Jews remain Jews and slaves remain slaves in the world he is writing to. He says they no longer determine membership, standing, or inheritance, which is precisely what circumcision was being offered to secure. And the closing verse makes the point unmistakable: belonging to Christ, the single Seed, is what makes a person Abraham's offspring, so the Galatians already possess what they were being asked to purchase. O foolish Galatians, who hath bewitched you, that ye should not obey the truth, before whose eyes Jesus Christ hath been evidently set forth, crucified among you? This only would I learn of you, Received ye the Spirit by the works of the law, or by the hearing of faith? Are ye so foolish? having begun in the Spirit, are ye now made perfect by the flesh? Have ye suffered so many things in vain? if it be yet in vain. He therefore that ministereth to you the Spirit, and worketh miracles among you, doeth he it by the works of the law, or by the hearing of faith? Even as Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness. Know ye therefore that they which are of faith, the same are the children of Abraham. And the scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the heathen through faith, preached before the gospel unto Abraham, saying, In thee shall all nations be blessed. So then they which be of faith are blessed with faithful Abraham. For as many as are of the works of the law are under the curse: for it is written, Cursed is every one that continueth not in all things which are written in the book of the law to do them. But that no man is justified by the law in the sight of God, it is evident: for, The just shall live by faith. And the law is not of faith: but, The man that doeth them shall live in them. Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us: for it is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree: That the blessing of Abraham might come on the Gentiles through Jesus Christ; that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith. Brethren, I speak after the manner of men; Though it be but a man’s covenant, yet if it be confirmed, no man disannulleth, or addeth thereto. Now to Abraham and his seed were the promises made. He saith not, And to seeds, as of many; but as of one, And to thy seed, which is Christ. And this I say, that the covenant, that was confirmed before of God in Christ, the law, which was four hundred and thirty years after, cannot disannul, that it should make the promise of none effect. For if the inheritance be of the law, it is no more of promise: but God gave it to Abraham by promise. Wherefore then serveth the law? It was added because of transgressions, till the seed should come to whom the promise was made; and it was ordained by angels in the hand of a mediator. Now a mediator is not a mediator of one, but God is one. Is the law then against the promises of God? God forbid: for if there had been a law given which could have given life, verily righteousness should have been by the law. But the scripture hath concluded all under sin, that the promise by faith of Jesus Christ might be given to them that believe. But before faith came, we were kept under the law, shut up unto the faith which should afterwards be revealed. Wherefore the law was our schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ, that we might be justified by faith. But after that faith is come, we are no longer under a schoolmaster. For ye are all the children of God by faith in Christ Jesus. For as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ. There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus. And if ye be Christ’s, then are ye Abraham’s seed, and heirs according to the promise.

label: Galatians 4
text: The schoolmaster image is extended into an estate. "The heir, as long as he is a child, differeth nothing from a servant, though he be lord of all," but is "under tutors and governors until the time appointed of the father" — a legal minority in which ownership is real and enjoyment is deferred, and in which the child's daily experience is indistinguishable from a slave's. That is Paul's verdict on the whole period before Christ: "Even so we, when we were children, were in bondage under the elements of the world." The pronoun is generous, sweeping Jew and Gentile alike into a single minority, and the phrase "elements of the world" is chosen to cover both the law and the cults the Galatians came from, which is why Paul can later accuse them of turning "again" to something they had never held. The turning point is announced with the language of a date arriving rather than a rescue improvised: "But when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law." The two participles are not decoration; the Son enters the human condition and enters it at its most constrained point, born into the very jurisdiction he came to end, "To redeem them that were under the law, that we might receive the adoption of sons." Then a second sending answers the first: "because ye are sons, God hath sent forth the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, Abba, Father." The order matters — the Spirit comes because they are sons, not in order to make them so — and the evidence offered is not an argument but a cry, in the Aramaic word Jesus himself used, spoken from inside the believer. Paul lets the whole movement land on a single reader: "Wherefore thou art no more a servant, but a son; and if a son, then an heir of God through Christ." Against that, the Galatian regression looks not merely wrong but unaccountable. "When ye knew not God, ye did service unto them which by nature are no gods" describes their pagan past; "But now, after that ye have known God, or rather are known of God" corrects itself mid-sentence, since being known by God is the prior and safer fact. And then the accusation: "how turn ye again to the weak and beggarly elements, whereunto ye desire again to be in bondage? Ye observe days, and months, and times, and years." Paul is watching them adopt a sacred calendar and he calls it a return, which means he regards a religion of prescribed times, taken up as the way of standing before God, as the same species of thing they left. His fear is stated without pastoral cushioning: "I am afraid of you, lest I have bestowed upon you labour in vain." The tone then changes completely. "Brethren, I beseech you, be as I am; for I am as ye are: ye have not injured me at all" — he clears the ground of any personal grievance before appealing to memory. He reminds them that he first preached to them by accident of illness, "through infirmity of the flesh," that his condition was the kind of thing ancient people took as a mark of divine disfavour, and that they nonetheless "despised not, nor rejected; but received me as an angel of God, even as Christ Jesus." The affection was extravagant: "if it had been possible, ye would have plucked out your own eyes, and have given them to me." Then the question that hurts: "Am I therefore become your enemy, because I tell you the truth?" He diagnoses the rival teachers by their technique rather than their doctrine — "They zealously affect you, but not well; yea, they would exclude you, that ye might affect them" — exposing the mechanism of the whole campaign, which is to shut people out in order to be courted for readmission. Paul does not object to zeal itself, only to its object and its constancy: "it is good to be zealously affected always in a good thing, and not only when I am present with you." Then the letter's most startling image, in which the apostle becomes a mother in labour for a second time: "My little children, of whom I travail in birth again until Christ be formed in you." What he wants is not their agreement but a shape, Christ formed in them, and he admits he cannot tell from a distance whether it is happening — "I desire to be present with you now, and to change my voice; for I stand in doubt of you." The chapter closes by turning the opponents' own text against them. "Tell me, ye that desire to be under the law, do ye not hear the law?" Abraham had two sons, "the one by a bondmaid, the other by a freewoman," and the difference between them was the difference between flesh and promise: Ishmael came by the ordinary means of a slave woman's body, Isaac by a word spoken to a couple past hope. "Which things are an allegory: for these are the two covenants; the one from the mount Sinai, which gendereth to bondage, which is Agar." The identification is deliberately shocking, since it puts Sinai and present-day Jerusalem on the side of the slave woman and her son — "answereth to Jerusalem which now is, and is in bondage with her children" — while the free city is elsewhere: "But Jerusalem which is above is free, which is the mother of us all." Paul then quotes the prophet's summons to a barren woman to sing, "for the desolate hath many more children than she which hath an husband," because a community of Gentiles who produced nothing by descent is exactly the barren mother's unexpected family. The application is direct and consoling before it is severe: "Now we, brethren, as Isaac was, are the children of promise," and the harassment they are suffering fits the pattern, since "he that was born after the flesh persecuted him that was born after the Spirit, even so it is now." The last word is Sarah's demand, quoted as Scripture's own verdict: "Cast out the bondwoman and her son: for the son of the bondwoman shall not be heir with the son of the freewoman." And the conclusion, stated as a fact about identity rather than a command: "we are not children of the bondwoman, but of the free." The estate analogy makes a claim about history that is easy to miss under the family imagery. The heir in his minority is not mistreated and the tutors are not villains; the arrangement is the father's own and it is appropriate to the child's age. What Paul objects to is not the period of custody but its indefinite extension, since the whole point of a date "appointed of the father" is that it arrives. This is why he can call the pre-Christian condition bondage without condemning the law that produced it, and why the Galatian move looks to him like a legal absurdity rather than an excess of devotion: they are heirs of full age petitioning to be placed back under guardianship. The sentence "differeth nothing from a servant, though he be lord of all" also concedes something to the opponents, admitting that the outward difference between a child and a slave is invisible, which is exactly the anxiety the agitators were exploiting. Verse four packs an entire Christology into a single sentence built on three verbs. God "sent forth his Son" implies the Son was already his to send; "made of a woman" locates the entrance in a real human birth; "made under the law" places him inside the jurisdiction he came to end. The redemption is therefore not accomplished from outside the human situation but from within it, by one who submitted to the very custody being lifted. The pairing of the two sendings — the Son into the world, the Spirit into the heart — gives the chapter its architecture: the first changes the status, the second communicates it, and the second is described as "the Spirit of his Son," so that what believers receive is not a generic empowerment but the Son's own relation to the Father. The cry "Abba, Father" is the evidence Paul offers, and it is significant that he does not say believers cry it but that the Spirit does, in them. The accusation in verses nine and ten is one of the most disorienting sentences in the letter, because Paul describes Gentile Christians taking up the Jewish calendar as turning "again" to what they had left. He is not saying that Israel's law and pagan religion are morally equivalent; he has just called the law a tutor appointed by God. He is saying that both function the same way when made the ground of acceptance — as "weak and beggarly elements," powerless to give what they promise and enslaving to those who trust them. The adjectives are precise: weak because they cannot produce the sonship in question, beggarly because they have nothing of their own to give. The self-correction of "ye have known God, or rather are known of God" belongs to the same argument, since the security Paul wants them to rest in is not the quality of their knowledge but the fact that they have been known. The personal appeal from verse twelve to twenty is not a digression from the argument but its emotional proof. Paul reminds them that the whole Galatian mission began in weakness, through an illness that detained him among them, and that his physical condition was repellent enough to be a test — "my temptation which was in my flesh" — which they passed by receiving him as though he were an angel or Christ himself. That memory matters because their present teachers come with credentials and prestige, and Paul is pointing out that the gospel reached them in the opposite package. His analysis of the rival technique is unsparing and durable: "they would exclude you, that ye might affect them" describes a strategy of manufactured exclusion, in which people are made to feel outside so that they will court the ones who can let them in, which is precisely what an added requirement for full membership accomplishes. The image of verse nineteen breaks the letter's own register, and the strain is deliberate. Paul has been an apostle, a defendant, a prosecutor; here he is a woman in labour, and in labour "again" for children already born, which is not how childbirth works and is exactly his point about how unnatural the situation is. What he is waiting for is not their assent to his position but a formation — "until Christ be formed in you" — language of shape taking hold in a body over time. This is the chapter's answer to the question of what replaces the law: not a lighter code but a person being formed within a community. It also explains his admission of helplessness, "I stand in doubt of you," since formation is not something an absent teacher can enforce by argument, and Paul knows that a letter is a poor substitute for a voice that can change its tone. The Hagar reading is the most aggressive move in the letter and Paul knows it, which is why he prefaces it by daring his opponents to actually listen to the text they invoke: "ye that desire to be under the law, do ye not hear the law?" The reversal is total. His readers would expect Isaac's line to be the circumcised and Ishmael's the outsiders; Paul assigns the slave woman to Sinai and to "Jerusalem which now is," and puts the uncircumcised Galatians in Isaac's place. The hinge is the manner of the two births: Ishmael was produced by ordinary human capacity acting to secure a promise it doubted, Isaac by a word given to bodies that had nothing left to contribute. Anyone attempting to obtain the inheritance by what he can do is therefore repeating Hagar rather than Sarah, whatever his ancestry. The quotation of Sarah's demand at the end is not a call to persecute anyone; it is Paul telling the Galatians what to do with the teaching that has come among them, since two heirs on incompatible terms cannot share the estate. Now I say, That the heir, as long as he is a child, differeth nothing from a servant, though he be lord of all; But is under tutors and governors until the time appointed of the father. Even so we, when we were children, were in bondage under the elements of the world: But when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law, To redeem them that were under the law, that we might receive the adoption of sons. And because ye are sons, God hath sent forth the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, Abba, Father. Wherefore thou art no more a servant, but a son; and if a son, then an heir of God through Christ. Howbeit then, when ye knew not God, ye did service unto them which by nature are no gods. But now, after that ye have known God, or rather are known of God, how turn ye again to the weak and beggarly elements, whereunto ye desire again to be in bondage? Ye observe days, and months, and times, and years. I am afraid of you, lest I have bestowed upon you labour in vain. Brethren, I beseech you, be as I am; for I am as ye are: ye have not injured me at all. Ye know how through infirmity of the flesh I preached the gospel unto you at the first. And my temptation which was in my flesh ye despised not, nor rejected; but received me as an angel of God, even as Christ Jesus. Where is then the blessedness ye spake of? for I bear you record, that, if it had been possible, ye would have plucked out your own eyes, and have given them to me. Am I therefore become your enemy, because I tell you the truth? They zealously affect you, but not well; yea, they would exclude you, that ye might affect them. But it is good to be zealously affected always in a good thing, and not only when I am present with you. My little children, of whom I travail in birth again until Christ be formed in you, I desire to be present with you now, and to change my voice; for I stand in doubt of you. Tell me, ye that desire to be under the law, do ye not hear the law? For it is written, that Abraham had two sons, the one by a bondmaid, the other by a freewoman. But he who was of the bondwoman was born after the flesh; but he of the freewoman was by promise. Which things are an allegory: for these are the two covenants; the one from the mount Sinai, which gendereth to bondage, which is Agar. For this Agar is mount Sinai in Arabia, and answereth to Jerusalem which now is, and is in bondage with her children. But Jerusalem which is above is free, which is the mother of us all. For it is written, Rejoice, thou barren that bearest not; break forth and cry, thou that travailest not: for the desolate hath many more children than she which hath an husband. Now we, brethren, as Isaac was, are the children of promise. But as then he that was born after the flesh persecuted him that was born after the Spirit, even so it is now. Nevertheless what saith the scripture? Cast out the bondwoman and her son: for the son of the bondwoman shall not be heir with the son of the freewoman. So then, brethren, we are not children of the bondwoman, but of the free.

label: Galatians 5
text: The letter turns here from argument to consequence, and the whole weight of four chapters lands on one imperative: "Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage." Freedom is described as ground already occupied, so the danger is not failure to advance but a voluntary return to a yard the Galatians have already left. Paul then stakes his own name on the stakes of the choice — "Behold, I Paul say unto you, that if ye be circumcised, Christ shall profit you nothing" — and gives the arithmetic behind the threat: to take the sign as a requirement is to sign for the entire system, since "every man that is circumcised... is a debtor to do the whole law." There is no partial enrolment, and the verdict is stated in the letter's coldest sentence: "Christ is become of no effect unto you, whosoever of you are justified by the law; ye are fallen from grace." Over against that stands the posture Paul commends, patient rather than acquisitive — "we through the Spirit wait for the hope of righteousness by faith" — and then the compressed formula that has been fought over ever since: "in Jesus Christ neither circumcision availeth any thing, nor uncircumcision; but faith which worketh by love." The tone slips into grieved bewilderment at the athletics of it: "Ye did run well; who did hinder you that ye should not obey the truth?" The interference is disowned at its root — "This persuasion cometh not of him that calleth you" — and diagnosed as contagion rather than opinion, "A little leaven leaveneth the whole lump." Paul balances confidence in the congregation against judgment on the agitators, "I have confidence in you through the Lord, that ye will be none otherwise minded: but he that troubleth you shall bear his judgment, whosoever he be," and produces his own scars as evidence that he has not softened the message: "if I yet preach circumcision, why do I yet suffer persecution? then is the offence of the cross ceased." The rage breaks surface in the most savage line in his correspondence, a wish that the knife-men would not stop at the knife: "I would they were even cut off which trouble you." Then, abruptly, the guardrail: "ye have been called unto liberty; only use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh, but by love serve one another" — the freed man is put straight back into service, and the only thing that changes is the master. What follows is startling from the man who has just called the law a yoke: "all the law is fulfilled in one word, even in this; Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." The immediate peril at Galatia is not licence but cannibalism, and Paul names it as such: "if ye bite and devour one another, take heed that ye be not consumed one of another." His remedy is not a rule but a gait — "Walk in the Spirit, and ye shall not fulfil the lust of the flesh" — accompanied by an unsparing account of the interior war it does not abolish: "the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary the one to the other: so that ye cannot do the things that ye would." The release is jurisdictional: "if ye be led of the Spirit, ye are not under the law." Two catalogues then set the alternatives side by side. The works of the flesh "are manifest," needing no discernment to identify, and they run from "Adultery, fornication, uncleanness, lasciviousness" through "Idolatry, witchcraft, hatred, variance, emulations, wrath, strife, seditions, heresies" to "Envyings, murders, drunkenness, revellings, and such like," with a warning Paul insists is a repetition and not a novelty: "they which do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God." Against that scattered plural stands a single harvest, "the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, Meekness, temperance," closed with a quiet piece of irony aimed at the law-teachers, "against such there is no law." The chapter ends by naming what has already been done and what must therefore follow: "they that are Christ’s have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts," "If we live in the Spirit, let us also walk in the Spirit," and then, with the quarrelling congregation squarely in view, the small and unglamorous sins that had been doing the actual damage — "Let us not be desirous of vain glory, provoking one another, envying one another." Paul treats freedom as a position to be held rather than a prize to be won, which is why the verb is "Stand fast" and the danger is being "entangled again." The metaphor is agricultural and legal at once: a yoke is fitted to an animal that has been unhitched, and slipping back under it requires no effort at all, only passivity. What makes this more than rhetoric is that Paul immediately fences the freedom he has just defended — "only use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh, but by love serve one another" — so the chapter refuses both of the obvious reductions. Liberty is not permission to do as one pleases, since it terminates in servitude to the neighbour; and it is not achieved by taking on a code, since that is the very bondage in question. The freed man is still a servant; what has changed is whom he serves and why. The logic of verses two through four is deliberately all-or-nothing, and it is easy to misread as a condemnation of a rite. Paul has no quarrel with circumcision as such — elsewhere he calls it and its absence equally weightless — but with what accepting it now would mean at Galatia. To take the mark as a requirement for standing with God is to enter a system whole: "he is a debtor to do the whole law." One cannot enrol partially, adopting the ceremony while declining the ledger. The consequence, "Christ is become of no effect unto you," is not a punishment arbitrarily attached but the internal result of the choice, since a righteousness constructed by law-keeping leaves nothing for Christ to do.
