And "ye are fallen from grace" is Paul's own phrase for the possibility, which he plainly regards as real enough to write a letter about. Verse six is the letter in miniature and one of the most contested sentences in the New Testament. Two things are said at once: the ritual marker is void in both directions — "neither circumcision availeth any thing, nor uncircumcision" — so the anti-circumcision party has no more standing than the circumcision party; and what does avail is described with a working verb, "faith which worketh by love." Paul does not oppose faith to activity here. He opposes faith-that-works-through-love to a righteousness sought by legal observance, which means the alternative to law is not inertia but a different kind of energy with a different source. Whatever else the phrase settles or unsettles, it forecloses the reading that the faith Paul commends is a bare assent that leaves the person unchanged. The grammatical difference between the two lists carries most of their theology. The flesh produces "works," plural and various, a heap of unrelated items that need no explanation because they "are manifest"; the Spirit produces "fruit," singular, one organic yield described from nine angles. Works are manufactured and can be counted; fruit is grown and cannot be forced, only cultivated and awaited. This is why the ethical instruction of the chapter is a walk rather than a checklist, and why the closing barb, "against such there is no law," lands where it does — a life yielding love, joy, peace and the rest has nothing for a legal code to prohibit, so the teachers pressing law on the Galatians have no purchase on precisely the life they claim to be protecting. Verse seventeen is a remarkably unsentimental piece of Christian anthropology, and it sits oddly beside the confidence of verse sixteen unless both are held together. Paul promises that walking in the Spirit means not fulfilling the lust of the flesh, and in the same breath concedes an internal deadlock in which "ye cannot do the things that ye would." He is not describing serene progress. He is describing a real war with a decided outcome, and the decision is stated as an accomplished fact in verse twenty-four — "they that are Christ’s have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts" — while verse twenty-five still has to command the obvious: "If we live in the Spirit, let us also walk in the Spirit." Life in the Spirit is presented as a possession that must be enacted, and the gap between the possession and the enactment is where the Christian actually lives. The vice list is weighted in a direction most readers do not expect. Four items are sexual and two involve drink; eight — "hatred, variance, emulations, wrath, strife, seditions, heresies, Envyings" — are the sins of a community at war with itself, and the chapter's framing sentence about biting and devouring one another shows why. The Galatian crisis was a doctrinal fight, and Paul's point is that the fight itself was manufacturing works of the flesh in people who imagined they were contending for holiness. The closing verse makes this explicit and painfully small: "vain glory, provoking one another, envying one another." A church can lose the gospel through the content of what it believes, and it can lose it just as thoroughly through the temper in which it argues about belief. Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage. Behold, I Paul say unto you, that if ye be circumcised, Christ shall profit you nothing. For I testify again to every man that is circumcised, that he is a debtor to do the whole law. Christ is become of no effect unto you, whosoever of you are justified by the law; ye are fallen from grace. For we through the Spirit wait for the hope of righteousness by faith. For in Jesus Christ neither circumcision availeth any thing, nor uncircumcision; but faith which worketh by love. Ye did run well; who did hinder you that ye should not obey the truth? This persuasion cometh not of him that calleth you. A little leaven leaveneth the whole lump. I have confidence in you through the Lord, that ye will be none otherwise minded: but he that troubleth you shall bear his judgment, whosoever he be. And I, brethren, if I yet preach circumcision, why do I yet suffer persecution? then is the offence of the cross ceased. I would they were even cut off which trouble you. For, brethren, ye have been called unto liberty; only use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh, but by love serve one another. For all the law is fulfilled in one word, even in this; Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. But if ye bite and devour one another, take heed that ye be not consumed one of another. This I say then, Walk in the Spirit, and ye shall not fulfil the lust of the flesh. For the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary the one to the other: so that ye cannot do the things that ye would. But if ye be led of the Spirit, ye are not under the law. Now the works of the flesh are manifest, which are these; Adultery, fornication, uncleanness, lasciviousness, Idolatry, witchcraft, hatred, variance, emulations, wrath, strife, seditions, heresies, Envyings, murders, drunkenness, revellings, and such like: of the which I tell you before, as I have also told you in time past, that they which do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God. But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, Meekness, temperance: against such there is no law. And they that are Christ’s have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts. If we live in the Spirit, let us also walk in the Spirit. Let us not be desirous of vain glory, provoking one another, envying one another.

label: Galatians 6
text: Having set the works of the flesh against the fruit of the Spirit, Paul now tests the doctrine on the hardest case a congregation faces, which is what to do with a member who has failed. The instruction is addressed to the very people most likely to enjoy the moment — "ye which are spiritual" — and the verb chosen is medical and reparative rather than punitive: "if a man be overtaken in a fault... restore such an one in the spirit of meekness." The word "overtaken" grants that the man was caught rather than merely calculating, and the corrective is aimed straight back at the corrector: "considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted." From this comes the summary command, "Bear ye one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ" — a striking phrase from a writer who has spent five chapters dismantling law as a way of standing before God, and who now names the whole obligation of the Christian community by that word. What follows deflates the self-importance that makes burden-bearing impossible: "if a man think himself to be something, when he is nothing, he deceiveth himself," the deception being self-inflicted rather than imposed by anyone else. The alternative to comparison is examination — "let every man prove his own work, and then shall he have rejoicing in himself alone, and not in another" — and it is grounded in a sentence that sits in apparent contradiction to verse two: "every man shall bear his own burden." A brief practical note follows on supporting teachers, "Let him that is taught in the word communicate unto him that teacheth in all good things," and then the chapter's central warning, delivered with agricultural bluntness: "Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap." The two harvests are named without softening — "he that soweth to his flesh shall of the flesh reap corruption; but he that soweth to the Spirit shall of the Spirit reap life everlasting" — and the pastoral application is directed not at the reckless but at the exhausted: "let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not." The scope is then set as wide as opportunity allows, with a priority rather than a boundary: "let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith." At verse eleven Paul takes the pen from his secretary — "Ye see how large a letter I have written unto you with mine own hand" — and the closing paragraph is his own handwriting pressed hard into the page. He assigns a motive to his opponents that is neither theological nor sincere: "As many as desire to make a fair shew in the flesh, they constrain you to be circumcised; only lest they should suffer persecution for the cross of Christ," and he charges them with inconsistency as well as cowardice, since "neither they themselves who are circumcised keep the law; but desire to have you circumcised, that they may glory in your flesh." Against their boasting in other men's bodies he sets the only boast he will make: "God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom the world is crucified unto me, and I unto the world." The formula of the fifth chapter returns in its final form, with the positive term supplied at last — "in Christ Jesus neither circumcision availeth any thing, nor uncircumcision, but a new creature" — and a benediction is pronounced on those who measure by it: "as many as walk according to this rule, peace be on them, and mercy, and upon the Israel of God." Then the last word on the subject, weary and immovable: "From henceforth let no man trouble me: for I bear in my body the marks of the Lord Jesus." His opponents wanted a mark cut into Gentile flesh; Paul offers the scars already cut into his own. The letter closes with the only thing it has ever been arguing for, "the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen." The chapter opens where communities usually fail, and it does so by aiming the instruction at the strong rather than the fallen. Paul addresses "ye which are spiritual," and the address is not flattery but exposure, since the moment a man accepts that description of himself he is exactly the man most in danger. The prescribed manner, "in the spirit of meekness," is drawn straight from the fruit of the Spirit in the previous chapter, so the correction of a sinner becomes the test case for whether the Spirit is actually producing anything. And the clause that follows, "considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted," abruptly reverses the direction of scrutiny: the one doing the examining is himself under examination, and the singular pronoun after a string of plurals makes it personal. A church that cannot restore gently is not spiritually advanced; it has simply relocated the works of the flesh into its disciplinary procedures. The apparent contradiction between bearing one another's burdens in verse two and bearing one's own burden in verse five is deliberate rather than careless, and Paul uses two different words for the load. The first is a crushing weight, the kind that flattens a man and requires other hands; the second is closer to a soldier's pack or a traveller's kit, the assigned portion nobody else can carry for him. So the two verses are not in competition but in sequence: precisely because each person will answer personally for his own work, nobody is entitled to hand off responsibility, and precisely because some weights genuinely crush, nobody is meant to carry them alone. The self-deception of verse three sits between the two for a reason — the man who thinks himself something will neither stoop to carry another's load nor honestly examine his own. Paul's phrase "the law of Christ" ought to stop any reader of this letter. He has spent five chapters insisting that the law cannot justify, that returning to it is bondage, and that those led by the Spirit are not under it; then he names the obligation of mutual burden-bearing as a law and says it is fulfilled by keeping it. The point is not that he has quietly recanted but that he distinguishes two things a law can be. As a system for establishing standing before God it is finished; as the shape a Spirit-formed life takes toward the neighbour it is not only intact but intensified, since bearing someone else's crushing weight is a good deal more demanding than a rite. This is the same move as the previous chapter's summary of all the law in loving the neighbour, and it is the reason Galatians cannot be read as an argument against Christian obligation. The sowing and reaping warning is aimed at a specific self-flattery: "Be not deceived; God is not mocked." The verb suggests turning up the nose at someone, and the target is the man who supposes that inward disposition and outward outcome can be kept apart indefinitely, that one may sow in one field and harvest in another. Paul's answer is that the moral world is agricultural rather than arbitrary — what is planted determines what comes up, and the interval between the two changes nothing. What is notable is where he then applies it. The application is not a threat aimed at the profligate but encouragement aimed at the tired: "let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not." The same law that makes the flesh's harvest inevitable makes the Spirit's harvest certain, and the only thing at issue is whether one is still standing at the season. Paul's account of his opponents' motives is unusually specific and unusually unflattering, and it reframes the whole controversy. They want "to make a fair shew in the flesh"; they act "lest they should suffer persecution for the cross of Christ"; they do not themselves keep the law they are pressing; and what they are after is the ability to "glory in your flesh," counting converts as trophies. This turns the dispute from a theological disagreement into a question about the cross's social cost. Circumcising Gentiles kept the churches legible and safe within a recognized religious framework, and it spared the missionaries the trouble that came with preaching an executed messiah to anyone. The offence of the cross, which the previous chapter named directly, is thus not incidental to the gospel but the very thing the compromise was designed to avoid. The letter ends by replacing one mark in the flesh with another. Paul's opponents want a cut made in Gentile bodies as proof of belonging; Paul answers, "I bear in my body the marks of the Lord Jesus," pointing to the scars left by beatings, stonings and imprisonments incurred for preaching. Both are bodily, both are visible, and both signify allegiance, but one is a credential displayed for advantage and the other is damage taken for a person. The formula of verse fifteen sets the same contrast at the level of doctrine: neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything, and what does count is "a new creature" — something made rather than performed, and made by God rather than negotiated. The whole letter comes to rest on that, which is why the last word before the benediction is a request to be left alone about it. Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted. Bear ye one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ. For if a man think himself to be something, when he is nothing, he deceiveth himself. But let every man prove his own work, and then shall he have rejoicing in himself alone, and not in another. For every man shall bear his own burden. Let him that is taught in the word communicate unto him that teacheth in all good things. Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap. For he that soweth to his flesh shall of the flesh reap corruption; but he that soweth to the Spirit shall of the Spirit reap life everlasting. And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not. As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith. Ye see how large a letter I have written unto you with mine own hand. As many as desire to make a fair shew in the flesh, they constrain you to be circumcised; only lest they should suffer persecution for the cross of Christ. For neither they themselves who are circumcised keep the law; but desire to have you circumcised, that they may glory in your flesh. But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom the world is crucified unto me, and I unto the world. For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision availeth any thing, nor uncircumcision, but a new creature. And as many as walk according to this rule, peace be on them, and mercy, and upon the Israel of God. From henceforth let no man trouble me: for I bear in my body the marks of the Lord Jesus. Brethren, the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen.

label: Ephesians 1
text: The letter opens with the plainest of addresses — "Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, to the saints which are at Ephesus, and to the faithful in Christ Jesus" — and then, with no news, no crisis, and no complaint to report, breaks straight into a single vast movement of praise. "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who hath blessed us with all spiritual blessings in heavenly places in Christ" fixes the terms of everything that follows: the blessing is already given rather than promised, it is spiritual rather than territorial, its location is "heavenly places," and every clause in the long sentence will fall back into the same refrain — in Christ, in him, in whom, in the beloved. Paul then traces the blessing backward past all history to its source, "According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world," and immediately forward to its stated end, "that we should be holy and without blame before him in love," so that election is never an alternative to holiness but the appointed means of it. The choosing is filled out as adoption — "Having predestinated us unto the adoption of children by Jesus Christ to himself" — and its motive is located nowhere in the chosen: "according to the good pleasure of his will, To the praise of the glory of his grace, wherein he hath made us accepted in the beloved." Only now, with the eternal decision named, does Paul touch the cross: "In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace," and grace is at once said to have overflowed "toward us in all wisdom and prudence," since what God gives includes the capacity to understand what he is doing. That understanding is then named a disclosed secret — "Having made known unto us the mystery of his will, according to his good pleasure which he hath purposed in himself" — and the content of the secret is the largest sentence in the letter: "That in the dispensation of the fulness of times he might gather together in one all things in Christ, both which are in heaven, and which are on earth; even in him." The scope is cosmic, not merely personal; salvation is the reassembling of a fractured universe under one head. From that summit Paul descends to the readers' own experience in two movements marked by a shift of pronoun. First "we," those "who first trusted in Christ" and "have obtained an inheritance, being predestinated according to the purpose of him who worketh all things after the counsel of his own will"; then "ye also," the Gentile hearers, whose entry is described as an ordinary sequence of hearing and believing — "after that ye heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation: in whom also after that ye believed, ye were sealed with that holy Spirit of promise." The Spirit is called "the earnest of our inheritance until the redemption of the purchased possession," a down payment on an estate not yet entered, and the whole outpouring closes as it began, "unto the praise of his glory." The second half of the chapter turns the doxology into intercession. Having heard of their "faith in the Lord Jesus, and love unto all the saints," Paul does not cease "to give thanks for you, making mention of you in my prayers," and what he asks for is not relief or increase but sight: that "the Father of glory, may give unto you the spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him: The eyes of your understanding being enlightened." Three things are to come into focus — "the hope of his calling," "the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints," and "the exceeding greatness of his power to us-ward who believe" — and the third is then measured against the only event adequate to it: that power is "according to the working of his mighty power, Which he wrought in Christ, when he raised him from the dead, and set him at his own right hand in the heavenly places, Far above all principality, and power, and might, and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this world, but also in that which is to come." The chapter ends by attaching that enthroned Christ to a visible community: God "hath put all things under his feet, and gave him to be the head over all things to the church, Which is his body, the fulness of him that filleth all in all." Everything in the opening blessing is spoken in the past tense of a completed act and in the locative case of a single person. God "hath blessed," "hath chosen," "having predestinated," "hath made us accepted," "hath abounded," "having made known" — and each verb terminates in Christ rather than in the believer considered by himself. This is why Paul can address a congregation about eternity without producing anxiety: the question is not whether an individual can locate his name on a hidden list, but whether he is in Christ, which is a question about a visible and enterable reality. The chapter never invites introspective auditing of one's own election; it invites praise, and it places the whole weight of assurance on the one in whom the choosing was made. The purpose clauses are the discipline of the passage, and they are easy to skip. Election is "that we should be holy and without blame before him in love"; adoption is "To the praise of the glory of his grace"; the inheritance is "That we should be to the praise of his glory"; the sealing is "unto the praise of his glory." Paul states the doctrine three times and each time refuses to leave it as a bare fact about God's freedom, tethering it instead to an intended outcome in the chosen and a final outcome in God's own glory. A reading of predestination that produces either moral passivity or private complacency has severed the doctrine from the only ends the text assigns it. Verse ten is the sentence the whole letter will spend six chapters unpacking: "That in the dispensation of the fulness of times he might gather together in one all things in Christ, both which are in heaven, and which are on earth." The word behind "gather together in one" carries the sense of summing a column and writing the total at the head, and it presumes that the universe is currently in pieces. Redemption here is not primarily rescue of individuals out of a doomed world but the reunification of a divided one under a single head — which is why the ethical chapters will be preoccupied with walls broken down, walking worthy, and the knitting of a body. Personal salvation is real and assumed throughout, but it is presented as participation in something considerably larger than itself. Paul describes the Ephesians' conversion with unglamorous ordinariness — "after that ye heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation: in whom also after that ye believed, ye were sealed" — and sets it directly beside the choosing made "before the foundation of the world." The two are not in competition; the eternal decision is executed in time through a preacher, a message, a hearing, and a believing. Whatever else predestination means in this chapter, it does not mean that preaching is decorative or that human response is fictional. The sealing that follows is described as ownership and guarantee at once, "the earnest of our inheritance," a first instalment that both proves the buyer's intent and is itself part of the sum. The prayer of verses fifteen through nineteen asks for nothing the Ephesians do not already possess. Paul does not ask that they be given hope, an inheritance, or power; he asks that they may "know what is the hope of his calling, and what the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints, And what is the exceeding greatness of his power." The deficit he assumes in a healthy, believing congregation is a deficit of perception, and the remedy he asks for is not information but "the spirit of wisdom and revelation" and enlightened eyes. This is a distinctly unsentimental account of Christian growth: the chief thing lacking is the ability to see what is already true, and that ability is itself a gift to be prayed for rather than a skill to be acquired. The chapter's final clause refuses to leave Christ's exaltation in the abstract. He is raised, seated, and set "Far above all principality, and power, and might, and dominion" — and then, immediately, "gave him to be the head over all things to the church, Which is his body, the fulness of him that filleth all in all." The cosmic sovereignty is given as a gift to a particular community, and the community is described not as his organisation or his audience but as his body and his fulness. Two consequences follow that the rest of the letter will press: the Church's life is not a human project supplemented by divine help, and the powers Paul names are not defeated somewhere else while the congregation waits, since the one seated above them is the same one whose body the congregation is. Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, to the saints which are at Ephesus, and to the faithful in Christ Jesus: Grace be to you, and peace, from God our Father, and from the Lord Jesus Christ. Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who hath blessed us with all spiritual blessings in heavenly places in Christ: According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love: Having predestinated us unto the adoption of children by Jesus Christ to himself, according to the good pleasure of his will, To the praise of the glory of his grace, wherein he hath made us accepted in the beloved. In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace; Wherein he hath abounded toward us in all wisdom and prudence; Having made known unto us the mystery of his will, according to his good pleasure which he hath purposed in himself: That in the dispensation of the fulness of times he might gather together in one all things in Christ, both which are in heaven, and which are on earth; even in him: In whom also we have obtained an inheritance, being predestinated according to the purpose of him who worketh all things after the counsel of his own will: That we should be to the praise of his glory, who first trusted in Christ. In whom ye also trusted, after that ye heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation: in whom also after that ye believed, ye were sealed with that holy Spirit of promise, Which is the earnest of our inheritance until the redemption of the purchased possession, unto the praise of his glory. Wherefore I also, after I heard of your faith in the Lord Jesus, and love unto all the saints, Cease not to give thanks for you, making mention of you in my prayers; That the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give unto you the spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him: The eyes of your understanding being enlightened; that ye may know what is the hope of his calling, and what the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints, And what is the exceeding greatness of his power to us-ward who believe, according to the working of his mighty power, Which he wrought in Christ, when he raised him from the dead, and set him at his own right hand in the heavenly places, Far above all principality, and power, and might, and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this world, but also in that which is to come: And hath put all things under his feet, and gave him to be the head over all things to the church, Which is his body, the fulness of him that filleth all in all.

label: Ephesians 2
text: The chapter begins in the middle of a sentence whose main verb will not arrive for three verses, and the delay is the point. "And you hath he quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins" states the diagnosis first: not sick, not weakened, not badly instructed, but dead. Paul then describes the condition as a way of walking rather than a mere status — "ye walked according to the course of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that now worketh in the children of disobedience" — so that the death is simultaneously a captivity to an age, to a personal power, and to one's own appetites. Lest the Gentile readers hear this as an indictment of somebody else, Paul folds himself and his own people into it: "Among whom also we all had our conversation in times past in the lusts of our flesh, fulfilling the desires of the flesh and of the mind; and were by nature the children of wrath, even as others." The word "all" and the phrase "by nature" close every exit. Into that dead level ground drops the great adversative of the letter: "But God, who is rich in mercy, for his great love wherewith he loved us, Even when we were dead in sins, hath quickened us together with Christ." Three compound verbs follow, all of them shared with Christ and all in the past tense — quickened together, "hath raised us up together, and made us sit together in heavenly places in Christ Jesus" — so that the believer's biography is narrated as a participation in the resurrection and enthronement already described in the first chapter. The purpose is display over an unlimited horizon: "That in the ages to come he might shew the exceeding riches of his grace in his kindness toward us through Christ Jesus." Then comes the sentence that has carried more theological freight than any other in the letter: "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast." Paul immediately supplies the balancing clause that is too often left off: "For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them." Works are excluded as the cause and reinstated as the purpose, and the same verb of walking that described the old captivity now describes the new life. The second half of the chapter takes the vertical rescue and lays it on its side. "Wherefore remember" — Paul commands memory, and what is to be remembered is a social and religious exclusion: "ye being in time past Gentiles in the flesh, who are called Uncircumcision," and worse, "at that time ye were without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world." Five deprivations, ending with the bleakest phrase in the letter. Against them stands one reversal: "But now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ." Paul then presses the peace between Jew and Gentile back into the person of Christ himself — "For he is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us; Having abolished in his flesh the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances" — and states the constructive purpose twice, "for to make in himself of twain one new man, so making peace" and "that he might reconcile both unto God in one body by the cross, having slain the enmity thereby." Reconciliation with God and reconciliation between enemies are accomplished in a single act and cannot be separated. Christ then "came and preached peace to you which were afar off, and to them that were nigh," and the result is stated in the most Trinitarian sentence of the chapter: "For through him we both have access by one Spirit unto the Father." The closing images pile up citizenship, family, and temple. They are "no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God; And are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone," a structure that is not static but alive — "all the building fitly framed together groweth unto an holy temple in the Lord" — and whose purpose is habitation: "In whom ye also are builded together for an habitation of God through the Spirit." Paul's account of the human predicament is triple and refuses to settle on a single villain. The old walk was "according to the course of this world," an ambient current of the age; "according to the prince of the power of the air," a personal and hostile intelligence; and "in the lusts of our flesh, fulfilling the desires of the flesh and of the mind," a corruption running inward through appetite and thought alike. Blaming culture alone produces victims, blaming the devil alone produces excuses, and blaming appetite alone produces moralism. Holding all three explains why the remedy has to be resurrection rather than reform: a dead man is not improved by a better environment, a rescued hostage, or stronger resolve. The three compound verbs of verses five and six — quickened together, raised up together, made to sit together — put the believer's present position inside an event that has already happened to someone else. Chapter one described God's power as that "Which he wrought in Christ, when he raised him from the dead, and set him at his own right hand in the heavenly places"; chapter two says the same three things about the Ephesians. This is why the letter can move so freely between cosmic language and pastoral advice, and why it never treats Christian ethics as an attempt to climb toward a status not yet held. The sitting is the strangest of the three and the most consequential: a seated person is neither anxious nor still striving for position. Verses eight through ten form one argument and are habitually quoted as two. "By grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast" is immediately grounded by "For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works." The Greek word rendered "workmanship" means something made, so the same sentence that denies human making affirms divine making, and the works excluded at the door reappear as the very floor the house is built on. The one thing the passage will not permit is boasting; it neither permits a Christianity that earns its standing nor one that has nothing to walk in once standing is given. "Wherefore remember" is an imperative aimed at a specific amnesia. The Gentile converts are ordered to keep in mind that they were the outsiders, called "Uncircumcision" by others, "aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise." Paul is not indulging in nostalgia for guilt; he is preventing the newly included from forgetting that they were included, which is the root of every subsequent contempt for those still outside and of every fantasy that one's place was always deserved. The phrase "having no hope, and without God in the world" also refuses a sentimental view of pre-Christian religion — the ancient world was crowded with gods, and Paul still calls it godless. The peace of this chapter is not an attitude but a demolition. "He is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition" — peace is identified with a person and enacted by removing a barrier, and it costs the abolishing "in his flesh" of "the law of commandments contained in ordinances." What Paul sets aside is precisely the machinery of separation, the ceremonial and ritual boundary markers that made Jew and Gentile two peoples; he does not thereby set aside the moral demand, since he will spend chapters four through six issuing commands. The goal is stated constructively rather than merely negatively: not the assimilation of one group into the other, but the creation "in himself of twain one new man," a third thing that did not exist before. The chapter ends with three images that correct one another. Citizenship answers the political exclusion of the aliens; household answers the loneliness of the strangers; temple answers the religious exclusion of those barred from the sanctuary. The temple image is the most demanding, because it is under construction and growing — "all the building fitly framed together groweth" — and because its purpose is not the accommodation of worshippers but the housing of God: "builded together for an habitation of God through the Spirit." Individual Christians are not each a small temple in this passage; they are stones whose whole significance lies in being fitted to others, which makes disunity not a failure of manners but a structural defect in the dwelling God intends to occupy. And you hath he quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins; Wherein in time past ye walked according to the course of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that now worketh in the children of disobedience: Among whom also we all had our conversation in times past in the lusts of our flesh, fulfilling the desires of the flesh and of the mind; and were by nature the children of wrath, even as others. But God, who is rich in mercy, for his great love wherewith he loved us, Even when we were dead in sins, hath quickened us together with Christ, (by grace ye are saved;) And hath raised us up together, and made us sit together in heavenly places in Christ Jesus: That in the ages to come he might shew the exceeding riches of his grace in his kindness toward us through Christ Jesus. For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them. Wherefore remember, that ye being in time past Gentiles in the flesh, who are called Uncircumcision by that which is called the Circumcision in the flesh made by hands; That at that time ye were without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world: But now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ. For he is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us; Having abolished in his flesh the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances; for to make in himself of twain one new man, so making peace; And that he might reconcile both unto God in one body by the cross, having slain the enmity thereby: And came and preached peace to you which were afar off, and to them that were nigh. For through him we both have access by one Spirit unto the Father. Now therefore ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God; And are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone; In whom all the building fitly framed together groweth unto an holy temple in the Lord: In whom ye also are builded together for an habitation of God through the Spirit.

label: Ephesians 3
text: Paul begins a prayer and does not finish it for thirteen verses. "For this cause I Paul, the prisoner of Jesus Christ for you Gentiles" breaks off mid-thought, and the sentence is only resumed at verse fourteen with the same words, "For this cause I bow my knees." What interrupts is a digression about his own commission, and the interruption turns out to be necessary, because the readers cannot pray the prayer until they know why the man praying it is in chains. He describes his office as an administration entrusted rather than a career achieved — "the dispensation of the grace of God which is given me to you-ward" — and its content as something he did not work out but received: "by revelation he made known unto me the mystery." The word mystery here means a secret now disclosed rather than a truth permanently obscure, and Paul is careful to say both that it "in other ages was not made known unto the sons of men" and that it "is now revealed unto his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit," so the disclosure is neither private to him nor a novelty of his own devising. Then he states the secret in one line, and it is not what a religious imagination would predict: "That the Gentiles should be fellowheirs, and of the same body, and partakers of his promise in Christ by the gospel." The hidden purpose of the ages is a merger. Paul's own place in it is described with a superlative that outdoes ordinary modesty — "Unto me, who am less than the least of all saints, is this grace given" — and the commission has two parts, to "preach among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ" and "to make all men see what is the fellowship of the mystery, which from the beginning of the world hath been hid in God." Verse ten then makes the most startling claim in the letter: the audience for this disclosure is not only human. "To the intent that now unto the principalities and powers in heavenly places might be known by the church the manifold wisdom of God" — the united Church is itself the exhibition, and the watching intelligences are the ones being instructed. This is said to be "According to the eternal purpose which he purposed in Christ Jesus our Lord," and its practical fruit for the reader is immediate access: "In whom we have boldness and access with confidence by the faith of him." Only then does Paul return to his chains, and he does so to protect his readers rather than himself: "Wherefore I desire that ye faint not at my tribulations for you, which is your glory." The prayer resumes on his knees, addressed to "the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, Of whom the whole family in heaven and earth is named," and it asks for a series of things that escalate past what a petition normally dares. First strength — "according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with might by his Spirit in the inner man" — then indwelling, "That Christ may dwell in your hearts by faith," then stability in love, "being rooted and grounded in love," the metaphors of a plant and a building set side by side. What all of this is for is comprehension, and the object is given only in dimensions without a noun: "May be able to comprehend with all saints what is the breadth, and length, and depth, and height." Paul then names it and immediately concedes the impossibility: "And to know the love of Christ, which passeth knowledge." The final clause asks for more than any of the preceding: "that ye might be filled with all the fulness of God." Aware that he has prayed past the edge of what can be requested, Paul closes not with amen but with a doxology that makes the excess into the point: "Now unto him that is able to do exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think, according to the power that worketh in us, Unto him be glory in the church by Christ Jesus throughout all ages, world without end. Amen." Paul's self-description controls the whole chapter. He is "the prisoner of Jesus Christ for you Gentiles," which reassigns the credit for his imprisonment away from Rome and toward Christ, and away from his own misfortune toward their benefit. He calls himself "less than the least of all saints" — a deliberately impossible comparative, as though the superlative were not low enough — and describes his commission as grace given rather than authority earned. The effect is that the most consequential ministry in the letter is presented as entirely derivative: a secret he did not deduce, an office he did not seek, a power he does not supply, and a suffering whose value belongs to somebody else. The content of the mystery is the part most often blurred. Paul does not say the mystery is that God saves sinners, or that Christ died, or that grace is free; he says it is "That the Gentiles should be fellowheirs, and of the same body, and partakers of his promise in Christ by the gospel." Three compound words, each stressing togetherness, define the hidden purpose of the ages as the abolition of a religious frontier. That the epoch-making secret of God turns out to be the seating of former outsiders at the same table sets a permanent standard: any Christianity that quietly reinstates a first and second class of members has not merely failed at manners, it has obscured the specific thing God kept hidden for ages in order to reveal. Verse ten reverses the expected direction of instruction. The Church is not primarily being taught here; she is the lesson — "that now unto the principalities and powers in heavenly places might be known by the church the manifold wisdom of God." The word rendered "manifold" suggests something many-coloured or intricately variegated, and what displays it is the improbable composition of a congregation containing people who had no business being in the same room. Angelic and hostile powers alike learn God's wisdom by observation of a mixed community, which means that reconciled diversity in the Church is not a social bonus attached to the gospel but part of its public demonstration in the unseen world. The prayer of verses sixteen through nineteen is built as a sequence in which each request is the ground of the next, and the sequence moves from interior to immeasurable. Strength in "the inner man" makes room for Christ to "dwell in your hearts by faith"; indwelling produces rootedness "in love"; rootedness is what makes comprehension possible; comprehension terminates in knowing a love that "passeth knowledge"; and knowing that love ends in being "filled with all the fulness of God." Notably the comprehension is corporate — "with all saints" — so the dimensions cannot be measured alone. Paul assumes that the love of Christ is too large for any single Christian's perception and that the missing dimensions are held by other people. The four dimensions are given without an object, and the omission is probably deliberate. "The breadth, and length, and depth, and height" names a magnitude in every direction without saying of what, and only the next clause supplies a candidate in "the love of Christ." The construction leaves the reader momentarily measuring nothing at all, which is the correct posture, and it is immediately followed by the admission that the thing measured "passeth knowledge." Paul is not being vague; he is asking for a knowledge that includes the recognition of its own insufficiency, a comprehension that grasps enough to know it has not grasped the whole. Devotion that claims to have taken the measure of Christ's love has misunderstood the prayer. The doxology answers a problem the prayer itself created. Having asked for fulness with "all the fulness of God," Paul has requested something no petitioner can expect, and rather than retreat he escalates: God is "able to do exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think." The measure of that ability is then located not in heaven but in the reader — "according to the power that worketh in us" — so that the same power that raised and seated Christ is named as already operative in an ordinary congregation. And the glory is directed to a specific address, "in the church by Christ Jesus throughout all ages," pairing the community and her Lord as the joint site where God's praise is rendered in time. For this cause I Paul, the prisoner of Jesus Christ for you Gentiles, If ye have heard of the dispensation of the grace of God which is given me to you-ward: How that by revelation he made known unto me the mystery; ( as I wrote afore in few words, Whereby, when ye read, ye may understand my knowledge in the mystery of Christ) Which in other ages was not made known unto the sons of men, as it is now revealed unto his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit; That the Gentiles should be fellowheirs, and of the same body, and partakers of his promise in Christ by the gospel: Whereof I was made a minister, according to the gift of the grace of God given unto me by the effectual working of his power. Unto me, who am less than the least of all saints, is this grace given, that I should preach among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ; And to make all men see what is the fellowship of the mystery, which from the beginning of the world hath been hid in God, who created all things by Jesus Christ: To the intent that now unto the principalities and powers in heavenly places might be known by the church the manifold wisdom of God, According to the eternal purpose which he purposed in Christ Jesus our Lord: In whom we have boldness and access with confidence by the faith of him. Wherefore I desire that ye faint not at my tribulations for you, which is your glory. For this cause I bow my knees unto the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, Of whom the whole family in heaven and earth is named, That he would grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with might by his Spirit in the inner man; That Christ may dwell in your hearts by faith; that ye, being rooted and grounded in love, May be able to comprehend with all saints what is the breadth, and length, and depth, and height; And to know the love of Christ, which passeth knowledge, that ye might be filled with all the fulness of God. Now unto him that is able to do exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think, according to the power that worketh in us, Unto him be glory in the church by Christ Jesus throughout all ages, world without end. Amen.

label: Ephesians 4
text: The hinge of the letter falls at the first word: "I therefore, the prisoner of the Lord, beseech you." Everything from here is consequence, and the man drawing the consequence has no leverage but his chains and his affection — he beseeches rather than commands. The single demand is that they "walk worthy of the vocation wherewith ye are called," and its first content is not doctrinal correctness or moral achievement but temperament: "With all lowliness and meekness, with longsuffering, forbearing one another in love; Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace." The verb is strenuous and the object is not manufactured — unity already exists as the Spirit's work, and what is asked is that it be kept. Paul then grounds the appeal in a list of seven singulars that reads like a creed cut to the bone: "There is one body, and one Spirit, even as ye are called in one hope of your calling; One Lord, one faith, one baptism, One God and Father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in you all." Having pressed oneness to the limit, he immediately turns to difference without apology: "But unto every one of us is given grace according to the measure of the gift of Christ." The differences are distributions from a single source, and Paul proves it with a citation about a conquering king dividing spoil — "When he ascended up on high, he led captivity captive, and gave gifts unto men" — pausing to insist that the ascent presupposes a descent, since "He that descended is the same also that ascended up far above all heavens, that he might fill all things." The gifts he then names are not abilities but persons: "he gave some, apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, pastors and teachers." Their purpose is stated in a three-fold phrase, "For the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ," and the horizon is corporate maturity: "Till we all come in the unity of the faith, and of the knowledge of the Son of God, unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ." The alternative is childhood in its least attractive form, believers "tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men, and cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive." Against manipulation Paul sets the compound discipline of "speaking the truth in love," and describes growth as an organic operation in which every part contributes: "the whole body fitly joined together and compacted by that which every joint supplieth, according to the effectual working in the measure of every part, maketh increase of the body unto the edifying of itself in love." The second half turns to the walk itself. Paul "testifies in the Lord" that they must not walk "as other Gentiles walk, in the vanity of their mind," and traces the pagan condition through a chain of causes — darkened understanding, alienation "from the life of God through the ignorance that is in them," ignorance rooted in "the blindness of their heart" — ending in numbness: "Who being past feeling have given themselves over unto lasciviousness, to work all uncleanness with greediness." Against this stands a curiously personal formula, "But ye have not so learned Christ," as though Christ were himself the curriculum, and the lesson learned is stated as a change of clothes: put off "the old man, which is corrupt according to the deceitful lusts," "be renewed in the spirit of your mind," and put on "the new man, which after God is created in righteousness and true holiness." The chapter closes with concrete instances, each with a reason attached. Lying is put away because "we are members one of another"; anger is permitted but time-limited — "Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath" — because delay gives ground to an enemy, "Neither give place to the devil"; the thief is not merely stopped but redirected into work "that he may have to give to him that needeth"; speech is regulated by its effect on hearers, "that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers." Then the sharpest motive in the list: "And grieve not the holy Spirit of God, whereby ye are sealed unto the day of redemption" — the offended party in ordinary congregational unkindness is a person who can be grieved. Five hostile dispositions are to be carried out together, "all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking... with all malice," and three replacements installed in their place, with the pattern named last: "be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ’s sake hath forgiven you." Paul asks the Ephesians to keep a unity rather than to build one, and the distinction governs the whole chapter. "Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace" assumes that the oneness is already a fact created by God — the seven singulars of verses four through six are indicative statements, not goals — and that the human work is custodial. This rules out two opposite errors: treating unity as a negotiable achievement that the sufficiently diplomatic might construct, and treating it as an invisible reality so secure that visible fractures do not matter. The virtues named as its means are all unglamorous and all relational — lowliness, meekness, longsuffering, forbearance — which locates the practical threat to unity in ordinary personal friction rather than in theological complexity. The seven singulars are stacked in a deliberate order that moves outward and upward: one body and one Spirit, called in one hope; one Lord, one faith, one baptism; one God and Father of all. The middle triad is the confession, the first triad is the community it creates, and the last is the source of both. That "one baptism" sits inside a creedal list of things as non-negotiable as the one Lord and the one God is significant, since it treats a sacramental act as constitutive of the Church's oneness rather than as a denominational preference. The closing phrase then refuses every attempt to keep God at one distance only: he is "above all, and through all, and in you all" — transcendent, pervasive, and indwelling in the same breath. Verse eleven gives the Church offices rather than techniques, and verse twelve tells us what they are for in a phrase that has been read two ways with real consequences. "For the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ" either lists three parallel purposes of the ordained, or describes a chain in which leaders equip the saints so that the saints do the work of ministry and thereby build the body. The second reading is favoured by verse sixteen, where growth comes "by that which every joint supplieth, according to the effectual working in the measure of every part." Either way, the outcome is not a well-run institution but a body arriving "unto the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ," and the offices exist to make themselves less necessary rather than more. The picture of immaturity is unexpectedly specific: not ignorance but instability, believers "tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine." What makes them vulnerable is not lack of intelligence but the presence of "sleight of men, and cunning craftiness" — Paul assumes the existence of skilled religious manipulators who lie in wait, and he assumes that doctrinal weather is a permanent feature of church life. The stated antidote is neither a stronger authority structure nor a hardening against all novelty, but "speaking the truth in love," a compound that resists both the loveless truth-teller who wounds and the loving evader who lets error stand. Maturity in this passage is measured by settledness under pressure and by growth into a head, not by the accumulation of information. The transformation of verses twenty-two through twenty-four is described in a sequence that resists both moralism and passivity. The old man is put off, the mind is renewed, the new man is put on — an outer action, an inner alteration, and another outer action — and the new man is not constructed by the believer but is "after God... created in righteousness and true holiness." What the Christian does is dress in something already made. Behind the clothing image lies the phrase "ye have not so learned Christ," which treats a person rather than a code as the content of moral instruction; ethics here is not the application of principles but the wearing of a nature received. Every command in the closing section carries a stated reason, and the reasons are almost all relational rather than abstract. Truth-telling rests on membership — "for we are members one of another" — so that lying is treated as a body attacking itself rather than as a violation of a rule. Work is reframed away from self-support toward provision for others, "that he may have to give to him that needeth," so that even the reformed thief is not merely made harmless but made useful. Speech is judged entirely by its effect on hearers, and the whole is placed under the warning "grieve not the holy Spirit of God," which makes the tone of congregational conversation a matter of personal offence to God rather than of etiquette. The final clause sets the standard and the resource in the same sentence: forgiveness is required "even as God for Christ’s sake hath forgiven you," a measure no one can meet who has not first been on the receiving end of it. I therefore, the prisoner of the Lord, beseech you that ye walk worthy of the vocation wherewith ye are called, With all lowliness and meekness, with longsuffering, forbearing one another in love; Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. There is one body, and one Spirit, even as ye are called in one hope of your calling; One Lord, one faith, one baptism, One God and Father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in you all. But unto every one of us is given grace according to the measure of the gift of Christ. Wherefore he saith, When he ascended up on high, he led captivity captive, and gave gifts unto men. ( Now that he ascended, what is it but that he also descended first into the lower parts of the earth? He that descended is the same also that ascended up far above all heavens, that he might fill all things.) And he gave some, apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, pastors and teachers; For the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ: Till we all come in the unity of the faith, and of the knowledge of the Son of God, unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ: That we henceforth be no more children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men, and cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive; But speaking the truth in love, may grow up into him in all things, which is the head, even Christ: From whom the whole body fitly joined together and compacted by that which every joint supplieth, according to the effectual working in the measure of every part, maketh increase of the body unto the edifying of itself in love. This I say therefore, and testify in the Lord, that ye henceforth walk not as other Gentiles walk, in the vanity of their mind, Having the understanding darkened, being alienated from the life of God through the ignorance that is in them, because of the blindness of their heart: Who being past feeling have given themselves over unto lasciviousness, to work all uncleanness with greediness. But ye have not so learned Christ; If so be that ye have heard him, and have been taught by him, as the truth is in Jesus: That ye put off concerning the former conversation the old man, which is corrupt according to the deceitful lusts; And be renewed in the spirit of your mind; And that ye put on the new man, which after God is created in righteousness and true holiness. Wherefore putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour: for we are members one of another. Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath: Neither give place to the devil. Let him that stole steal no more: but rather let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth. Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers. And grieve not the holy Spirit of God, whereby ye are sealed unto the day of redemption. Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice: And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ’s sake hath forgiven you.

label: Ephesians 5
text: The chapter opens with the most audacious imperative in the letter, stated as though it were obvious: "Be ye therefore followers of God, as dear children." Imitation of God is made possible only by the family relation that precedes it, and its content is immediately narrowed to one thing — "walk in love, as Christ also hath loved us, and hath given himself for us an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweetsmelling savour." The pattern to be imitated is a self-donation described in the vocabulary of the altar, so love here is defined by a death rather than by an emotion. What follows is the negative image of that love, and Paul sets three vices side by side that the ancient world would not have grouped together: "fornication, and all uncleanness, or covetousness, let it not be once named among you, as becometh saints." Sexual disorder and greed belong to the same family because both take rather than give. The regulation extends past conduct to speech — "Neither filthiness, nor foolish talking, nor jesting, which are not convenient" — and the prescribed replacement is not solemnity but gratitude, "but rather giving of thanks," since thanksgiving is the speech of a person who has received rather than seized. Then a hard warning: "no whoremonger, nor unclean person, nor covetous man, who is an idolater, hath any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God," with covetousness explicitly named idolatry, and a caution against those who will soften it — "Let no man deceive you with vain words: for because of these things cometh the wrath of God upon the children of disobedience." Paul then reaches for the image that governs the middle of the chapter, and states it as identity rather than aspiration: "ye were sometimes darkness, but now are ye light in the Lord" — not in darkness and in light, but darkness and light. The command follows the fact: "walk as children of light," bearing "the fruit of the Spirit... in all goodness and righteousness and truth," and "Proving what is acceptable unto the Lord." The relation to surrounding corruption is neither participation nor silence: "have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them," a reproof that works by exposure, since "all things that are reproved are made manifest by the light: for whatsoever doth make manifest is light." The section closes with what sounds like a fragment of an early baptismal hymn: "Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give thee light." From there the tone becomes practical and urgent — "See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise, Redeeming the time, because the days are evil" — with wisdom defined not as insight in general but as "understanding what the will of the Lord is." The contrast that follows is the chapter's structural pivot: "be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit." Both are conditions in which a person is governed by something outside himself, and Paul specifies what Spirit-filling looks like in a series of participles that are all corporate and vocal: "Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord; Giving thanks always for all things unto God and the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ; Submitting yourselves one to another in the fear of God." That last participle carries directly into the household instructions, so mutual submission is presented as the fourth mark of a Spirit-filled congregation rather than as a new subject. "Wives, submit yourselves unto your own husbands, as unto the Lord" is grounded in a headship immediately qualified by rescue — "the husband is the head of the wife, even as Christ is the head of the church: and he is the saviour of the body." The husband's command is longer and costlier: "Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it," and the purpose clauses describe not the husband's benefit but the beloved's transformation, "That he might sanctify and cleanse it with the washing of water by the word, That he might present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without blemish." Paul then argues from bodily self-interest — "He that loveth his wife loveth himself. For no man ever yet hated his own flesh; but nourisheth and cherisheth it, even as the Lord the church: For we are members of his body, of his flesh, and of his bones" — and quotes the founding text of marriage, "For this cause shall a man leave his father and mother, and shall be joined unto his wife, and they two shall be one flesh." The comment that follows is the most consequential sentence in the chapter: "This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church." Then, having ascended to the union of Christ and his body, Paul comes back down to the room: "Nevertheless let every one of you in particular so love his wife even as himself; and the wife see that she reverence her husband." Paul groups fornication, uncleanness and covetousness as a single category and then calls the third of them idolatry, which is a more radical claim than it appears. What binds them is acquisition: each treats another person or thing as material for one's own satisfaction, and each is therefore the exact inverse of the love just defined as Christ "hath given himself for us." The chapter's ethics of sex and its ethics of money are not two topics but one, and both are measured against a self-donation. Naming greed as idolatry also removes the comfortable distinction by which a respectable congregation deplores sexual sin while treating acquisitiveness as ambition, since the letter puts them under the same verdict about inheritance in the kingdom. The command about speech is easy to misread as prudishness. "Neither filthiness, nor foolish talking, nor jesting, which are not convenient: but rather giving of thanks" is not a prohibition on humour but on a particular use of speech — the corrosive, knowing, degrading wit that makes other people material for amusement — and the alternative offered is not silence or gravity but thanksgiving. That substitution is precise: the person whose habitual speech is gratitude has already conceded that he is a recipient, which is the disposition that makes both greed and contempt impossible. Read alongside the previous chapter's rule that speech should "minister grace unto the hearers," Paul is treating a community's ordinary conversation as one of its principal spiritual disciplines. "Ye were sometimes darkness, but now are ye light in the Lord" states the change as a change of substance rather than of location or behaviour, and the imperative follows rather than produces it. This ordering is consistent across the letter and governs how the ethical chapters should be heard: the commands never construct an identity, they express one already conferred. The consequence for engagement with a corrupt world is equally carefully balanced — "have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them" — which is neither participation nor withdrawal but exposure. The mechanism is stated as almost passive: light does not argue, it makes things visible, so the first form of Christian reproof is the presence of a community whose ordinary life shows what the alternative actually costs. "Be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit" sets two states of being governed against each other, and the comparison is more exact than it is flattering. Both involve a person acting under an influence he has admitted, and both alter speech and inhibition. The difference lies in what the influence produces: dissipation and loss of self on one side, and on the other four participles that are all outward-facing — singing to one another, praise directed to the Lord, thanksgiving "always for all things," and mutual submission. Notably Paul defines Spirit-filling almost entirely in terms of what a congregation does together, not by private experience, and includes yielding to other people as one of its constituent marks. The household instructions begin under the heading of verse twenty-one, "Submitting yourselves one to another in the fear of God," and the grammar of verse twenty-two depends on it, since the Greek supplies no second verb for the wives. That structure means the specific submissions that follow are instances of a mutuality that binds everyone, not exceptions to it, and it sets the frame in which the asymmetry of the commands must be read. The asymmetry is real and should not be smoothed away: wives are told to submit, husbands are not told to submit in the same words. But the husband's assignment is by far the heavier, since it is defined by the cross rather than by authority, and its stated aim is his wife's holiness rather than his own convenience — a headship measured entirely by what it gives up. The sequence at the end moves in an unexpected direction. One would expect Paul to explain the union of Christ and the Church by appealing to marriage as an illustration; instead he treats the union of Christ and the Church as the reality and marriage as the thing that has been pointing to it since Eden. "This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church" claims that the one-flesh clause of the creation account was always about more than a household. This inverts the usual order of explanation and gives ordinary marriage a weight it cannot carry on its own terms: it is a sign of something, and its obligations follow from what it signifies. The final verse then prevents the whole discussion from floating off into symbolism, returning to a particular man, a particular wife, and the daily work of love and reverence. Be ye therefore followers of God, as dear children; And walk in love, as Christ also hath loved us, and hath given himself for us an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweetsmelling savour. But fornication, and all uncleanness, or covetousness, let it not be once named among you, as becometh saints; Neither filthiness, nor foolish talking, nor jesting, which are not convenient: but rather giving of thanks. For this ye know, that no whoremonger, nor unclean person, nor covetous man, who is an idolater, hath any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God. Let no man deceive you with vain words: for because of these things cometh the wrath of God upon the children of disobedience. Be not ye therefore partakers with them. For ye were sometimes darkness, but now are ye light in the Lord: walk as children of light: ( For the fruit of the Spirit is in all goodness and righteousness and truth;) Proving what is acceptable unto the Lord. And have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them. For it is a shame even to speak of those things which are done of them in secret. But all things that are reproved are made manifest by the light: for whatsoever doth make manifest is light. Wherefore he saith, Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give thee light. See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise, Redeeming the time, because the days are evil. Wherefore be ye not unwise, but understanding what the will of the Lord is. And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit; Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord; Giving thanks always for all things unto God and the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ; Submitting yourselves one to another in the fear of God. Wives, submit yourselves unto your own husbands, as unto the Lord. For the husband is the head of the wife, even as Christ is the head of the church: and he is the saviour of the body. Therefore as the church is subject unto Christ, so let the wives be to their own husbands in every thing. Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it; That he might sanctify and cleanse it with the washing of water by the word, That he might present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without blemish. So ought men to love their wives as their own bodies. He that loveth his wife loveth himself. For no man ever yet hated his own flesh; but nourisheth and cherisheth it, even as the Lord the church: For we are members of his body, of his flesh, and of his bones. For this cause shall a man leave his father and mother, and shall be joined unto his wife, and they two shall be one flesh. This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church. Nevertheless let every one of you in particular so love his wife even as himself; and the wife see that she reverence her husband.
